off.p: Small rewards can be useful at 5½. I’d stop the “rent” charge now, use bedtime rewards temporarily, and keep paid extra jobs separate from everyday helping.

A reward agreed beforehand can help a child practise a new habit. Offering more money after she refuses can instead teach her that holding out pays. Rewards work best with clear, achievable goals and specific praise; they don’t have to be cash. CDC guidance.
For your two examples:

off.li: Sleeping in her bed: A small incentive is reasonable if she’s capable of the goal. First find out why she comes into yours: habit, fear, nightmares, or wanting closeness. Nighttime fears and nightmares are common at this age, and money doesn’t resolve them. Offer reassurance, a predictable bedtime routine, and help settling back into her bed. You can maintain a boundary while comforting her. Children’s sleep guidance.

Charging “rent”: I’d drop this. My concern is that it could make seeking comfort feel costly—or make your bed seem available for a fee. A difficult night can simply mean she hasn’t earned that night’s reward; previously earned money stays hers. The CDC specifically recommends against taking back earned rewards.

Her brother’s Lego: Paying $1 for an occasional, optional extra job seems reasonable. I’d avoid making his mess routinely her responsibility. Have him participate with your help, and give her ordinary responsibilities of her own. Thank her specifically: “You helped make the floor safe for everyone.”

off.p: The concern about paying for everything is that helping can become a transaction. One experiment found that toddlers given material rewards for helping subsequently helped less than those given praise or no reward. That’s a reason for restraint, not evidence that your $1 arrangement will damage your daughter’s character. Study.

When to stop: There’s no particular birthday cutoff. For bedtime, phase rewards out once the habit is reasonably consistent. Explain the change beforehand, gradually space rewards farther apart, and keep encouragement and support. Reward charts are intended for specific goals over a short period. Reward-chart guidance.
If she starts demanding payment for every small request, or the arrangement creates anxiety or arguments, that’s a signal to revise it—not raise the price.

on.p: Small rewards can be useful. I’d stop the $1 “rent” now, use bedtime rewards temporarily, and keep paid cleanup as an optional extra job. The American Academy of Pediatrics supports rewards for clear, achievable goals and recommends gradually phasing them out as the behavior becomes routine. AAP guidance

For sleeping in her own bed: First find out what brings her into yours: fear, nightmares, wanting company, or an established habit. A reward can encourage practicing a bedtime routine; fear also needs reassurance and support.

I’d drop the charge because it risks making seeking comfort feel costly. Taking back money she has earned also undermines the reward arrangement: the CDC specifically advises keeping earned rewards. CDC guidance

Choose something she can deliberately do, such as getting into her bed after stories or returning there with your help after waking. Make clear that she can always call you when frightened or unwell. Keep a predictable bedtime routine and calmly help her settle. AAP bedtime guidance
Cash is one possible reward. A sticker or choosing tomorrow’s bedtime story may be just as appealing to her. Agree on the arrangement ahead of time, and acknowledge the specific effort she made.

For her brother’s Lego: Paying $1 seems reasonable if she freely accepts an extra job. I’d also give both children ordinary cleanup responsibilities appropriate to their abilities. Her brother can practice putting pieces in a bin with your help; she shouldn’t become responsible for his mess simply because she’s older. Thank her specifically: “You put the Lego away—that helped us.”

When to stop: Follow the habit, rather than a particular birthday. Once bedtime is consistently manageable, explain that you’ll gradually reduce the rewards. For example, move from a reward each successful night to one for several nights, then retire the chart while continuing encouragement. Forgetting to ask for the reward can be a sign she’s ready. AAP guidance on phasing out rewards

If she starts bargaining over every routine task, or bedtime remains distressing despite support, reassess the arrangement. The useful question is whether she’s becoming more capable and comfortable—and whether the system is making family life easier.

off.p: Repeated trips to the principal and growing dislike of school are good reasons to seek a different approach. Boredom is a plausible explanation, but it’s worth investigating rather than assuming—and each child may need a different solution.
I’d start with these steps:

off.li: Find out when things go wrong. Ask each child, calmly and separately, which parts of school feel too easy, difficult, frustrating, or enjoyable. Ask teachers for specific examples: Does disruption happen during repetitive work, after finishing early, during transitions, or throughout the day? “Not paying attention” alone doesn’t tell you what needs to change.

Ask for evidence of their learning level and a trial of more challenging work. Meet with the teacher and, if available, the gifted education coordinator. Request pre-assessment in subjects where they seem advanced. If they already know the material, ask whether they can skip some repetition and use that time for deeper problems, advanced reading, or a meaningful project. This approach, called *curriculum compacting*, is supported by the National Association for Gifted Children. The key is appropriate challenge, rather than extra worksheets.

Pair academic changes with practical behavior support. Agree on movement breaks, a discreet reminder from the teacher, and something worthwhile to do when work is finished. Teach your children how to ask for help or challenge without interrupting others. You can acknowledge that boredom feels unpleasant while still helping them practice respectful classroom behavior.

Set a review date. Try the agreed changes for a few weeks, then compare engagement, completed work, office visits, and how the children feel about school. A useful opening is: “We want them learning and participating successfully. Could we check what they already know and try a plan that addresses both challenge and behavior?”

Keep other explanations open. If difficulties persist, discuss them with the school’s support team and their pediatrician. Being bright does not rule out attention or learning difficulties. An ADHD assessment, for example, considers functioning across settings and information from multiple adults; classroom disruption alone is insufficient. The American Academy of Pediatrics explains that process here.

off.p: At home, protect opportunities for play, movement, friendships, and interests they choose. Enrichment can keep curiosity alive, but the school day itself also needs attention.

If the school cannot provide appropriate challenge after a serious attempt, exploring subject acceleration, gifted programs, or another school setting is reasonable. Start by identifying what each child needs, then judge any alternative by how well it meets those needs.

on.p: Repeated trips to the principal’s office and growing dislike of school are good reasons to ask for a different approach. Boredom is a plausible explanation, and it’s worth checking what each child needs academically and what makes classroom participation difficult.
I’d start with these steps:

on.li: Talk with each child separately. Ask for specifics: “What work feels too easy?” “When do you get into trouble?” “What part of the day do you enjoy?” They may have different needs, even if their behavior looks similar.

Request a meeting focused on a concrete plan. Include the teacher and, if available, the gifted coordinator or school psychologist. Bring examples of work they find easy. Ask the teacher to track when disruptions happen—during repeated practice, waiting, difficult assignments, or transitions. That gives everyone something useful to work from.

Ask the school to assess what they already know. For material they have mastered, propose reducing repetitive practice and providing deeper problems, advanced reading, or a supervised project. Ask what gifted assessment and services are available. Pre-assessment can help teachers match instruction to a child’s learning needs. National Association for Gifted Children guidance

Discuss acceleration where appropriate. A child might attend a higher-level math class while staying with their age group for other subjects. Whole-grade acceleration is another possibility requiring individual consideration. NAGC supports both subject and grade acceleration for advanced learners. NAGC’s position on acceleration

Build support for behavior into the plan. Agree on scheduled movement breaks, a quiet signal from the teacher, and a clear activity to start after finishing work. Practice how to request help or a harder task politely. Your message can be: “We’ll help you get work that challenges you. You still need to let other people learn.”

Keep other explanations open. Bright children can also have attention or learning difficulties. If problems persist despite classroom changes, or occur in several settings, discuss them with their pediatrician and ask about an evaluation. School observations will help that conversation. American Academy of Pediatrics guidance

on.p: Set a review date in three or four weeks. Look for fewer disruptions, better engagement, and a change in how the children feel about school.

At home, make room for their interests and physical activity. If the school cannot provide suitable challenge and support, explore other schools or homeschooling, checking how each option would meet each child’s actual needs.
A useful opening for the meeting is: “They’re becoming unhappy at school. Can we agree on a short trial of more challenging work and movement breaks, then review what changes?”

off.p: Yes—a netbook or laptop can be appropriate for a fifth grader. Having their own computer doesn’t have to mean unrestricted or private access. You can still require it to be used in a shared room and stored there overnight.
I’d treat it as an opportunity to teach responsible use:

off.li: Set clear rules about homework, games, downloads, and when the computer goes away.
Use parental controls, while recognizing that they can’t replace conversations and supervision.
Teach children to protect personal information and to tell an adult when something online makes them uncomfortable.
Spend time using it together, so supervision includes interest in what they’re learning.

off.p: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a family media plan with agreed boundaries and parental controls, including for school devices.

I’d also ask the school what the laptop is intended for, what safeguards work at home, and who handles repairs. My bigger reservation is the reward policy: if laptops help children learn, students struggling with homework may need that support too. Rewarding effort is understandable, but access to a useful learning tool deserves separate consideration.
Your shared-space rule and the school’s laptop program can coexist quite comfortably.

on.p: Yes—a netbook can be appropriate for a fifth grader, with clear rules and adult guidance. Your preference for keeping computers in shared areas is compatible with a child having a laptop: you can require that it be used in the living room or kitchen and stored there overnight.
I’d set a few expectations from the start:

on.li: Agree on when it’s used for homework and when entertainment is allowed.
Keep it out of the bedroom at bedtime.
Use parental controls alongside regular conversations about privacy, online behavior, and anything upsetting they encounter.
Spend some time using it together so you understand what they’re doing.

on.p: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a family media plan with agreed rules and screen-free times and places.

I’d also ask the school what support comes with the laptop: safety settings, instruction on responsible use, and arrangements for repairs. Completing homework shows effort, but online judgment is a separate skill that needs teaching.

My bigger reservation is making a useful school tool a reward for achievement. If students need computers for learning, I’d want the school to ensure that children who struggle with homework also have access. With sensible supervision and support, though, I’d be comfortable with a fifth grader using one.

off.p: A useful method is to follow your toddler’s interests, name what they’re attending to, and revisit those words during play and everyday activities. Talking about routines, sharing picture books, and adding to what a child says are recommended ways to support early language learning. ASHA’s guidance
You can keep this going without an endless supply of new objects:

off.li: Go beyond names. A familiar cup gives you *pour, spill, full, empty, wet, dry, inside,* and *under*. Demonstrate the meaning as you talk: “Pour the water. Now the cup is empty.” ASHA’s household play ideas
Use ordinary outings. A walk, grocery trip, or bus ride supplies things to name and actions to describe. Follow what catches your child’s attention: “A pigeon! The pigeon is walking.”

Make books interactive. Follow their pointing, talk about the pictures, and connect them to real life. One duck picture can prompt “The duck swims,” “Here’s its beak,” or “Remember the duck at the pond?” You don’t have to read every printed word. Early language guidance
Expand their contributions. If they say “dog,” respond with “Yes, a dog! The dog is running.” That gives them a little more language connected to something they already understand.

Keep a growing picture collection. Printed photos of outings, family members, animals, and vehicles make a reusable conversation book. Add pictures as you encounter new things; borrow library books for subjects you can’t easily see in person.

off.p: For checking whether it’s sticking, try a relaxed sequence: name the item together, encounter it again later, then offer an opportunity to point or name it. “Where’s the duck?” checks understanding; “What’s that?” checks whether they can produce the word. If they don’t answer, simply supply it and continue playing.

Naming something on the second encounter is a nice success, but it shouldn’t be the deadline. Look for recognition and spontaneous use over time, including with another example—a different dog or a duck in a different book. Keep revisiting familiar material while introducing new words; knowing an object’s name still leaves plenty to talk about.

on.p: A useful, sustainable method is to follow your toddler’s interests, name what they notice, and revisit those words during play and everyday routines. Speech-language specialists recommend talking about what children see and do, responding to them, and adding a little to what they say. ASHA’s guidance
You can keep this going in several ways:

on.li: Expand the vocabulary around familiar objects. A cup gives you *pour*, *empty*, *full*, *spill*, and *handle*. Say “You’re pouring water” while it happens. Household objects offer plenty of actions and descriptions after their names are familiar. ASHA’s household activity suggestions

Turn ordinary outings into conversations. At the grocery store, name a vegetable your child examines. On a walk, talk about the puddle they stop beside. Follow their attention and use a short phrase: “A puddle! Your boot splashed.”

Use books repeatedly, with a different focus. On one reading, name the dog; on another, talk about it digging or hiding behind a chair. Pause for your child’s comments, and build on them: “Dog!” → “Yes, the dog is digging.” Library books provide a continuing supply of new subjects. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends conversational book sharing and expanding children’s words this way. Book-sharing guidance

Make a small photo book. Printed photos of relatives, places you visit, and things your child enjoys give you personally meaningful material to discuss. For wildlife, borrow illustrated animal books and act out the animals together.

on.p: A practical example: if your child becomes interested in ducks, name one on a walk, find one in a book later, and play with a toy duck at bath time. Each encounter gives the word another meaningful use.

To notice progress, look for understanding as well as speech. Finding the duck when you ask “Where’s the duck?” shows understanding; naming it independently shows spoken recall. Both are useful observations. ASHA includes pointing to named objects and following simple directions among early communication milestones. Early toddler milestones

Naming something on the second encounter is an encouraging moment, but it’s a demanding benchmark for every new word. Give words repeated opportunities over time, leave room for your child to respond, and keep the activity enjoyable.

off.p: Aim for a calm voice, a short instruction, and predictable follow-through. At four, a child can understand a rule and still struggle to stop himself when he really wants something. More explaining in that moment often won’t help.

It’s exhausting when shouting seems to be the only thing that works. But stopping when frightened isn’t the same as learning self-control. Physical punishment and yelling are ineffective long-term discipline strategies; the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends clear limits, redirection, and positive reinforcement. AAP guidance
For the toy-grabbing example, try this sequence:

off.li: Get close and stop the grabbing. Gently block his hand if necessary to protect his brother. Say, “I won’t let you take it. He’s using it.”
Give one concrete direction: “Give the truck back.” Avoid a long explanation or asking “Will you give it back?” when it isn’t optional.

Follow through. If he doesn’t return it after a brief opportunity, calmly help return it. If he keeps grabbing, separate their play for now: “You’re having trouble leaving his toy alone. We’ll play over here.”
Acknowledge the feeling while keeping the limit: “You really want that truck. It’s hard to wait. You can ask for a turn or choose another toy.” He can be upset; the toy still goes back.
Notice the behavior you want: “You waited until he finished—that was helpful.” Practise asking and taking turns later, when he’s calm.

off.p: Clear, age-appropriate directions and immediate, related consequences are consistent with CDC parenting guidance. Your calm words become meaningful because you consistently act on them.

To help yourself stay calm, decide on your sentence beforehand: “I can be firm without being loud.” Take one slow breath, lower your voice, and use fewer words. You don’t have to feel perfectly calm to respond calmly. If you’re close to hitting him, put both children somewhere safe and take a brief pause, or have another adult take over. The AAP also recommends taking a parent time-out.

Outside conflicts, give him regular individual attention, watch for tiredness and hunger, and praise small instances of cooperation. Offer choices before trouble starts rather than negotiating a reward each time he grabs something.

Success doesn’t mean he agrees or stops crying; it means the limit holds without anyone being hurt. Expect repetition. If aggression is frequent, causes injuries, or you’re regularly struggling to avoid physical punishment, ask his pediatrician for help and parent coaching. AAP guidance on aggression

on.p: That sounds exhausting, especially while you’re also protecting his younger brother. A useful approach is a short instruction, calm follow-through, and practice when he’s settled. At four, children still need help managing impulses; understanding a rule and following it when they desperately want something are different skills.

Yelling or physical punishment may stop him in the moment. Physical punishment is associated with increased aggression, and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends avoiding hitting and spanking. You can set firm limits with calm words and actions. AAP guidance
For the toy situation, try this sequence:

on.li: Move close and give one clear instruction. Get down to his level and say, “Give the truck back to your brother.” Use a steady, ordinary voice. Allow a few seconds for him to respond.
Follow through. If he keeps grabbing, gently block the grab or return the toy yourself: “He’s using it. I’ll help you give it back.” If he tries again, separate their play for now and stay nearby.

Acknowledge the feeling and keep the limit. “You really want that truck. Waiting is hard. You can choose another toy while he finishes.” He may cry or protest; the limit can stay in place while you comfort him.
Teach the alternative once he’s calm. Practise saying, “Can I have a turn when you’re finished?” Notice his attempts: “You waited until he finished. That helped him enjoy his turn.”

on.p: The CDC recommends giving one specific direction at a time, using a calm tone, following through consistently, and praising cooperation. CDC guidance

To stay calm, decide on your words and action beforehand. For example: “Give it back,” followed by helping return it. This gives you something predictable to do when you’re frustrated. Take a slow breath, lower your voice deliberately, and keep explanations brief during the conflict.

If you feel close to hitting him, put both children in safe, separate places and take a brief pause, or ask another adult to take over. If you’ve shouted or hit, repair it once calm: “I shouted/hit you. That was wrong. Next time I’ll pause and use a calm voice.” The toy rule still applies.

Between conflicts, give him some regular individual attention and practise taking turns during easy play. Watch for patterns such as hunger, tiredness, or conflict when you’re occupied with his brother.

Expect to repeat this many times. If aggression causes injuries, you frequently feel close to losing control, or difficulties also occur at preschool, speak with his pediatrician and ask about parent coaching. AAP advice on aggression

off.p: You can make a real difference here, but you don’t have to become your father to help your family. You’ve also lost something, and moving back home doesn’t make you responsible for repairing everyone’s feelings.

Your sisters’ behavior may reflect hurt, fear, or uncertainty after your father left. Children can respond to parental separation with anger and changes in behavior; that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ve become less mature or are deliberately manipulating people. AACAP’s guidance on children and divorce describes these reactions.
A few changes to your approach could help:

off.li: Step out of the “mini-father” role. Telling a sister to be mature or explaining what’s wrong with her behavior may sound like a sibling claiming authority over her. Try: “I know I’ve been lecturing you. I’m worried about us, but I want to understand what you need from me.”

Ask about your part when things are calm. “When you say I’m the problem, what specifically do I do that bothers you?” Listen before defending yourself. You can acknowledge a fair criticism without accepting every accusation.

Set boundaries around behavior, without debating feelings. If she says she isn’t angry, you don’t need to prove otherwise. Say: “I want to hear you, but I’m going to take a break if we’re shouting. We can try again in a little while.” Follow through calmly and return to the conversation.

Help the younger sister settle before trying to teach anything. Use fewer words: “This is really upsetting. I’m here.” Keep reasonable limits, but save explanations for when she can listen. Acknowledging a feeling doesn’t require giving in to a demand. Child Mind Institute’s guidance explains this approach.

Build ordinary connection. Share a meal, go for a walk, help with homework, or do something enjoyable together. Let them experience you as a dependable brother whose attention isn’t mostly correction.

off.p: Talk privately with your mother about a manageable division of responsibilities: “I can handle dinner and homework on these days, but I need you to lead on rules and consequences.” If your sisters are adults, focus on shared household agreements instead. Your mother may need practical and emotional support to regain her footing; another trusted adult can help carry some of that load.
If the outbursts persist, worsen, or interfere with school, sleep, or relationships, involve a school counselor, doctor, or family therapist. You can seek support for yourself too.
Your strongest contribution is consistency: listening, keeping promises, setting respectful limits, and showing up. You don’t have to fill the entire void to be someone your sisters can rely on.

on.p: You can help a great deal by being a dependable older brother. You don’t have to take responsibility for replacing your father or keeping everyone emotionally together. You’re dealing with his departure too.

What you describe may be your sisters struggling with the upheaval. Anger and changes in behavior can follow a parent’s departure; that doesn’t establish that they’re deliberately manipulating anyone. The American Academy of Pediatrics describes these reactions in its guidance on parental separation.
A useful shift is to focus on your relationship with each sister and on specific behavior:

on.li: Stop trying to get the older sister to admit she’s angry. You can address shouting even if you disagree about her feelings: “I want to hear what you’re saying. I’m getting overwhelmed, so I’m taking a break. We can talk again in twenty minutes.” Follow through and come back.

Ask about your part when things are calm. “When you said I was the problem, what did I do that upset you?” Listen for a concrete example. If you interrupted, lectured, or spoke condescendingly, acknowledge it and change that behavior. You can take her feedback seriously while setting limits on insults.

Give the younger sister simple support and limits. During a tantrum, keep your words brief: “I’m here. I won’t let you hit me. We can talk when you’re ready.” Once she settles, help her put the problem into words and ask for what she needs. Adjust this to her age.

Retire “be mature” and “you’re manipulating people.” Those statements judge her character and intentions. Name the action and its effect: “When you shout over me, I can’t follow what you’re asking.” Make a clear request: “Tell me one thing you need.”

Spend time together that involves no correction. Cook, take a walk, watch something, or help with homework. Ask how they’re doing and leave room for an answer. Listening and maintaining familiar routines are central recommendations in the Child Mind Institute’s guidance.

on.p: With your mother, discuss a manageable division of responsibilities privately: “I can handle dinner and school pickups. I need you to decide the household rules and consequences.” Agree on what authority you have when caring for a younger sibling. With an adult sister, focus on shared household agreements and your own boundaries.

If your mother is too overwhelmed to manage basic care, help bring in another trusted adult or professional support. A relative, school counselor, or family therapist can share the load. If the conflict keeps worsening or disrupts school, sleep, or everyday functioning, that is a good reason to seek help.

For now, aim for something achievable: fewer lectures, calmer boundaries, and regular time together. Their immediate reactions won’t tell you everything about whether your support is helping. Keep room for your own grief and a life outside the household, too.

off.p: No—crib use is not universal, even in affluent countries. Infant sleeping arrangements vary considerably with culture, rather than simply with the ability to afford a crib.

For example, a 2010 study surveyed parents of 29,287 children aged birth to three years in 17 countries and regions. Reported bed-sharing ranged from 5.8% in New Zealand to 83.2% in Vietnam. These were internet survey results, including toddlers, so they are not a worldwide census of infant crib use—but they clearly contradict the assumption that almost everyone uses cribs. Cross-cultural sleep study
Alternatives include:

off.li: Floor futons or sleeping mats, particularly in Japan, either separate from or shared with parents. Research specifically documents infant futons, including firm mattresses made for babies. A Japanese infant futon should not be assumed equivalent to an adult futon or a Western sofa-bed mattress. Japanese infant-bedding study
Sharing a parent’s bed, as the international survey above illustrates. Its prevalence does not establish its safety.

Bassinets, approved bedside sleepers, and portable cribs or play yards. These provide separate infant sleeping spaces without requiring a conventional wooden crib, although bassinets have relatively limited size and developmental allowances. AAP recommendations

off.p: Your intuition about cribs does identify a practical benefit: containment. A mobile baby stays within a small, controlled space while the parent sleeps. With an open floor bed, the room becomes the accessible space, so furniture, cords, small objects, and gaps around the mattress all matter. Elevation primarily makes reaching a young baby more convenient; height itself is not a requirement for safe infant sleep.

For your decision, though, fall prevention is only one part of sleep safety. A floor mattress reduces fall height but can still present suffocation or entrapment hazards. For babies under one year, current American Academy of Pediatrics guidance recommends a safety-approved crib, bassinet, portable crib, or play yard with its intended firm, flat mattress, a fitted sheet, and no soft objects or loose bedding. It recommends sleeping on the back and sharing the parents’ room on a separate surface, ideally for at least the first six months. An ordinary adult futon on the floor does not meet that recommendation simply because it is low. AAP safe-sleep guidance

So your friends’ arrangement has cultural precedents, but that does not establish either its claimed developmental advantages or its safety for an infant. A crib or approved play yard is the straightforward option after the bassinet; a floor bed is a separate decision to revisit as your child gets older.

on.p: No—crib use is far from universal, including in wealthy countries. Sleeping arrangements vary with culture as well as housing and income.

For example, a 2010 study of 29,287 children from birth to age three across 17 countries and regions found that reported bed-sharing ranged from 5.8% in New Zealand to 83.2% in Vietnam. Those figures include toddlers and come from a parent survey; they establish substantial variation, rather than a precise worldwide rate of crib use. Mindell and colleagues, *Sleep Medicine*

Japan provides a counterexample to your assumption about families who can afford cribs. Research documents babies sleeping on their own futons beside their parents’ bedding, sharing a futon or bed with a parent, and sleeping in cribs. A 2014 study examined these arrangements among Japanese mothers, although its small sample of online discussions cannot establish national prevalence. Shimizu and colleagues, *Frontiers in Psychology*
The alternatives therefore include:

on.li: A separate floor futon or mattress, sometimes beside the parents’ bedding.
Sharing the parents’ bed or futon, common in some cultures.
A portable crib or sleep-approved play yard, which provides a separate, enclosed sleeping space. Bassinets serve that purpose earlier, within their size and developmental limits.

on.p: For your decision, prevalence and safety are separate questions. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that infants sleep on their backs on a firm, flat surface in a safety-compliant crib, bassinet, portable crib or play yard, with only a fitted sheet. It recommends sharing the parents’ room, ideally for at least the first six months, and advises against bed-sharing. An ordinary adult futon or floor mattress does not automatically meet infant sleep standards. AAP safe-sleep guidance

A crib’s practical benefits are its contained sleeping area, regulated construction and convenient access for caregivers. Adjustable mattress height can reduce bending while the baby is small; the mattress must be lowered as the child develops to prevent falls. AAP guidance on sleeping spaces

Your friends’ point about fall height is reasonable: a floor mattress reduces the distance of a fall. Overall safety also depends on mattress firmness, gaps where a baby could become trapped, bedding and everything the child can reach after leaving the mattress. Baby-proofing the room addresses only part of that problem.

For the transition from a bassinet, a safety-compliant crib or play yard is the option supported by current infant safe-sleep guidance. You can still give your son opportunities to explore his room during supervised awake time.

off.p: I’d move her out of the crib now, then calmly return her to her new bed when she gets up. Once she can climb out, repeated climbs create a fall risk—even at 22 months. A toddler bed or a crib mattress on the floor is an option recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics.
For nighttime:

off.li: Make the whole room safe for unsupervised movement. Anchor furniture, secure windows, remove accessible cords and small objects, and block access to stairs. Position a floor mattress away from gaps where she could become trapped.
Keep the usual bedtime routine. When she gets up, check briefly for discomfort or a needed diaper change, then guide her back with a simple phrase: “It’s nighttime. Time for bed.”
Keep returns gentle, brief, and boring. Avoid turning them into playtime or lengthy negotiations. Repeat consistently; it may take many returns initially. This follows the AAP’s bedtime guidance.

off.p: Between your two options, I’d choose returning her to a safe bed, rather than putting her back into the crib or making “play until you collapse” the routine. You can set the expectation that nighttime is for resting without expecting her to fall asleep immediately.

on.p: Since she can climb out, I’d stop using the crib and move her to a safe toddler bed or a firm crib mattress on the floor. Climbing creates a fall risk; the CPSC recommends stopping crib use when a child begins climbing out.
Of your two options, I’d choose calmly returning her to her new sleeping spot when you notice she’s playing. Try this:

on.li: Keep the usual bedtime routine and explain simply: “It’s nighttime. Time to sleep.”
If she gets up, check whether she needs comfort or a diaper change, then quietly guide her back.
Keep lights low and interactions brief. Repeat the same response each time, and praise her in the morning for staying in bed.

on.p: This follows the American Academy of Pediatrics’ guidance for moving out of a crib. Expect to repeat it quite a few times during the transition.

Childproof the whole room before making the switch. Anchor furniture, remove accessible cords and small objects, secure windows, and prevent access to stairs and other hazards. Position the mattress so she cannot become trapped between it and a wall or furniture. A monitor helps you check on her, but the room itself needs to be safe. See the CPSC’s childproofing guidance.

I wouldn’t make “play until she falls asleep” the nightly plan. Aim for a predictable bedtime and a gentle, consistent return to bed. If she regularly stays awake for long stretches, review her nap timing and bedtime with her pediatrician; toddlers this age generally need 11–14 hours of sleep in 24 hours, including naps. Nemours KidsHealth

off.p: You can encourage her through play, but at 13 months, not putting any weight on her feet—even when supported—is a reason to arrange a pediatric appointment soon. Walking ages vary, and this alone doesn’t mean she won’t walk. However, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends discussing an inability to stand with support by 12 months with a doctor. AAP milestone guidance
While waiting for that appointment:

off.li: Give her plenty of supervised floor play. Reaching for toys, rolling, moving into sitting, and crawling if she does it help build strength and coordination.
Make pulling up inviting. Put a favorite toy on a low, sturdy sofa or securely anchored piece of furniture. Let her reach or kneel at it, staying close to prevent falls.
Keep attempts brief and relaxed. Encourage and praise her efforts, but don’t force her feet down, straighten her legs, or continue if she resists or seems uncomfortable.

Let her play barefoot on a safe, nonslip surface. This can help grip and balance. Avoid seated baby walkers; they don’t teach walking and can cause injuries. NHS standing advice, NHS barefoot advice, AAP walker guidance

off.p: Tell her doctor whether she sits independently, moves around, uses both legs equally, and has ever supported weight. Mention prematurity, if applicable. They can assess her development and decide whether pediatric physiotherapy or early intervention would help with exercises suited to her needs. CDC guidance

If this is a sudden change, or she has pain, swelling, fever, or appears unwell, seek urgent medical care rather than practicing standing. Also report any loss of previously acquired skills promptly. NHS urgent signs

on.p: You can encourage her through gentle play, but at 13 months, putting no weight through her feet—even when supported—deserves a prompt appointment with her pediatrician or GP. They can assess her movement and decide whether pediatric physiotherapy would help. This is a reason to get advice now, rather than waiting for walking to develop. Raising Children Network

Walking develops at different ages; being unable to walk independently at 13 months alone can fall within normal variation. Most babies pull up to stand by their first birthday, and most walk independently by 18 months. These milestones guide assessment; they cannot predict your daughter’s eventual walking ability. CDC: one year, 18 months
While arranging the appointment, try:

on.li: Plenty of supervised floor play. Put toys nearby to encourage reaching, changing position and crawling if she already crawls.
Play with her feet supported. Sit her on your lap with her knees bent and feet resting flat on the floor. Encourage her to lean forward toward a toy.
Offer a reason to rise. Put a favorite toy on a low, sturdy sofa. If she willingly pushes through her feet, gently support her hips as she tries to stand.

on.p: Keep attempts brief and playful. Stop if she appears uncomfortable or resists; don’t force her legs straight or make her bear weight. These activities come from NHS children’s physiotherapy guidance. Avoid seated baby walkers; they can delay standing and walking.
If she previously bore weight and suddenly stops, or has pain, swelling, fever or seems unwell, seek urgent medical assessment. NHS guidance

At the appointment, explain whether she sits independently, gets into sitting, crawls or bottom-shuffles, and uses both legs equally. Mention if she was born prematurely, since that affects how milestones are interpreted.

off.p: You can gently influence her behavior, but at six months you shouldn’t expect her to understand and reliably follow “don’t blow raspberries with food in your mouth.” She can learn from repeated interactions, but understanding a rule and controlling herself consistently are still developing.
Blowing raspberries is normal at this age—the CDC actually lists it as a six-month developmental milestone. With solids, she’s also discovering new tastes, textures, and what her mouth can do.
I wouldn’t make an issue of it. A practical approach is to:

off.li: Respond calmly and matter-of-factly; avoid making the food spraying an entertaining game.
Pause briefly, let her finish what’s in her mouth, then offer the next small spoonful when she’s ready.
Use a gentle, consistent phrase such as “Let’s swallow first,” without expecting immediate obedience.
Watch for fullness cues. If she closes her mouth, turns away, or pushes food away, stop offering food. These are recognized signs of fullness; raspberries alone don’t necessarily mean she’s finished.

off.p: Treat the pause as part of feeding at her pace, rather than a punishment or withholding food until she “behaves.” For infants, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends positive guidance and redirection.
For now, a bib and a washable feeding area are likely to accomplish more than correction. The useful lesson is a calm, pleasant feeding routine; tidier table manners can come later.

on.p: You can gently influence her behavior at six months, but understanding and consistently following “don’t blow raspberries with food in your mouth” is too much to expect yet. Babies learn from repetition and your responses; understanding a rule and controlling an impulse take further development. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends modeling, positive language, and redirection for infants.
Blowing raspberries is a normal skill at this age—the CDC lists it as a six-month communication milestone. She’s also learning how food feels and how to move it around her mouth.
I’d keep your response calm and predictable:

on.li: When she blows a raspberry, pause the spoon, clean up calmly, and give her a moment before offering another small bite.
Keep your reaction low-key. A big laugh or dramatic response may make repeating it more interesting.
You can use a gentle phrase such as “Time to eat,” while expecting that its meaning will develop through repetition.
If she turns away, closes her mouth, or loses interest, let the feeding end. Follow her appetite; don’t withhold food as punishment.

on.p: The NHS’s guidance on starting solids emphasizes going at the baby’s pace and allowing time to learn.

I wouldn’t make an issue of it. A consistent, gentle response is reasonable, but expect some food spray while she practices. A washable bib and a mat under the high chair may be your most effective tools for now.

off.p: Yes—10–12 hours at night can be okay for a healthy 4-month-old. It isn’t automatically abnormal or harmful. The key is whether your baby gets enough milk overall and is growing well; healthy, growing babies generally don’t need to be awakened for feeds. American Academy of Pediatrics

Reassuring signs include steady weight gain, good daytime feeding, normal wet diapers, and being alert and responsive when awake. The recommended sleep amount at 4–12 months is 12–16 hours over 24 hours, including naps—a guide rather than a strict limit. American Academy of Sleep Medicine

The main potential downside is missing needed feeds. If your baby was premature, has poor weight gain or a medical condition, or has been prescribed overnight feeds, check with their pediatrician before allowing such long stretches. Otherwise, mention the pattern at the next routine visit so they can confirm that growth and feeding are on track. Mayo Clinic
Seek medical advice promptly if sleepiness increases suddenly alongside poor feeding or fewer wet diapers. Difficulty waking, limpness, or breathing trouble warrants emergency care. NHS
Continue safe sleep: place baby on their back on a firm, flat, empty sleep surface, in their own crib or bassinet in your room for at least the first six months. NIH

on.p: Yes—10–12 hours at night can be okay for a healthy 4-month-old. Babies vary widely in their sleep patterns. The key is whether your baby gets enough milk over 24 hours and continues growing well. The American Academy of Pediatrics says healthy, growing babies usually don’t need to be awakened for feeds. AAP guidance
Letting your baby sleep is generally reasonable if they:

on.li: Gain weight steadily along their growth curve.
Feed well during the day and have their usual wet diapers.
Wake normally and are alert and responsive during awake periods.
Have no medical instructions requiring scheduled overnight feeds.

on.p: For babies aged 4–12 months, the recommended total is 12–16 hours of sleep per day, including naps. Long nighttime sleep can fit within that range. The main potential downside is missing needed nutrition; premature babies and babies with feeding or growth problems may need overnight feeds. Confirm the feeding plan with your pediatrician if any of those concerns apply. Sleep recommendation, Mayo Clinic feeding guidance

Continue safe sleep practices: place your baby on their back in a separate crib or bassinet with a firm, flat mattress and fitted sheet; keep blankets, pillows and toys out, and share your room for at least the first six months. CDC guidance
If sleepiness suddenly increases alongside poor feeding or fewer wet diapers, seek medical advice promptly. Difficulty waking, limpness or breathing trouble needs emergency care. NHS warning signs

off.p: There is no scientifically established “right birthday” to start preschool. For your two-year-old, the more useful question is whether a particular program offers better care and learning opportunities than his current arrangement.

“Nursery,” “preschool,” and “school” mean different things in different countries. A toddler program centred on play and attentive care is quite different from a classroom expecting children to sit through formal lessons.
There is research, but it does not give a universal starting age:

off.li: One large US study found that children starting centre-based care between ages two and three had larger reading and maths gains at kindergarten entry than children starting earlier or later. It also found some less favourable social-behaviour ratings, particularly with earlier entry. This was an observational study: differences between families and programs mean it cannot establish that starting at two or three *caused* those outcomes. Loeb and colleagues, published in 2007.

The NICHD longitudinal study found that higher-quality care was associated with modest improvements in language, cognition, and some social outcomes. Family characteristics were generally stronger predictors. Again, these are associations, rather than proof of an ideal starting age. Research summary.

off.p: For your son, I would use those findings this way: you do not need to rush him into preschool at two solely to get an academic head start. Equally, age two alone is not a reason to rule out a good toddler program.
When visiting, look for:

off.li: Warm, responsive teachers with experience caring for two-year-olds.
Small groups and enough adults to give individual attention.
Plenty of play, conversation, stories, music, and movement.
Support for his actual needs, including naps, toileting, and comfort when upset.

off.p: These priorities align with the American Academy of Pediatrics’ childcare guidance and NAEYC’s guidance on developmentally appropriate education.

If childcare is optional, a gradual introduction with shorter sessions is a reasonable practical approach—not a scientifically proven optimum. Judge the fit by how he settles with the caregivers and engages over time. The best choice depends on your child, the program, the hours, and the care available at home, rather than age alone.

on.p: Research has not established one ideal preschool starting age for every child. For your two-year-old, a good nursery can be a reasonable choice now; starting preschool at three or four is also reasonable. The decision depends on the care available, your child’s needs, and your family’s circumstances.
The terms can be confusing: “nursery,” “preschool,” and “childcare” often overlap. Look at what the programme actually provides for children his age.
There is useful scientific evidence:

on.li: The US NICHD study, summarised in 2006, followed more than 1,000 children from birth. Higher-quality childcare was associated with modestly better language and learning outcomes. Family experiences also had strong associations with development. This was an observational study, so it could not establish cause and effect or identify an ideal starting birthday. NICHD findings

England’s SEED study, reported in 2020, examined early education and later school outcomes. Associations varied with family disadvantage and hours of attendance. Earlier attendance was linked to better learning outcomes for some disadvantaged children, while greater group-care attendance was associated with poorer scores on some social and emotional measures. These findings do not establish a universal starting age. SEED research brief

on.p: My practical advice is to assess the particular nursery before deciding on the age. For a two-year-old, look for warm, responsive carers, small groups, and activities suited to toddlers. Staff should accommodate his naps, feeding, and toileting needs. The American Academy of Pediatrics provides a useful centre-selection checklist.

If you enrol him, visit together first and arrange a gradual introduction where possible. Notice whether he develops trust in a caregiver and settles into the day; discuss persistent distress with staff. AAP guidance on preparing for childcare

If his current care provides attentive interaction, shared reading, play, and opportunities to meet other children, the evidence gives you no deadline to enrol him at two. You can choose the start date around a suitable programme and your family’s needs.

off.p: I’d aim for regular family connection and opportunities to maintain friendships, rather than a fixed split of the available hours. There is relevant research, but I didn’t find evidence establishing an ideal number of playdates or a playdate-to-family-time ratio.
A few studies help put the decision in perspective:

off.li: More parental hours don’t automatically mean better outcomes. A 2015 study examined 1,605 children ages 3–11 and 778 adolescents. The amount of time mothers spent with younger children wasn’t associated with the measured emotional, behavioral, or academic outcomes after accounting for other factors. Some associations with engaged parental time appeared in adolescence. This doesn’t mean family time is unimportant; it cautions against treating hours together as a scorecard. Milkie, Nomaguchi & Denny, 2015

The quality and reciprocity of friendships matter. A study of 314 children ages 7–11 found that reciprocated friendships—where both children identified each other as friends—and friendship quality were associated with self-worth and identification with peers. It studied relationships, however, rather than how many playdates children attended. Maunder & Monks, 2019

Friendships and loneliness can influence each other over time. A three-wave study of 212 children, initially around age nine, found that better friendship quality predicted lower subsequent loneliness, while loneliness also predicted poorer subsequent friendship quality. Again, this supports helping children nurture friendships, without establishing a scheduling quota. Liu and colleagues, 2024

off.p: These are observational studies, so they don’t prove that changing a family’s schedule will cause a particular outcome.
Practically, I’d use this approach:

off.li: Protect a few dependable family routines. Dinner, reading at bedtime, a walk, or cooking together can provide connection without requiring a whole free afternoon.

Schedule around actual friendships. Consider whether your child has someone they enjoy and enough opportunity to play freely together. School provides peer contact, but how much relaxed play it allows varies.
Keep some time uncommitted. Neither family activities nor playdates need to fill every available slot.

Adjust to the child and the week. A child struggling to build friendships may benefit from more opportunities with a compatible peer; a child exhausted after school may prefer a quiet afternoon together.

off.p: For example, you could try one manageable playdate a week, a protected family weekend block, and everyday moments of connection. That’s a starting experiment, not a research-based prescription. Adjust according to whether your child feels connected to you, has satisfying friendships, and still has room to rest.

on.p: I’d protect a few predictable family routines and make room for regular time with friends, then adjust according to your child’s needs. I didn’t find research establishing an ideal ratio of playdates to family time. The relevant studies mostly examine relationships and time together; they don’t tell parents how many playdates to schedule.
Two studies help frame the decision:

on.li: Friendships: Maunder and Monks’s study, published online in 2018, surveyed 314 children aged 7–11. Children whose best friend also named them as a best friend reported better friendship quality and stronger identification with peers. Friendship relationships were also associated with self-worth. This supports paying attention to whether your child has mutual, satisfying friendships. It doesn’t establish a required frequency of playdates. Read the study.

Time with parents: Milkie and colleagues’s 2015 study examined time diaries and outcomes for 1,605 children aged 3–11 and 778 adolescents. For younger children, the amount of maternal time wasn’t associated with the measured behavioral, emotional, or academic outcomes. Among adolescents, more engaged time with mothers was associated with fewer delinquent behaviors. The study measured time and selected outcomes, so it cannot establish how much family time an individual child needs. Read the study.

on.p: Both are observational studies, which limits conclusions about cause and effect.
For a school-age child, I’d use this practical approach:

on.li: Keep everyday family connection predictable. A shared meal or bedtime conversation can be part of this. Add a family activity you all enjoy when the schedule allows.

Look at the friendship opportunities your child already has. Consider how much actual free play happens at recess, aftercare, or in the neighborhood. Being around classmates gives you only part of that picture.

Use playdates to support friendships your child wants. If scheduling feels difficult, try one playdate a week or every other week as a starting point. That’s a scheduling suggestion, not a research-based minimum.
Leave some time open. Protect sleep and room to decompress. The American Academy of Pediatrics emphasizes the value of free, unscheduled play alongside family engagement. AAP report.

on.p: After a few weeks, check whether your child seems connected to you, enjoys their friendships, and has enough energy for the schedule. A child who wants more time with a particular friend may benefit from another opportunity; a child who feels exhausted after school may prefer a weekend visit. Your family’s capacity belongs in that decision too.

off.p: For your daughter, I’d put warm, responsive caregivers, safe routines, and consistent staffing at the top of the list. A good infant program should give her plenty of individual attention and caregivers who learn her cues.
About the ratios: legal limits depend on your country or state, and meeting those limits doesn’t by itself establish quality. As reference points:

off.li: 1 adult to 4 infants matches ZERO TO THREE’s recommendation for children under three, with a maximum group size of eight. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a stricter 1:3 for babies under 12 months.
1:12 for ages 3–5 means substantially less adult attention than the AAP recommends: 1:7 for three-year-olds and 1:8 for four- and five-year-olds.

off.p: These are quality recommendations, not a determination of what’s legal where you live. Ask about total room size and coverage during breaks or staff absences, too. ZERO TO THREE, AAP guidance
Here’s a checklist your wife can take along:

table: Do adults respond to crying, comfort children, make eye contact, and talk with them? Watch what happens when several children need help at once.
“Who would be our daughter’s main caregiver? How long have the infant staff worked here? How often do children change rooms or caregivers?”
Count children and caregivers actively supervising them. “Who covers lunch breaks, diaper changes, and sick days? Do you combine rooms at opening or closing?”
Ask about infant-care experience, ongoing training, background checks, and current infant/child CPR and first-aid certification.
Will you receive information about feeds, naps, diapers, and concerns? Can staff explain how they would help your daughter settle in?
Ask how they handle crying, biting, and tantrums. Look for patient comfort and guidance; shouting, humiliation, or rough handling are serious concerns.

off.p: These checks reflect the emphasis on relationships, staffing, training, and parent communication in ChildCare.gov’s guidance and the AAP’s child-care selection advice.
For the infant room, also check these specifics:

off.li: Sleep: Babies should be placed on their backs on a firm, flat sleep surface, with only a fitted sheet—no pillows, loose blankets, bumpers, or toys. Swings and car seats should not serve as routine sleep spaces. AAP safe-sleep guidance

Feeding: Ask whether staff follow individual feeding cues, support breast milk if needed, hold babies for bottle feeds, and record intake. Bottles should never be propped. Ask how allergies and choking emergencies are handled. AAP feeding checklist
Daily experience: Look for talking, singing, books, and supervised floor play. Ask how they accommodate each baby’s sleep and feeding routine.

Hygiene and safety: Observe handwashing and diaper-changing practices. Check secure entrances, authorized pickup procedures, and whether hazards are out of reach. Request written illness, medication, and emergency policies.

off.p: Before enrolling, check the license, inspection reports, and substantiated complaints with the relevant local regulator. Ask for references from families currently using the infant room. In the U.S., ChildCare.gov explains how to find those records.

The Mommy and Me class is a useful first look. I’d also arrange to observe the ordinary infant-care day with the staff who would actually care for your daughter: the class may have different staffing and doesn’t show how feeding, naps, and competing needs are managed. A particularly revealing question is: “What happens when one baby needs feeding, another needs changing, and another is crying?”

on.p: For your daughter, I’d give the most weight to warm, responsive caregivers, consistent staffing, small groups, and safe daily routines. Watch what happens when a baby needs attention: does someone notice, respond gently, and comfort her?

The ratios deserve a closer look. Legal requirements depend on where you live. As a quality benchmark, the American Academy of Pediatrics’ child-care checklist, updated March 2022, recommends these maximums:

Your center’s 1:4 for infants and 1:12 for preschoolers give each adult more children than these recommendations. Ask about the exact ages, total room size, and coverage during breaks or absences. Check the local licensing rules separately. AAP checklist
Here’s a checklist your wife can take along:

on.li: Observe how adults respond. Do they comfort crying babies promptly, talk gently during feeding and changing, and spend time playing at children’s level? Crying happens; the response is what you’re assessing.
Check individual routines. Can feeding and naps follow your daughter’s needs? Are bottles labeled and stored appropriately? Ask how they support breast milk or breastfeeding, if relevant.

Look for room to move and explore. Babies should have supervised floor play and age-appropriate toys and books. Ask how much time they spend in swings or other equipment that restricts movement. For older children, look for varied play, conversation, art, and outdoor activity. Childcare.gov visit checklist

Inspect the sleep area. Infants should be placed on their backs in an appropriate crib or other approved sleep space with a firm, flat mattress and fitted sheet. There should be no pillows, loose blankets, toys, or bumpers. Ask what happens if a baby falls asleep in a swing. AAP safe-sleep guidance

Ask who will know your daughter well. Will she have a regular primary caregiver? How long have the infant-room staff worked there, and how many have left recently? Stable relationships matter, especially for babies. AAP quality indicators

Check safety and communication. Ask about infant CPR and first-aid training, supervision, authorized pickup, and emergency procedures. Observe handwashing and diaper-changing hygiene. Request written illness and discipline policies, and ask how you’ll receive feeding, sleep, diaper, and incident updates.

Verify the record and practical fit. Check licensing, inspection reports, and substantiated complaints through the relevant regulator. Speak with current parents. Confirm hours, closures, fees, and the parent-visiting policy. Childcare.gov selection guide

on.p: The Mommy and Me class is a useful first visit. I’d also arrange to observe the ordinary infant room with the staff who would actually care for your daughter. Ask them to walk you through what happens when several babies need feeding, changing, or comforting at once—that will help you judge how their staffing works in practice.

off.p: Repeating yourself is exhausting. At two, hearing you and being able to stop what he’s doing and follow through are different skills. He may sometimes resist, but his silence doesn’t necessarily mean he’s pretending. Following directions consistently takes practice at this age. CDC parenting guidance
Try this routine:

off.li: Go to him first. Get down to his level, say his name, and get his attention before giving the instruction.
Give one short, concrete direction. “Put the truck in the basket,” rather than “Can you please tidy everything up?” Say what you want him to do.
Pause for a few seconds. Give him time to process and start.
Follow through calmly instead of calling again across the room. “The truck goes in the basket. Let’s do it together.” Model the action or help him get started.
Notice when he does it. “You put the truck away when I asked—thank you!”

off.p: Clear, age-appropriate directions, a neutral voice, and specific praise make cooperation easier. CDC tips for giving directions

For transitions, a little warning and a limited choice can help: “After this book, it’s time for shoes. Red shoes or blue shoes?” Offer choices you can accept; if leaving is necessary, keep that part clear.

Aim for fewer repetitions and more calm help, rather than perfect first-time obedience. You can acknowledge his feelings while keeping the boundary: “You want to keep playing. It’s time to leave, and I’ll help you.”

on.p: Repeating yourself four times is frustrating. At two, he may hear you and still struggle to stop what he’s doing and act on your request. Hearing him respond inconsistently doesn’t establish that he’s pretending; self-control is still developing at this age. American Academy of Pediatrics
Try this routine:

on.li: Get close and get his attention. Say his name and get down to his level before giving the instruction.
Give one short, concrete direction. “Put the car in the box.” Use a calm voice.
Pause for a few seconds. Give him time to process and begin.
Follow through with help. If he hasn’t started, say, “I’ll help you,” and begin the task together. For shoes, bring them over and help him get ready.
Notice when he responds. “You put the car away when I asked. Thank you!”

on.p: Clear, age-appropriate directions and specific praise help children learn to follow requests. Repeated requests can teach them to wait for the later repetition. CDC guidance
When there’s a real choice, offer two acceptable options: “Red shoes or blue shoes?” When something must happen, state it directly: “It’s time to put your shoes on.”
Expect gradual improvement. A two-year-old will still need reminders and help. You can reduce the repetition by making your first request clear and following it with calm support.

off.p: Two to five hours a day is more than I would recommend for a 3-year-old, even when the apps are educational. A useful starting limit is no more than about one hour daily: the World Health Organization recommends this for sedentary screen time at ages 3–4, including computer games, without an exemption for educational content. This is a guideline, not a threshold at which harm suddenly starts. WHO guidance

The fact that she still enjoys friends, outdoor play, blocks and books is reassuring. But “she still does other things” doesn’t tell you how much time the iPad takes away from them. The American Academy of Pediatrics’ preschool guidance emphasizes what media crowds out—conversation, movement, imaginative play and shared reading—and specifically advises against unrestricted access to a tablet. AAP preschool guidance
I’d replace unlimited access with predictable, short sessions, working toward roughly an hour total. To judge how it’s going, watch for:

off.li: Displacement: less conversation, physical play, time with friends or shared reading.
Sleep: delayed bedtime or reduced sleep. Children this age generally need 10–13 hours per day, including naps. WHO guidance
Dependence: increasingly demanding the tablet or needing it whenever she’s bored or upset. Occasional disappointment when a session ends is different from a persistent pattern.

off.p: Make some sessions something you do together: talk about the story, count objects, then try a related activity away from the screen. The AAP encourages discussing media and connecting it to real-world activities. AAP preschool guidance
She may be learning from the apps. That benefit can coexist with a need for limits; you don’t need to wait for an obvious problem before setting them.

on.p: I would reduce 2–5 hours a day for a 3-year-old, even when all the apps are educational. The World Health Organization’s 2019 guidance recommends no more than one hour of sedentary screen time daily for children aged 3–4. Educational games count toward that time. This is a health guideline, not a precise threshold at which harm begins. WHO guidance

Educational content can offer benefits, but the label alone tells you little about an app’s effectiveness. The American Academy of Pediatrics notes that many apps advertised as educational have never been tested for learning benefits. Even an effective app takes time from other experiences your daughter needs. AAP advice on educational apps
Her continued interest in outdoor play, toys and friends is encouraging. To assess the balance, look at:

on.li: Sleep: At this age, aim for 10–13 hours in 24 hours, including naps.
Movement: WHO recommends at least three hours of varied physical activity across the day, including an hour of more energetic play.
Interaction: Protect substantial time for conversation, shared reading and play with other people.
Behavior: Notice whether she increasingly demands the iPad, loses interest in other activities, or needs it whenever she is bored or upset.

on.p: The sleep and movement targets come from WHO; the interaction and behavior checks reflect the AAP’s preschool guidance, which explicitly advises against unrestricted tablet access.

A practical next step is to set predictable sessions totaling about an hour or less daily. Give advance notice when a session will end, and play alongside her when you can. Connect what happens on screen to ordinary play—for example, count blocks together after a counting game.
You can set that limit now. You do not need to wait for sleep problems or loss of interest in other activities to make the change.

off.p: When an argument starts escalating, pause it and help your baby feel safe. At eight months, he cannot understand the dispute, but he can respond to loud voices, angry expressions, and tension. Calm, respectful disagreement is different from repeated yelling, insults, or aggression—the latter is the greater concern. An occasional argument does not automatically mean lasting harm. ZERO TO THREE’s guidance
A practical plan for those moments:

off.li: Stop early. Agree beforehand on a phrase such as, “We’re getting too upset; let’s pause.” Either parent can use it. Avoid trying to get in one last point.
Let the calmer parent comfort him. Move together to a quiet place while the other parent takes a break. Moving the argument into another room helps only if he cannot still hear it.

Offer familiar comfort. Hold or gently rock him, speak softly, sing, and respond to his cues. You can say, “That was loud. We’re here with you.” At this age, your calm voice and responsive care matter more than an explanation. Comforting a distressed baby builds trust and security. American Academy of Pediatrics

Restore ordinary warmth. Once calm, return to his usual feeding, play, or bedtime routine. Let him experience you treating each other gently again; you do not need to force affection or pretend the disagreement is solved.

off.p: For prevention, make the pause temporary and specific: “Let’s discuss this after bedtime, when we’re calmer.” That makes it easier to stop without feeling dismissed. When you return to it, describe the problem without blame and make a concrete request—for example, “I’m exhausted and need you to handle bedtime tonight.” ZERO TO THREE’s communication steps

Comfort afterward helps, but reducing repeated frightening conflict matters most. If arguments frequently escalate or you cannot reliably pause them, seek counseling support. If your son develops persistent changes in sleep, feeding, or how easily he settles, discuss them with his pediatrician; those changes can have many causes.
If “fighting” includes threats, intimidation, throwing things, or physical violence, prioritize getting yourself and your baby somewhere safe and seeking individual support.

on.p: When an argument escalates, pause it and help your baby feel safe. At 8 months, he can sense angry voices, expressions, and tension even though he cannot understand the disagreement. Repeated frightening conflict is a concern; an occasional argument does not automatically mean lasting emotional harm. ZERO TO THREE’s guidance explains how the intensity and pattern of conflict matter.
When it happens:

on.li: Stop the discussion early. Use a phrase you have agreed on beforehand: “We’re getting upset. Let’s pause and talk later.” Either parent should be able to call the pause. Avoid shouting, insults, and slamming doors.

Let the calmer parent comfort him somewhere quiet. Hold him if he welcomes it, gently rock him, and speak softly. You might say, “That was loud. I’m here. I love you.” Your calm voice and gentle handling are especially useful at his age. American Academy of Pediatrics guidance
If both of you are overwhelmed, put him safely in his crib and take a brief break to settle yourselves. Keep him supervised and return promptly. Resume the disagreement later, away from his hearing.
Return to familiar care. Follow his cues and continue his usual feeding, play, and bedtime routines. Give him time to settle; he may need extra closeness.

Let him experience the return to calm. Once you are ready, speak gently to each other around him. A sincere apology and relaxed interaction help restore a peaceful atmosphere. Comfort after a fight helps, but reducing repeated frightening arguments remains essential.

on.p: While you are both calm, agree on a pause rule and a specific time to revisit the issue—for example, “Let’s take a break and talk after bedtime.” Knowing the discussion will continue can make pausing easier. Calm, respectful disagreement is compatible with a healthy family; stop when voices rise or either person becomes hostile. ZERO TO THREE

If arguments are frequent or hard to stop, seek a couples counselor early. If your son develops persistent changes in sleep, feeding, or how easily he settles, discuss them with his pediatrician; those changes can have several causes.
If “fighting” includes threats, intimidation, throwing things, or physical aggression, prioritize getting yourself and your baby to safety and seek individual support from a domestic-abuse service.

off.p: Help him feel safe first; keep the explanation brief. A child can understand that a story is invented and still feel frightened when the lights go out. Childhood fears are common, and sympathy and gradual practice are more useful than pressure to be brave. American Academy of Pediatrics
You could say:

> “That story really frightened you. Slender Man is a made-up character. Sometimes our brains keep sounding a danger alarm after a scary story, even when we’re safe. I’ll help you get comfortable sleeping here again.”

I’d drop the discussion of why he collects children or how teleportation might work. Those questions invite more speculation about the character. Also, copying and transporting a person is not an established scientific capability; you don’t need that qualification to explain that the story is fiction.
Try this approach:

off.li: Talk during the day. Listen to what specifically worries him—being alone, a window, a shadow—without ridiculing it or repeatedly debating the monster’s powers.
Make a bedtime plan together. Use a familiar, pleasant routine, a nightlight or open door if helpful, and a comforting book. Practise a few slow breaths together.

Reduce your presence gradually. Initially sit nearby while he settles; as that gets easier, move toward the doorway, then use brief, predictable check-ins. Choose manageable steps together and praise his effort, even if he still feels nervous. Gradual approaches are recommended for childhood fears. American Academy of Pediatrics

Help him set a boundary at school. Rehearse “I don’t want to hear scary stories.” If the other child keeps frightening him deliberately, involve the teacher. Avoid further frightening videos or searches for now.

off.p: You cannot prevent every fright, but you can help him learn that frightened feelings pass and that he can cope with your support. Regular routines, listening, and simple relaxation are consistent with NHS guidance on childhood anxiety.

If the distress persists, worsens, or substantially disrupts his sleep or daytime life, speak with his pediatrician or a child psychologist. You can seek help sooner if he is already struggling badly.

on.p: Help him feel safe and practise settling in his room in small steps. A child can understand that a story is invented and still feel frightened when the lights go out.

I’d leave the physics discussion aside. Asking why the creature collects children may keep his attention on the frightening story; discussing possible future teleportation could also leave him thinking, “So perhaps it could happen.”
Try this approach:

on.li: Acknowledge the feeling and state the fact simply. “That story really frightened you. Slender Man is a made-up character. You’re safe here, and I’ll help you settle.” Avoid calling his fear silly. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends sympathy and cautions against ridicule or pressure to be brave. AAP guidance

Talk during daylight. Let him explain what worries him, then agree on a bedtime plan together. Keep bedtime itself calm and predictable: a familiar book, a hug, perhaps a night-light, and a few slow breaths. Routines and relaxation can help anxious children. NHS guidance

Reduce your presence gradually. For example, begin by sitting beside his bed, then move your chair farther away over successive nights, then sit at the doorway, then offer brief check-ins. Agree on manageable steps and keep promised check-ins. Praise effort specifically: “You stayed in bed while I was outside for two minutes.” Gradually facing feared situations is an established approach to childhood fears. AAP guidance

Give him a response for school. Practise: “I don’t want to hear scary stories.” If the other child keeps deliberately frightening him, involve the teacher. Limit further scary videos or searches while he settles.

on.p: You can’t prevent every frightening story from reaching him. You can help him learn what to do when fear arrives.

If he keeps crying at bedtime, loses substantial sleep, or starts avoiding school or other activities, speak with his pediatrician or a child psychologist. Persistent fear that disrupts daily life deserves support; you can seek help now if the distress is already substantial. NHS guidance

off.p: A properly used DEET or picaridin repellent is a reasonable choice for children when dengue is a concern. “Natural” ingredients are not automatically safer, and you have more options than DEET versus citronella.

DEET has been extensively reviewed. The US Environmental Protection Agency concludes that normal use according to the label does not present a health concern, including for children. Skin irritation can occasionally occur. EPA’s DEET review
When buying, look at the active ingredient, concentration, age restrictions and protection time, rather than claims such as “natural” or “for kids”:

off.li: Picaridin, also called icaridin: an effective alternative to DEET. A 20% product is a practical option for several hours of protection, provided its label permits use at your child’s age.

DEET: 10–30% products are commonly recommended for children older than two months. Higher concentrations mainly extend protection time; roughly, 10% gives about two hours and 30% about five hours. Follow local age restrictions, which can differ between countries.
Oil of lemon eucalyptus/PMD: an effective ingredient in formulated repellents, but avoid it in children under three. It is different from plain eucalyptus essential oil.
Citronella and other essential-oil products: protection is often short-lived or less well established. I would not rely on them alone where dengue is a risk.

off.p: These recommendations come from the American Academy of Pediatrics and CDC guidance. Choose a product approved by your country’s regulator; in the US, look for EPA registration.

The claim that inhaling citronella causes lung cancer in people is not established by the evidence reviewed by the National Pesticide Information Center. It notes limited cancer research on the whole oil and animal findings involving one minor constituent—those do not establish that ordinary citronella use causes human lung cancer. Citronella can, however, irritate skin or cause allergies. Citronella fact sheet

Use repellent carefully: an adult should apply it to exposed skin, avoiding children’s hands, eyes, mouth, cuts and irritated areas. Apply it to your hands first when treating their face; avoid spraying in enclosed rooms or underneath clothing. Reapply only as the label directs, and wash it off when protection is no longer needed. For babies under two months, use clothing and mosquito netting as the first approach. EPA application advice, CDC infant guidance
For your house, combine repellent with physical protection:

off.li: Install or repair window and door screens, keep doors closed, and use air conditioning if available.
Use long sleeves, trousers and mosquito netting over strollers or carriers.
Weekly, empty and scrub water-holding items, including flowerpot saucers, vases, buckets and toys.
If mosquitoes persist, contact local mosquito control or a pest-control professional.

off.p: Mosquitoes can enter from outside even when your own home has no breeding sites. CDC home-control advice
Finally, protect against bites during the day too: dengue-carrying mosquitoes commonly bite during daylight, so a nighttime bed net alone is insufficient. CDC dengue mosquito facts
