How old are your children, and which country are you in? That would help narrow down the appropriate label restrictions.

on.p: A repellent containing DEET or picaridin, labelled for your child’s age, is a sensible choice when dengue is a concern. Combine it with window screens, protective clothing and mosquito netting. CDC considers registered repellents safe and effective when used as directed. CDC guidance
The safety claims you found need some context:

on.li: DEET: EPA’s assessment found that normal use according to the label does not present a health concern, including for children. Skin irritation can occur. The concentration mainly affects how long protection lasts. EPA assessment

Citronella: The claim that inhaling citronella repellent causes lung cancer in people is not established. Its cancer potential has not been adequately studied, and it can cause irritation or allergic reactions. Many essential-oil repellents provide only brief protection, which makes them a less dependable choice for dengue prevention. National Pesticide Information Center, American Academy of Pediatrics

on.p: When buying, check the active ingredient, age restrictions, stated protection time and approval by your country’s regulator. In the US, look for an EPA registration number. Picaridin—also called icaridin—is an effective alternative to DEET. For young children, CDC’s travel guidance describes 20–30% DEET applied sparingly as a prudent option; the individual product’s label governs its use. For newborns or premature babies, use clothing and netting and discuss skin repellents with their clinician. CDC advises avoiding oil of lemon eucalyptus/PMD in children under three. CDC guidance for children
Apply it yourself:

on.li: Use only enough to cover exposed skin; keep it off hands, eyes, mouth, cuts and irritated skin.
Apply it to your hands first when treating the child’s face.
Choose a lotion, stick or unpressurised spray to control application; avoid breathing spray mist.
Follow the label’s reapplication instructions and wash treated skin when protection is no longer needed.
Use separate sunscreen and repellent: sunscreen first. AAP application advice

on.p: For your house, mosquitoes can enter from neighbouring areas even when you have removed breeding sites. Repair door and window screens, keep doors closed, and use mosquito netting over strollers and sleeping areas. Check water-holding containers weekly, including flowerpot saucers and vases; empty and scrub them to remove eggs. Persistent indoor mosquitoes warrant help from building management or a pest-control professional. CDC home-control guidance

Dengue-carrying mosquitoes can bite during the day, so include daytime naps in your protection plan. Repellent bracelets and ultrasonic devices have no proven protective effectiveness. Avoid burning mosquito coils indoors around children because their smoke contributes to harmful indoor air pollution. CDC dengue prevention, AAP, WHO
How old are your children, and which country do you live in? Those details help narrow the suitable products and age limits.

off.p: What you describe sounds more like ordinary night waking or a brief partial awakening than sleepwalking, although a description alone cannot establish the cause. Sitting or standing in the crib and crying does not, by itself, mean she is sleepwalking.
At 13 months, several things can contribute:

off.li: Needing help to settle again. Children briefly wake during the night. If feeding, rocking, or a parent’s presence helps them fall asleep initially, they may seek that help again after waking. Night feeds can be part of this pattern, but they aren’t necessarily the cause. American Academy of Pediatrics
Separation anxiety. This commonly disrupts sleep around her age: a child wakes, notices a parent is absent, and cries for reassurance. AAP guidance
Hunger or discomfort, including teething, illness, or being too hot or cold. NHS guidance

off.p: She doesn’t need to be having nightmares for this to happen. Sleepwalking and night terrors involve incomplete awakening from deep sleep, usually early in the night. During a typical night terror, a child looks frightened or confused, may scream or sweat, and often doesn’t recognize or respond to a parent. Your daughter’s ability to respond to your calm voice and settle makes an ordinary awakening more likely—though it doesn’t conclusively rule out a partial awakening. AAP explanation

Your quiet reassurance is a reasonable approach. Keep lights low, interactions brief, and bedtime and naps consistent. Note when episodes happen, how long they last, and whether she seems to recognize you; a short video can help her pediatrician assess unusual episodes. You don’t have to stop breastfeeding to address sleep, and night-weaning decisions can take her growth, daytime intake, and your family’s preferences into account.

Discuss it with her pediatrician if episodes worsen, she seems in pain, or she has habitual loud snoring, gasping, breathing pauses, or unusual stiffening or repetitive jerking. Seek urgent help for breathing difficulty or abnormal unresponsiveness.

on.p: This sounds most consistent with ordinary night waking and needing help settling back to sleep. Sitting or standing and crying is not enough to identify sleepwalking. Her responding to your calm voice and quickly settling supports that interpretation, though a description alone cannot establish the cause.
At 13 months, several things can contribute:

on.li: Brief awakenings between sleep cycles. If she usually falls asleep feeding or with a parent’s help, she may seek that same help when she wakes. American Academy of Pediatrics
Separation anxiety. This can cause repeated waking and crying for a parent at this age; reassurance may be enough to settle her. AAP guidance
Hunger or discomfort, including teething or illness. Night feeds may provide food, comfort, or both. Continuing breastfeeding does not by itself establish why she wakes. NHS guidance

on.p: Sleepwalking or another partial awakening is possible, but sleepwalking is more typical in older children. During sleepwalking, children often look blank or confused and respond poorly. Night terrors usually occur early in the night and involve intense distress, difficulty comforting the child, and apparent failure to recognize a parent. Her settling when you speak makes a classic night terror less likely. Nightmares can occur at this age, but nightly crying does not establish that she is having them. AAP explanation

Keep using the gentle reassurance that works. Maintain a consistent bedtime routine and keep nighttime interactions quiet with dim lighting. For a week, record when episodes happen, how long they last, whether she recognizes you, and whether she needs a feed. That can help her pediatrician distinguish ordinary waking from a sleep-related episode. If you want to reduce night feeds, discuss her growth and daytime intake with the pediatrician first.

Arrange a pediatric review if episodes worsen, cause injury, or accompany pain, poor growth, or daytime tiredness. Habitual loud snoring, gasping, or breathing pauses also warrant review, because breathing problems can repeatedly interrupt sleep. AAP guidance on sleep problems

off.p: For a nine-month-old, I’d start with songs you sing yourself, simple action songs, and a few gentle recordings. Classical music is an option, but you don’t need a special “baby music” collection.
Your concern about sudden loud passages is sensible. I’d treat “dramatic” as a matter of your son’s reaction, rather than a reason to exclude a whole genre.
Other useful criteria are:

off.li: Comfortable volume. Keep recordings quiet enough that you can speak normally over them, and place the speaker away from his head. Overall loudness and listening duration matter more for hearing safety than musical style. NIDCD guidance

Opportunities to interact. Choose music you can sing along with, sway to, or accompany with gentle clapping. Your familiar voice is a particularly good starting point: babies recognise caregivers’ voices and associate them with comfort. American Academy of Pediatrics
Repetition and a clear pulse. Repeated verses and a recognisable beat make it easy to turn a song into a shared game. These are useful selection preferences, not requirements.
A match for the moment. Try slow, gentle music when settling down and livelier songs during play. Music for an awake, interested baby needn’t all sound like a lullaby.
His response. Watch for smiling, babbling, reaching or moving along. If he becomes upset or loses interest, lower the volume, change the music or stop.
Quiet breaks. Music can be an activity rather than continuous background sound. A noisy environment can make speech harder for young children to understand. AAP guidance on noise

off.p: Here are some starting suggestions, chosen for their musical character rather than any proven special benefit for babies:

table: “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” or “Row, Row, Row Your Boat,” sung by you
Short, repetitive melodies; easy to sing softly and pair with swaying
“The Wheels on the Bus” or “If You’re Happy and You Know It”
Repeated verses and gestures for shared play; increasingly useful as he becomes a toddler
Bach: Prelude in C major, BWV 846, on piano
Saint-Saëns: “The Swan”, for cello with piano accompaniment
A smooth melody with flowing accompaniment
Softly performed folk songs or acoustic songs you enjoy
A way to introduce variety while singing or moving together

off.p: Preview the actual recording, including its loudest passage: arrangements and performances can differ considerably.
There’s no need to favour Mozart for intelligence benefits; research does not establish that playing Mozart to babies raises their IQ. Harvard’s review
For your son, try one or two songs while sitting together, repeat whichever catches his interest, and follow his lead. You don’t have to sing well to make that enjoyable.

on.p: For a nine-month-old, your own singing is an excellent place to start. Try a familiar song while he watches your face, add simple hand movements, and pause to let him babble back. ZERO TO THREE recommends singing, movement, and these back-and-forth musical exchanges for babies. Getting in Tune
Your criteria are useful for choosing calming music. For playtime, a lively beat and some changes in expression can also be enjoyable. The key is how your son responds.
A few practical criteria:

on.li: Comfortable volume. Start quietly, with the speaker away from his head. You should easily hear each other over the music. Hearing risk depends on loudness and duration; a recording with little variation can still be too loud. NIDCD hearing guidance

Repetition. Familiar melodies, repeated verses, and a clear beat give him patterns to recognize. Repeating a favourite song is useful; you do not need a constantly changing playlist. ZERO TO THREE’s music guidance
Opportunities to join in. Choose songs you can sing, clap, or gently sway to together. As he becomes a toddler, action songs offer more ways to participate.
A match for the moment. Try gentle singing for settling down and more rhythmic music for active play.
His response. Watch for interest, smiles, or movement. Turning away or becoming upset is a cue to pause or change the activity. Include quiet periods too. Getting in Tune

on.p: These are reasonable starting choices, selected for their musical character—not a scientifically established infant playlist:

table: “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” or “Row, Row, Row Your Boat”, sung by you
Short, repetitive melodies; easy to sing gently
“Itsy Bitsy Spider” or “The Wheels on the Bus”
A familiar lullaby; try singing it or a gentle recording
Bach: Prelude in C major, BWV 846
Slow pace and a relatively sparse piano texture
Acoustic folk songs or gentle jazz
Alternatives with voices, clear melodies, or a steady pulse

on.p: Preview the particular recording: arrangements and performances can change the volume and character considerably. Classical music is one option; family songs and music you enjoy are also worth exploring.

For your son, I would begin with a few minutes of singing and gestures, then try one short recording together. Repeat whatever he seems to enjoy. That gives you a useful selection method: his interest, at a comfortable volume.

off.p: At two, I’d treat this as curiosity that needs gentle coaching. Your explanation is plausible: he is noticing rules and trying to understand what happens when people break them. Understanding other people’s feelings is still developing at this age, so expecting consistent tact is a big ask. ZERO TO THREE’s guidance on empathy supports teaching through simple explanations and your own example.
Try a predictable response:

off.li: Describe the behavior without labeling the child. “He’s crying and looks upset. I don’t know why.” If someone hits: “Hitting hurts. His grown-up is helping him stop.” This preserves the rule without agreeing that someone is “bad.”
Give him a concrete way to ask privately. Get close and say softly, “You can ask me in a quiet voice. Let’s give them some space.” Model the volume yourself; “be discreet” is too abstract.

Answer briefly, then redirect. “He seems upset. His dad is helping. Let’s go to the swings.” If the question repeats, calmly repeat the short answer rather than supplying increasingly elaborate explanations.

Acknowledge an old incident without reopening it. “Yes, you remember that Sam threw a toy. Throwing toys can hurt people. That happened earlier; now we’re drawing.” If he seems worried, ask, “Did that scare you?” Repetition may be his way of processing something.
Notice kindness, too. “You saw her help him pick up the blocks!” Give him language and attention for observations beyond rule-breaking.

off.p: These scripts are practical ways to apply guidance about modeling empathy and responding patiently; they aren’t a guarantee that he’ll stop immediately.

Avoid calling him a “tattletale” or making a blanket rule against telling. Keep the door open for help: “If someone hurts you, you feel scared, or you need help, always tell me.” At two, he still needs you to judge which situations require intervention.

This will likely become easier with maturity, but gentle teaching now is useful. Aim first for him to accept a brief explanation and move on with your help. Remembering to speak privately will take more practice.

on.p: At two, I’d treat this as curiosity about rules and feelings, and begin teaching him a simple way to ask privately. Your explanation is plausible; his comments alone don’t establish that he wants to get anyone into trouble.

Two-year-olds are still developing empathy and self-control, and need repeated help with social situations. Keep your explanations short and your expectations modest. ZERO TO THREE’s guidance for ages 24–36 months supports this approach.
Try a consistent response:

on.li: Describe what you can see. “He’s crying. He seems upset. His grown-up is helping him.” If you don’t know why, say, “I don’t know.”
Give him a concrete privacy cue. Get close and quietly say, “You can ask me in a quiet voice.” Practice this when he’s calm, and acknowledge success: “Thank you for asking quietly.”
Answer briefly, then redirect. If he repeats the question, say, “We talked about that. Let’s give him some space and go to the swings.” You can stay warm while ending the discussion.
Use specific descriptions of behavior. When he says “Sam was bad,” respond, “Sam hit. Hitting hurts.” This gives him words for the action and its effect.

Acknowledge an old incident once. “Yes, you remember that he threw the toy. The teacher helped.” If he keeps returning to it, check gently: “Did that scare you?” He may need reassurance or help understanding what happened.

on.p: Keep asking for help welcome: “You can always tell me if someone hurts you, you feel scared, or you need help.” At this age, let adults decide which reports need action; avoid making him sort everything into “tattling” and “telling.”

You can start teaching quiet questions now, but expect plenty of reminders. Maturity and practice should help; there’s no reliable age when this particular habit will disappear. Avoid calling him a tattletale or punishing his questions—give him the words and routine you want him to use.

off.p: Plan on gradually getting your house back during the preschool years—roughly ages 4–5 for many everyday restrictions. That’s a practical planning estimate, not an age at which everything becomes safe. Your youngest child’s behavior and the particular hazard matter more than their birthday.
Remove precautions individually:

off.li: Protecting possessions: You can put decorations back when your child reliably leaves them alone. Start with inexpensive, unbreakable things.

Preventing everyday injuries: Look for demonstrated skills, such as consistently navigating stairs safely. Follow each safety device’s instructions; a gate that your child can climb may itself become hazardous.

Preventing serious injuries: Keep medicines and cleaners secured, furniture anchored, and dangerous windows and pools protected. Those precautions can still matter well beyond toddlerhood. CPSC home-safety guidance

off.p: The tricky period is that physical ability develops ahead of judgment: a toddler who can open cupboards and climb furniture still cannot reliably remember safety rules while exploring. The American Academy of Pediatrics specifically warns about this at ages 2–4. AAP guidance

So there is a light at the end of the tunnel, but it’s a gradual transition. Use observed, consistent behavior to relax low-risk restrictions; keep barriers where one mistake could cause serious harm.

on.p: Think in terms of gradually easing baby-proofing through the preschool years, with age 4–5 as a rough time to reassess much of it. That’s a planning estimate, not a safety cutoff. Your youngest child’s abilities and behavior determine which precautions can come down.

Expect to need substantial protection throughout toddlerhood. The American Academy of Pediatrics cautions that children aged 2–4 can climb and open drawers while still failing to understand dangers or remember prohibitions during play. AAP guidance
Different safeguards have different lifetimes:

on.li: Baby gates: Often come down around age 2, or earlier if the child starts climbing over or opening them. Follow the gate’s limits, and supervise and teach stair use as you make that transition. Nationwide Children’s guidance
Locks on cupboards containing harmless items: You can reassess these as your child reliably handles the contents safely. Understanding a rule is one step; consistently following it is another.

Protection against serious hazards: Keep medicines and cleaners locked away, furniture and TVs anchored, and appropriate window and pool barriers in place. These protections remain useful beyond the baby years. CPSC guidance

on.p: Your house can become progressively more “normal.” Review each precaution by asking what could happen if your child reached this while your attention was elsewhere. For ordinary mess or minor breakage, you can gradually allow more access. For poisoning, drowning, or a serious fall, keep a physical safeguard.

off.p: Swaddling probably calms babies through a combination of comforting body contact and limiting movements that can startle them awake. The soothing effect is supported by research; the exact mechanism is less certain.
Two explanations are particularly relevant:

off.li: It limits sudden arm movements and their progression into waking. Young infants make involuntary startles during sleep. Swaddling contains those movements, which may help prevent a brief startle from becoming a full awakening with crying. In a study of 26 infants, swaddling reduced startles and reduced the likelihood that a startle progressed to full arousal during quiet sleep. Those babies were about 3 months old, so this is evidence for the mechanism, rather than a direct study of 4-day-olds. Gerard, Harris & Thach, *Pediatrics*, 2002.

It provides a familiar feeling of containment. A newborn has just moved from a confined environment into one where their limbs can move freely. A snug wrap provides continuous contact and boundaries around the body. The American Academy of Pediatrics describes this as resembling the womb and helping soothe newborns. That is a plausible explanation, but “it reminds them of the womb” should not be treated as a proven account of what babies experience. AAP guidance.

off.p: Research also shows an effect on sleep itself: a 2022 systematic review found that swaddling tended to increase quiet sleep and reduce transitions between sleep states. However, only six studies met its criteria, and swaddling methods varied, so the evidence cannot tell us precisely why it works for your particular newborn. *The effect of swaddling on infant sleep and arousal*, 2022.
“Snug” is the aim; tighter is not necessarily better. For your 4-day-old, the AAP recommends:

off.li: Enough room for two or three fingers between the chest and wrap, allowing unrestricted breathing.
Loose wrapping around the hips and legs so they can bend up and outward.
Sleeping on their back, on a firm, flat surface, with the head uncovered and no loose bedding.
Avoiding overheating and weighted swaddles, and stopping swaddling as soon as the baby shows signs of trying to roll.

off.p: These precautions matter because excessive tightness can restrict breathing or harm hip development, and swaddling does not prevent SIDS. AAP safe-swaddling guidance.

on.p: Swaddling probably calms newborns through a combination of comforting body contact and fewer startle-driven movements. The calming effect is supported by research; the precise contribution of each mechanism is less certain.

on.li: It limits the movements that can wake or upset a baby. Newborns have a strong Moro reflex: they suddenly throw their arms outward when startled, sometimes waking themselves and crying. A snug wrap contains those movements. The American Academy of Pediatrics describes this as one reason swaddling helps babies settle. AAP explanation

It makes a startle less likely to become a full awakening. In a 2002 study, Gerard and colleagues observed 26 infants during swaddled and unswaddled naps. Swaddling reduced startles and reduced the likelihood that a startle progressed to waking during quiet sleep. This provides a physiological explanation for some of the calming you see. These infants were about 80 days old, so the study does not establish the exact response in a four-day-old. Study in *Pediatrics*

The surrounding contact may feel familiar and soothing. Swaddling provides bodily boundaries resembling the confined environment of the womb. The AAP offers this as an explanation for its soothing effect. “It resembles the womb” is a plausible explanation, though the baby's subjective experience is difficult to establish experimentally. AAP guidance

on.p: The sleep effect has also been measured directly: a 2005 study of 16 infants aged 6–16 weeks found that swaddling increased sleep efficiency and reduced spontaneous awakenings. That supports your observation, while leaving some uncertainty about exactly why it works. Franco and colleagues, *Pediatrics*

For your four-day-old, aim for snug, with room for breathing and hip movement. Increasing tightness can affect breathing: a study found that greater swaddle pressure increased respiratory rate during quiet sleep. Gerard and colleagues, 2002

The AAP recommends allowing two or three fingers between the wrap and the chest, leaving the legs free to bend up and outward, and avoiding overheating. For sleep, always place your baby on their back on a firm, flat surface; keep the head uncovered, use an unweighted swaddle, and stop swaddling at the first signs of trying to roll. Swaddling has not been shown to prevent SIDS. AAP safe-swaddling guidance

off.p: Simply touching your gums with your fingers is unlikely to explain severely crooked teeth. Prolonged thumb or finger *sucking*, or sustained pressure against teeth, can affect their position; occasional touching is different. Dental guidance emphasizes how long and how often pressure acts. Your childhood habit alone does not establish the cause. AAPD guidance
Crooked teeth can develop for several reasons:

off.li: Inherited traits and insufficient space: Teeth may be too large for the available jaw space, causing overlap or rotation. Jaw growth and bite patterns can also run in families. Your mother’s similar teeth make an inherited contribution plausible, although that cannot be confirmed from family history alone. American Association of Orthodontists, explanation of crowding
Development and tooth loss: Extra, missing or unusually positioned teeth, eruption problems, and premature loss of baby teeth can interfere with alignment. AAPD guidance

Persistent oral habits: Prolonged thumb/finger sucking and pacifier use are associated particularly with front teeth that do not meet and crossbites. Their effects depend on duration, frequency and intensity. AAPD guidance

off.p: Prevention can reduce some risks, but cannot guarantee straight teeth. For children, useful measures are:

off.li: Establish dental care by the first birthday so development, decay and habits can be monitored.
Gently help children stop thumb/finger sucking and pacifier habits by about age three, using encouragement rather than punishment. AAPD recommendations
Protect baby teeth from decay and obtain dental advice if one is lost early; some children need an appliance to preserve space for the permanent tooth. AAPD guidance
Arrange an orthodontic assessment by age seven, or sooner if a dentist identifies a concern. An assessment does not automatically mean starting braces. AAO guidance

off.p: Two other common misconceptions are that good brushing alone prevents crowding, and that straightened teeth stay straight permanently. Brushing protects dental health but cannot correct inadequate space; after orthodontic treatment, retainers help prevent teeth from shifting again. AAO guidance on crowding, retainers

If your teeth remain crooked, a dentist or orthodontist can assess the crowding and bite and discuss whether treatment would help. There is no sound basis, from what you describe, to blame yourself for touching your gums.

on.p: Ordinary touching or rubbing of your gums with your fingers is unlikely to explain severely crooked teeth. Dental guidance links changes in tooth position to habits that apply pressure frequently and for long periods, particularly thumb or finger sucking. Occasional touching is a different exposure. American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD)

Heredity is a common contributor. Tooth size, jaw size and jaw relationships can run in families. When teeth need more room than the jaw provides, they can overlap or rotate. Your mother having crooked teeth makes an inherited contribution plausible, although that alone cannot establish the cause in your case. MedlinePlus
The main facts and myths are:

table: “Crooked teeth are always caused by childhood habits.”
They often have several contributors, including inherited anatomy, extra or missing teeth, and problems with tooth eruption.
Yes. Persistent sucking can contribute to protruding front teeth, an open bite or a crossbite. Duration and frequency matter.
“Baby teeth do not matter because they fall out.”
Losing them prematurely can let neighbouring teeth move into the space needed by permanent teeth.
Evidence does not support removing otherwise healthy wisdom teeth solely for this purpose.

on.p: Sources: MedlinePlus, AAPD guidance, Imperial College Healthcare NHS wisdom-tooth information.
Prevention can reduce some risks, but it cannot guarantee straight teeth. Inherited crowding and jaw differences may develop despite good care. MedlinePlus
For children, useful measures include:

on.li: Address prolonged sucking habits. AAPD recommends stopping thumb, finger and pacifier sucking by about age three. Use encouragement and comfort; ask a dentist for help if the habit persists. AAPD, American Dental Association

Protect baby teeth and monitor their loss. Regular dental care helps detect decay and eruption problems. If a baby tooth is lost early, a dentist can assess whether a space-maintaining appliance would help. AAPD

Arrange an orthodontic assessment by age seven, or earlier if a problem is apparent. This identifies developing problems and helps determine treatment timing; many children initially need monitoring. American Association of Orthodontists

on.p: For teeth that are already crooked, an orthodontist can assess whether braces or clear aligners would help. Adults can also be treated. After treatment, wearing retainers as prescribed helps prevent teeth shifting back. MedlinePlus, NHS

The childhood explanation you were given is too definite: an examination and history would be needed to judge the contributors, and simply touching your gums does not establish that you caused the crookedness.

off.p: You haven’t spoiled him or caused this. Needing help to fall asleep—and waking when put down—is common at nearly 3 months. That doesn’t make it any less exhausting, especially for your wife. NHS guidance describes babies initially sleeping only in a parent’s arms.

At this age, focus on gentle practice. Formal sleep training, including timed crying methods, is generally considered around 4–6 months, depending on the baby’s development and health. Night feeds may still be needed. Cleveland Clinic guidance
Try these steps:

off.li: Use a short, repeatable routine: feed, change if needed, dim the lights, cuddle and sing quietly. Start settling when he looks sleepy, before he becomes very upset.
Practise one crib nap each day. You can rock or feed him to sleep first and then gently transfer him. Falling asleep independently isn’t a requirement right now.

Help him settle in the crib: try quiet shushing and a gentle hand on his chest while you’re beside him. If he becomes distressed, pick him up, calm him and try again. Keep attempts manageable; there’s no need to turn every nap into a prolonged struggle.

Share the carrying and settling. Take a regular shift yourself, or enlist someone trusted, so your wife gets predictable time to eat, shower and rest. Consistent routines and help from another caregiver are recommended for exhausted parents. AAP advice

off.p: The sleep arrangement is the change to prioritise now: put him on his back in his own crib or bassinet beside your bed, with a firm, flat mattress and only a fitted sheet. Bed-sharing increases the risk of suffocation and sleep-related death, particularly under 4 months. Avoid pillows, blankets, nests and positioners, and never fall asleep holding him on a sofa or armchair. If you bring him into bed to feed, return him to his crib before you sleep. AAP safe-sleep guidance

If lying flat consistently seems painful, or he has feeding difficulties, poor weight gain or unusually persistent crying, discuss that with his pediatrician rather than assuming it’s a habit. For now, aim for small gains in crib sleep and more rest for both parents—not perfect independent sleep.

on.p: This sounds exhausting, especially for your wife. Needing to be held to sleep is common at this age, and it doesn’t mean you’ve caused a problem. Sleep rhythms are still developing around three months. You can start gentle crib practice now; formal sleep training, including timed crying methods, generally waits until at least four months and a discussion with your pediatrician. NHS infant sleep guidance, Mount Sinai sleep-training guidance
Here’s a manageable approach:

on.li: Start with one nap a day. Choose a time when he’s fed, comfortable and getting sleepy. Use a short, repeatable routine, such as a diaper change, dim lights and a lullaby.
Help him settle, then try the crib. At this age, it’s reasonable to rock or feed him to sleep before transferring him. Falling asleep independently can develop gradually.
If he wakes, soothe him responsively. Try a quiet voice and gentle touch. If he becomes upset, pick him up, calm him and try again when you both feel ready. Keep attempts manageable.
Share the settling work. You can take over holding and crib attempts after feeds so your wife gets a dependable break. A trusted relative can help too. AAP advice for tired parents

on.p: The immediate safety priority is a separate sleep space beside your bed. For every nap and nighttime sleep, place him on his back in a crib or bassinet with a firm, flat mattress and fitted sheet; keep pillows, blankets and toys out. Share your room for at least the first six months. Bed-sharing raises the risk of suffocation and sleep-related death, particularly under four months. Avoid falling asleep while holding him, especially on a sofa or armchair. AAP safe-sleep guidance

Bring this up with his pediatrician, especially if lying down seems painful, feeding is difficult or weight gain is poor. For now, aim for small opportunities to sleep in the crib and regular breaks for both parents. He may still need considerable help settling and feeding overnight.

off.p: There is specialist literature on this question, but little direct evidence comparing early disclosure with waiting until adolescence or adulthood. I found no controlled study establishing an optimal age, or showing that disclosure at 18 produces better outcomes. The usual professional recommendation is truthful, developmentally appropriate disclosure, with further conversations as children grow. That recommendation rests largely on clinical expertise rather than trials of disclosure timing.

The most directly relevant paper is Albert C. Cain’s “Children of Suicide: The Telling and the Knowing”, *Psychiatry* 65(2), 124–136 (2002). Cain, a University of Michigan psychologist, examines precisely the question you ask. He describes the limited literature and challenges an absolute rule that every child must receive the whole truth immediately. His discussion is based primarily on clinical and preventive work, rather than a controlled comparison of disclosure strategies. He emphasizes that being told does not necessarily mean understanding, and that the parent’s explanation of *why* the suicide happened also matters. Paper abstract and citation.

It helps to distinguish that literature from research on the effects of parental suicide itself. For example, Cerel and colleagues followed 26 suicide-bereaved children aged 5–17 and compared them with 332 children bereaved by other parental deaths over two years. They found more anxiety, anger and shame in the suicide-bereaved group. This comparison does not establish whether telling children earlier or later causes better outcomes; the groups differed in the cause of death, and some difficulties predated the bereavement. Cerel et al., 1999.
The advantages and disadvantages below are therefore clinical considerations, not experimentally demonstrated effects of disclosure timing:

table: The child hears from a trusted caregiver; misunderstandings and self-blame can be addressed; there is less opportunity to discover the truth accidentally.
Younger children may understand only part of the explanation. Information needs to be given in small amounts and revisited.
Allows time to prepare an explanation and arrange support; an older child may understand more complex information.
The child may learn elsewhere, imagine explanations, or later feel misled. Greater understanding at an older age does not establish that the news will be emotionally easier.

off.p: These considerations are reflected in guidance from the National Child Traumatic Stress Network and Winston’s Wish, a specialist childhood bereavement service. Both favor honest explanations adapted to the child’s understanding. They identify possible problems with secrecy, including confusion, accidental discovery and damage to trust. These are professional guidance documents, not comparative studies. NCTSN caregiver guide, Winston’s Wish: *Beyond the Rough Rock*.
For how to disclose, those services recommend:

off.li: Give a simple, truthful explanation, using words the child understands and avoiding unnecessary details.
Allow questions and check what the child understood.
Expect to return to the subject rather than treating disclosure as one completed conversation.
If an earlier explanation was incomplete or inaccurate, acknowledge that and explain again.

off.p: Winston’s Wish specifically addresses correcting an earlier account; it does not suggest that having delayed means the opportunity for an honest conversation has passed. *Beyond the Rough Rock*.

The NCTSN guide additionally recommends explicitly addressing guilt, acknowledging uncertainty about why the person died, and explaining that one family member’s suicide does not mean others will die that way. Mental illness should be discussed where appropriate, without inventing a diagnosis or presenting suicide as inevitable. NCTSN caregiver guide.

Taking your timeline as stated, your younger children are now approximately 13 and 11. The sources do not provide an evidence-based reason to wait until 18. Applying the specialist guidance to your circumstances would favor planning a supported, age-appropriate conversation now. Given the several suicide deaths in your family and the long interval, a clinician experienced in childhood suicide bereavement could help tailor the explanation and follow-up to each child. That is an application of professional guidance—not a claim that research has proved one disclosure age best.

on.p: There is published work specifically on telling children about a parent’s suicide, but the evidence on *when* to disclose is limited. I found no study establishing an optimal age, or demonstrating that waiting until 18 produces better outcomes. Specialist guidance generally favors truthful, developmentally appropriate explanations, with further discussion as children grow.
The distinction between research findings and clinical recommendations matters here.
The research most relevant to your question

on.li: Albert C. Cain (2002), *Children of Suicide: The Telling and the Knowing*. This is the most directly relevant paper I found. Cain reviews the limited disclosure literature and draws primarily on clinical and preventive work. He questions an absolute requirement to tell every child the whole truth immediately. He also distinguishes being *told* from understanding what happened, and examines how the surviving parent’s explanation of *why* the suicide occurred affects the child. It provides expert analysis, but does not establish a best disclosure age through a controlled comparison. Abstract and publication details.

Natalie C. Hung and Laura A. Rabin (2009), *Comprehending Childhood Bereavement by Parental Suicide*. This review covers quantitative and qualitative research, including communication about the suicide, stigma, and the surviving parent’s functioning. It describes substantial methodological gaps. It is useful background for understanding the family circumstances that influence bereavement; it does not supply a validated age threshold for disclosure. Abstract and publication details.

Julie Cerel and colleagues (1999), *Suicide-Bereaved Children and Adolescents: A Controlled Longitudinal Examination*. Researchers followed 26 suicide-bereaved children aged 5–17 and compared them with 332 children bereaved by other parental deaths, over approximately two years. The suicide-bereaved group experienced more anxiety, anger and shame. This comparison concerns the cause of death; it cannot establish whether early disclosure or delayed disclosure caused those outcomes. Study abstract.

on.p: Studies of children’s age when a parent dies also need to be distinguished from studies of their age when they learn the cause. They answer different questions.
The advantages and disadvantages of timing
The following considerations come from specialist clinical guidance. Their relative effects have not been quantified in a reliable early-versus-late disclosure comparison.

table: Gives the child a consistent explanation; provides opportunities to address self-blame; allows a trusted adult to explain before others do.
The information can be upsetting or misunderstood. Young children may need brief explanations repeated over time.
Waiting until the child is older
Greater maturity may help with understanding. A short delay can allow the caregiver to prepare and arrange support.
The child may learn elsewhere, develop frightening explanations, or later feel hurt about information being withheld. Waiting until adulthood has no established protective benefit.

on.p: These considerations are described in the National Child Traumatic Stress Network’s caregiver guide and Winston’s Wish’s specialist suicide-bereavement booklet. Your concern about your eldest finding out at school is explicitly recognized in that guidance.
How specialists recommend approaching disclosure

The guidance treats disclosure as an ongoing conversation. Ireland’s Health Service Executive describes staged explanations whose timing depends on the child’s needs and family circumstances. It recommends preparing what to say, using simple language, and allowing questions to set the pace. HSE guidance.

The NCTSN recommends giving basic facts, returning to questions over time, explicitly addressing blame, and acknowledging uncertainty about why the person died. It also recommends explaining that mental health problems can be treated and that another family member’s suicide does not mean the child will die that way. These are clinical recommendations informed by bereavement research. NCTSN guide.

For your younger children, now approximately 13 and 11, the available guidance supports planning a truthful conversation at their current level of understanding. Winston’s Wish specifically addresses revisiting an earlier explanation and acknowledging why fuller information was withheld. Given the multiple suicides in your family and the ten-year interval, a clinician experienced in childhood suicide bereavement could help you prepare the conversation and follow-up support. The evidence supports that individualized approach; it cannot retrospectively establish that one particular disclosure age would have been best for your children.

off.p: Chilled, soft fruit or cooked vegetables are good food-based options, provided your baby is ready for solids. At around six months, she should be able to sit upright with a steady head, bring food to her mouth, and swallow it. Mouthing everything alone doesn’t establish readiness. NHS feeding guidance
Try these preparations:

table: Peel a ripe banana and offer a long, soft piece. No cooking needed.
Wash, peel, remove the stone or core, and cut into finger-length slices. Cook pear if it is firm.
Peel, core, and steam or simmer until soft; then cool and refrigerate.
Peel and cook until soft throughout, then cool and offer finger-length sticks.

off.p: Pieces should be long enough to protrude from her fist and soft enough to squash easily between your fingers. Firm produce needs cooking; simply chilling it does not make it suitable. These preparations follow NHS first-food and food-safety guidance.

Avoid hard raw carrot or apple as teethers: pieces can break off and cause choking, even when an adult is watching. Also avoid whole grapes, nuts, and hard or chewy dried fruit. Have her seated upright in a high chair and stay within reach throughout. CDC choking guidance

Use the refrigerator for cooling. Don’t give food frozen solid directly to chew—it can hurt tender gums. If she isn’t ready for food, or simply wants something to gnaw on between meals, a clean, chilled damp washcloth or gentle gum massage with a clean finger is a useful alternative. American Academy of Pediatrics teething guidance

on.p: Soft, chilled foods are good options once your baby is ready for solids. At around six months, readiness includes holding her head steady while sitting upright, bringing food to her mouth, and swallowing it. Chewing her fists alone doesn’t establish readiness. NHS feeding guidance
Here are some practical choices:

table: Peel and offer a soft, finger-length piece, or mash it if she’s still learning to handle textures.
Wash, peel, remove the stone/core, and cut into soft finger-length slices. Cook firm pears first.
Peel, core, and steam or simmer slices until soft. Cool completely before serving.
Peel, cut into finger-length sticks, and steam or boil until easily mashed with a fork. Cool completely.

on.p: These are suitable first-food examples from the NHS. For cooked foods, the CDC recommends a texture soft enough to mash easily with a fork. You can refrigerate prepared portions for a cool sensation; keep them soft.

Avoid hard raw apple or carrot as teethers. Pieces can break off and cause choking. Whole grapes, whole nuts, and dried fruit are also choking hazards. Sit her upright in a high chair and stay within reach, watching throughout—even soft foods can cause choking. CDC choking guidance

For sore gums, avoid letting her chew directly on food frozen solid, which can hurt tender gums. If she hasn’t started solids yet, a clean, cool damp washcloth or gentle gum massage with a clean finger can provide relief. American Academy of Pediatrics teething advice

off.p: That sounds tiring, especially when you’ve worked hard to be consistent. You can keep the “no” and still comfort her. At five, she may need help managing disappointment; crying alone doesn’t mean she is deliberately trying to change your answer. Calm support can help children learn to regulate their feelings. Child Mind Institute
Try using the same short response each time:
> “You really wanted that, and you’re disappointed. The answer is still no. I’m here if you want a hug.”
Then give her time. Avoid repeated explanations, bargaining, or asking her to think differently while she’s upset. You don’t need to make the tears stop before continuing your day.
A few changes may help:

off.li: Make the goal recovery, rather than no crying. She can feel sad and still accept the limit. If she hits or throws things, set a separate boundary: “You can be upset. I won’t let you hit.”
Offer a calming space instead of sending her away for crying. She might choose to sit beside you or take some quiet time nearby.

Practice when she’s calm. Use toys to act out disappointment and rehearse one simple response: “I’m disappointed,” followed by slow breathing or asking for a hug. Notice specific progress: “You were upset and then found something else to do.” Guidance on teaching self-regulation

Look for patterns. Hunger, tiredness, and transitions can make small disappointments harder. Offer choices within the boundary when appropriate: “We’re leaving the park. Would you like to walk or hold my hand?” American Academy of Pediatrics

off.p: I’d drop the comparisons with her friends and “no big deal” language. Something can feel like a big deal to her even when your limit is reasonable.

Brief tears followed by recovery are different from prolonged, intense episodes. If these reactions regularly disrupt school, friendships, or family activities—or involve aggression or difficulty recovering—discuss them with her pediatrician. When to seek help
How long does she usually cry, and does this happen at school too?

on.p: That sounds tiring, especially when even small requests end in tears. At five, children are still learning to handle disappointment. You can keep the “no” and help her through the feeling. Naming emotions and offering calm support can help children develop that skill. Child Mind Institute
I’d try a consistent response:

on.li: State the limit briefly. “We’re not buying a toy today.”
Acknowledge the disappointment. “You really wanted it. You’re disappointed.”
Offer quiet support. “I’m here. Would you like a hug?” Let her cry, keep your answer consistent, and pause the discussion until she settles.

on.p: I’d stop sending her to her room solely for crying. Offer a quiet space if she wants one, and remain available. Save conversations about coping for when she’s calm; children who are overwhelmed often need time and support before they can problem-solve. CDC guidance

At a calm moment, practice one small coping skill together: three slow breaths, asking for a hug, or saying, “I’m disappointed.” You could use stuffed animals to rehearse hearing “no.” Notice specific progress: “You were upset, and you took a breath and joined us again.” Shorter episodes and easier recovery are useful signs of progress. Child Mind Institute
I’d also drop the comparisons with friends. Focus on what helps *her*. Notice whether hunger, tiredness, or transitions make the crying more likely.
If episodes are prolonged, worsening, involve aggression, or disrupt school and family activities, discuss them with her pediatrician.
One detail would help tailor this: does she cry briefly and then move on, or stay distressed for a long time?

off.p: It may help to frame this as asking them to care for you in a different way. If withholding painful news has long been their way of protecting you, they may need reassurance that sharing it can also be an act of care.
Choose a calm moment, rather than waiting until someone is seriously ill or has died. You could say:

> “I know you’ve kept difficult news from me because you love me and don’t want me to worry. But being far away, finding out later makes me feel more alone and less able to support you. I’d like you to tell me when someone is ill or dies, even when it’s upsetting. You don’t have to make it easier for me before telling me.”
A few things can make that request easier for them to act on:

off.li: Ask for something specific. “Please tell me when a relative goes into hospital or gets a serious diagnosis” is clearer than “You can talk to me about anything.” You can ask for a brief update first, with details later.

Ask what makes sharing difficult. They may worry about upsetting you, disrupting your work, or leaving you feeling helpless at a distance. Understanding their concern gives you something concrete to address.
Make room for uncertainty. Tell them they can say, “We don’t know much yet.” They needn’t wait until they have a full explanation.

Show that sharing is welcome. When they do tell you something painful, try to begin with “Thank you for telling me,” rather than “Why didn’t you tell me sooner?” You can discuss delays afterward. You don’t have to hide your sadness to prove you can handle the news.

off.p: With the distance and time difference, agree on a simple communication routine: a regular call with room to ask how they and their friends are doing, plus a way to share important news between calls. For example:
> “For news that can wait, send me a message and we’ll arrange a call. If someone has died or something urgent happens, it’s okay to call outside our usual time.”
Tell them explicitly whether waking you is okay; don’t leave them guessing.

You might also separate two conversations: keeping you informed about other people’s illnesses and deaths, and talking about their own wishes as they get older. The second may feel much more threatening and deserves its own time.

Expect this to take more than one conversation. A useful first goal is simply: “Next time something happens, please let me know.” Small experiences of telling you—and feeling supported afterward—may persuade them more than one big discussion.

on.p: Make a specific request to be included in difficult family news, and explain what knowing allows you to do. You can acknowledge their wish to protect you while telling them what you need now.
For example:

> “I know you’ve tried to spare me painful news because you care about me. I want you to tell me when someone in the family is seriously ill or has died. These people matter to me, and knowing gives me a chance to contact them, support you, and decide whether to visit. I may be upset, but I want to share that part of family life.”

If finding out late has hurt you, give one concrete example and describe its effect: “When I learned about Aunt Jane’s illness afterward, I felt left out, and I wished I’d had a chance to call her.” Keep the focus on what you want to happen next.
Then ask what makes telling you difficult:
> “What worries you about sharing this kind of news with me?”

Their answer may reveal a concern you can address—for example, that you’ll feel helpless so far away, lose sleep, or feel obliged to travel. Listen before offering reassurance. You can say, “You can tell me what’s happened, and I can decide what I’m able to do.”
A few practical steps may help:

on.li: Start with a particular person or event. “How is Uncle David doing?” is a manageable opening. Follow with “How are you feeling about it?” if they seem willing.
Respond warmly when they share something. “Thank you for telling me. I’m glad you called.” Let them see that telling you leads to connection.
Allow some sadness. You don’t have to demonstrate that bad news leaves you untouched. “This is upsetting, and I’m glad I know” communicates both your feelings and your preference.

Return to the request gently. A longstanding family habit may take several conversations to change. Hospice UK also recommends giving people time and allowing difficult conversations to happen in stages. Talking about dying

on.p: For the distance, make contact predictable and agree on how important news should reach you:

on.li: Arrange a regular call at a time when everyone has privacy and enough time to talk.
Send a short message beforehand: “On Sunday, I’d like to talk about how we keep each other informed when someone is ill.”
Offer an asynchronous option: “If saying it on a call feels difficult, you can email or message me.”
Agree that urgent news can interrupt the usual schedule: “For a serious illness or death, please contact me as soon as you can. If I’m asleep, leave a message asking me to call.”

on.p: You can also be explicit about the value of sharing ordinary updates: “I’d like to hear how you’re coping, even when there’s nothing I can do from here.”
You can’t guarantee their openness. You can make your preference clear, make sharing easier, and show through your responses that you welcome their trust.

off.p: At three, start with one specific action and a reward soon afterward. “Behave well for a while” asks him to track time, remember earlier behavior, and control his emotions—all skills he is still developing. A clearer explanation alone may not solve that mismatch.
You can teach earning and waiting in small steps:

off.li: Define what earns the reward beforehand. “First we put the blocks in the basket, then we watch your show.” Help him get started. Avoid “if you’re good,” which leaves him guessing about what counts.

Reward the action promptly and name it. “You put your blocks away! Now it’s time for the show.” Specific praise and immediate rewards help young children connect their actions to the outcome. CDC guidance

Practice waiting separately, when he is calm. Start with a few seconds during an ordinary activity: “Your turn after I finish mine.” Gradually lengthen the wait as he succeeds. Make the endpoint visible and predictable.
Teach a replacement for yelling. Practice “Help, please,” or “I’m frustrated,” together. Notice and praise attempts, including when he needs prompting.

off.p: When he says, “I’ll behave,” you can answer with something he can actually do:
> “You want your show. First the blocks go in the basket. I’ll help.”
If he melts down, keep the explanation short:
> “You’re upset because you want it now. I’m here. We can put the blocks away when you’re ready.”

Keep the agreed boundary, keep everyone safe, and offer help calming down. Save teaching and discussion for afterward; tantrums are common at this age, and calm, consistent responses are more useful than arguing through them. American Academy of Pediatrics guidance
Once he completes the agreed task, honor the reward. Avoid extending the requirement because he protested along the way. Otherwise, the finish line becomes unpredictable.

For now, replace “you’ve been a terror today, so no TV” with several small, clear opportunities to succeed. Over time, those experiences give him the foundation for earning rewards over longer periods.

on.p: At three, start with one specific action and a reward that follows soon afterward. “Behave well for a while” asks him to understand an unclear time period, remember several rules, and control his impulses throughout it. That is a demanding starting point. The CDC recommends simple, achievable behaviors and immediate rewards for toddlers and preschoolers. CDC guidance
Your observation about the catch-22 is useful: he needs to see exactly how he can succeed.
Try this approach:

on.li: Set the rule beforehand: “First put the blocks in the box, then we can watch one episode.”
Make the task manageable: “You put these three blocks away; I’ll help with the others.”
When he says, “I’ll behave,” give him the next action: “You can start now. These blocks go in the box.”
Follow through when he finishes: “You put the blocks away. Now it’s time for your show.”

on.p: That gives him practice earning something through an action. Avoid adding new requirements once he has completed the agreed task. If you use stickers, give each sticker immediately and let him keep earned stickers even after a later difficult moment. CDC reward guidance

Practice waiting separately, in tiny steps. When he is calm, try: “I’ll blow more bubbles after we count to five.” Help him count, then deliver. As that becomes easy, gradually lengthen the wait. The exact starting time should fit what he can already manage; repeated successes give you something to build on.

For frustration, teach an action he can use: “Say ‘Help, please,’” or “Come get me when it’s hard.” Notice attempts: “You were frustrated and asked me for help.” Expect him to need reminders and help calming down.
During a tantrum, keep your words brief:
> “You really want the show. First the blocks go away. I’m here to help.”

Keep the limit steady, allow disappointment, and stop hitting or other unsafe behavior. Save explanations for when he is calm. Tantrums are common at this age, and calm, consistent responses help. American Academy of Pediatrics guidance

For now, I would drop “good behavior over a period of time” as the condition for television. Give him frequent, clear opportunities to complete a small task, experience success, and try again after a difficult moment.

off.p: I’d try an activated-carbon filter inside the pail, preferably one designed for your model. For example, Diaper Genie carbon filters fit the Complete, Deluxe and Platinum pails; the manufacturer recommends replacing them every 30 days. Treat it as extra odor control, rather than a complete fix.

The biggest clue is “jamming the lid open.” Empty the liner *before* diapers interfere with the lid or internal closure—even if the bag has space left. An absorber beside the pail is unlikely to keep up with odor continually escaping.
I’d also:

off.li: Check that the liner isn’t caught in the closure and that the lid seals fully.
Clean around the lid, seals and bag opening according to your pail’s instructions.
Take especially smelly diapers straight to the outside trash, or empty the pail daily for a few days to see whether that solves it.

off.p: My first move would be earlier emptying, then a compatible carbon filter. Keep any odor-absorbing product out of your toddler’s reach.

on.p: I’d try an unscented activated-carbon filter made for your pail. If you have a Diaper Genie Complete, Deluxe, or Platinum, its carbon filters fit inside the lid; the manufacturer recommends replacing them every 30 days. Treat it as an extra layer of odor control.

The detail that stands out is waiting until the diapers jam the lid open. Empty it while the lid can still close fully, and try taking out poopy diapers daily for a week. A room that smells even with the pail closed suggests escaping odor or residue around the closure.
Also check the lid, seal, and liner seating, and clean according to your model’s instructions. Cleaning guidance varies: Ubbi specifies wiping its pail with a dry cloth.
For especially smelly diapers, tie each in a small disposal bag and take it straight to the outside trash. Keep spare bags and odor absorbers out of your toddler’s reach.

off.p: There are daily nutrient reference values for 10-month-olds, but no universal daily cheese allowance. Cheese can be part of her diet; the amount needs to fit alongside her milk feeds and other foods.
For the numbers you’re looking for, Health Canada’s nutrient reference tables give these values for babies aged 7–12 months:

table: 11 g, or about 1.2 g per kg of body weight

off.p: These include breast milk or formula plus solid food. Protein is a recommended dietary allowance; carbohydrate and fat are “adequate intakes,” estimates used where evidence is insufficient to establish an RDA. They are average intake guides, not strict daily quotas or maximum limits.
For the other nutrients you mentioned:

off.li: Added sugar: avoid it. This does not mean avoiding naturally occurring sugars in milk or whole fruit. CDC guidance
Saturated fat: there is no established infant allowance in grams. The familiar limit of less than 10% of calories does not apply below age 2. US dietary guidance
Salt: UK guidance recommends less than 1 g daily under age 1, including salt already present in foods—approximately 400 mg sodium. NHS salt guidance

off.p: For cheese specifically: choose pasteurised, full-fat cheese and lower-salt varieties. Full-fat dairy is appropriate at this age. Offer cheese as one part of a varied diet, alongside iron-rich foods such as meat, beans, lentils or fortified infant cereal. The NHS guide for 10–12 months recommends three meals daily plus usual milk feeds, with vegetables, fruit, starchy foods, protein foods and dairy.

To assess the amount she currently eats, the useful details are which cheese, roughly how many grams, and her usual milk feeds and other meals. Her paediatrician or health visitor can review those together with her growth; the nutrient table alone cannot establish a suitable cheese portion.

on.p: There are daily nutrient reference values for this age, but no universal daily cheese allowance. Two useful resources are Health Canada’s nutrient tables and the NHS feeding guide for 10–12 months.
For healthy babies aged 7–12 months, the US/Canadian reference values are:

These totals include breast milk or formula and all solid foods. Protein has a recommended dietary allowance; carbohydrate and fat have “adequate intake” estimates. These are nutritional reference values, not maximum limits or exact amounts your baby must eat every day. Health Canada’s macronutrient table
For the other nutrients you mentioned:

on.li: Added sugar: Avoid it at this age. Naturally occurring sugars in milk and whole fruit are a different category. CDC guidance

Saturated fat: There is no established daily gram allowance for infants. Full-fat dairy is recommended for young children because they need its energy and nutrients. FDA explanation, NHS dairy guidance
Salt: UK guidance recommends less than 1 g of salt daily, equivalent to about 400 mg sodium, for babies under one. That includes salt already present in food and milk. NHS infant feeding leaflet

on.p: For cheese specifically: Pasteurised, full-fat cheese is suitable from around six months; choose lower-salt varieties. Offer it as part of a varied diet, with regular iron-rich foods and continued breast milk or formula. At 10 months, NHS guidance recommends three meals daily alongside milk feeds, with portions guided by hunger and fullness. NHS feeding guidance

To assess your daughter’s cheese intake, the useful details are the type of cheese, roughly how many grams she eats daily, and her usual milk and other foods. A paediatrician or paediatric dietitian can use those details and her growth pattern to advise on an appropriate amount.

off.p: At one month, a fixed, repeatable timetable isn’t necessary. A gentle rhythm can help, but responding to his hunger, tiredness and need for comfort matters more. His day–night pattern is still developing, so variable naps and unsettled evenings are expected. NHS sleep guidance
He can notice light, noise, handling and familiar soothing cues at this age. That doesn’t mean he needs every feed and sleep to happen at the same time or in the same cot.

Your observation about outings is plausible: extra stimulation, tiredness or changes in feeding could make settling harder. But it doesn’t establish that a disrupted routine is the cause—evening fussiness is common at this age, including on quiet days. NHS guidance on crying
A practical approach is to:

off.li: Continue ordinary outings, making room for feeds and sleep as he needs them.
Follow hunger and sleepy cues rather than delaying either to preserve the cycle.
Keep evenings calm, with dim lights, quiet voices and a familiar cuddle or song.
If outings consistently precede difficult evenings, try shorter trips or a quieter period afterwards and see whether it helps.

off.p: These fit guidance to respond to newborn cues and gradually introduce the difference between day and night. AAP newborn guidance, NHS sleep guidance

Two details relevant to your setup: if “seven cycles” means only seven breastfeeds in 24 hours, that is below the usual 8–12; check with your midwife or health visitor, particularly if weight gain or wet nappies are a concern. Also, transfer him from the car seat to a firm, flat sleep surface when you arrive. For all sleeps, place him on his back and keep his cot or Moses basket in the same room as a caregiver for the first six months, including daytime naps. AAP feeding guidance, NHS crying guidance, NHS safe sleep guidance

on.p: At one month, a gentle, repeatable pattern can help, but a fixed timetable isn’t necessary. His sleep pattern is still developing. The priority is responding to hunger, tiredness and the need for comfort. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends following newborns’ cues and helping them settle before they become overtired.

He can respond to his surroundings at this age, and you can begin helping him learn the difference between day and night. Daylight and normal household activity during the day, followed by dim lights and quiet care at night, provide useful cues. A short, familiar settling sequence can also help. Expect the timing to vary. NHS sleep guidance

Your observation about outings is plausible: tiredness or extra stimulation could contribute to a harder evening. However, evening fussiness is also common at this age, so the pattern alone doesn’t establish the cause. You could jot down feeds, naps and crying for a few days and try shorter outings or a quieter period afterwards. NHS crying guidance
Practically:

on.li: Feed when he shows hunger cues, including while you’re out.
Offer sleep when he seems tired, even if that changes the usual sequence.
Keep a familiar way of comforting him wherever you are.

on.p: One detail to check: if “seven cycles” means seven breastfeeds in 24 hours, that is below the usual 8–12 feeds cited by the AAP. Ask your health visitor or clinician whether his feeding frequency and weight gain are appropriate, especially before encouraging longer overnight stretches. Bottle-fed babies may feed less frequently. AAP feeding guidance

For sleep on outings, transfer him from the car seat to a firm, flat sleep surface when you arrive. Place him on his back, keep the sleep space clear, and have him in the same room as you for daytime and nighttime sleep during the first six months. Your downstairs cot and bedroom Moses basket can fit that guidance. NHS safer sleep advice

off.p: Use thin, warm layers under the car-seat harness, and add the bulky warmth over it. Your clothes-and-blankets approach was sensible, provided the blankets went over the buckled harness.
A thick snowsuit can compress during a crash, leaving the harness dangerously loose—even if you managed to buckle it. A bigger seat doesn’t solve that problem. American Academy of Pediatrics guidance
For everyday trips:

off.li: If you carry him in a removable infant seat: buckle him indoors wearing snug layers, then add a blanket over the harness. Carry the seat to the car and into the building with the blanket in place and his face uncovered. Use this approach only while he remains within the seat’s size limits.

If the seat stays in the car: carry him outside wrapped in a blanket or wearing his coat. Remove the bulky layer before buckling, then place it over the secured harness. At your destination, unbuckle him and wrap him up or put his coat on before carrying him inside.
For a longer walk: put on his outdoor coat or snowsuit after unbuckling. Allow more protection for wind, wet weather and extreme cold than for a quick doorway-to-car transfer.

off.p: A bodysuit, trousers, sweater or thin fleece, plus a hat, mittens and warm socks or booties, makes a practical starting outfit. Young children generally need about one more layer than an adult in the same conditions. AAP cold-weather guidance

You don’t need a special snowsuit-and-seat combination. Avoid padded inserts or bunting that goes beneath him or between him and the harness; follow the seat manufacturer’s accessory instructions. Remove extra blankets as the car warms up.
You’re right to keep him warm—the useful adjustment is making the warm outer layer easy to add for the walk and remove for buckling.

on.p: Thin, warm layers under the car-seat harness, with a blanket over the buckled harness, are the usual solution. Your approach of clothing plus blankets can work well—as long as the blankets go on after he is strapped in.

Avoid bulky snowsuits or puffy coats under the harness. Their padding compresses in a crash, leaving the straps dangerously loose, even when they seemed snug before. A larger car seat doesn’t solve that problem. NHTSA’s winter car-seat guidance
For everyday trips, you have two practical options:

on.li: If you carry him in a removable infant car seat: Keep the seat indoors before departure. Dress him in close-fitting clothing, a thin fleece layer, a hat, mittens, and socks or booties. Buckle him indoors, tighten the harness, then tuck a blanket over him for the walk to the car. Keep his face uncovered. At your destination, carry the seat inside with the blanket still over him.

If the seat stays in the car: Carry him to the car wearing his coat, or wrapped in a blanket with a secure hold. Remove the bulky outer layer, buckle him in, then place the blanket or coat over the harness. At your destination, unbuckle him and put his coat on or wrap him before stepping outside.

on.p: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends thin layers, blankets over the harness, and removing outer coverings as the car warms up. Avoid padded inserts or bunting that goes beneath him or between him and the straps; follow your seat manufacturer’s instructions for accessories. AAP winter safety tips

Wanting to keep him warm is reasonable. Dress for the temperature, wind, and length of the outdoor walk. A short transfer needs less insulation than an extended walk or outdoor play. For longer exposure, put his full outdoor clothing on before leaving the car. One additional layer compared with a comfortable adult is a useful starting point. AAP cold-weather guidance
At around a year old, also check that he still fits the removable seat’s height and weight limits. Keep him rear-facing within his seat’s limits. NHTSA rear-facing guidance

off.p: Yes, a book that feels persistently too difficult can be discouraging—but I wouldn’t assume that one challenging birthday gift will put her off science. How she gets to explore it matters.

There are two separate difficulties: reading the words and understanding the ideas. A book she cannot yet read independently may still be enjoyable with an adult reading and explaining it. Reading Rockets explicitly recommends sharing challenging books this way.
For the picture-and-fact format you describe, my suggestion would be to make it an invitation to browse:

off.li: Let her choose a picture or page that catches her eye.
Read short bits together and follow her questions.
Let her skip anything confusing or uninteresting.
Avoid expecting her to finish it, remember facts, or answer quizzes correctly.

off.p: You could introduce it with: “I thought these pictures and experiments looked fun. We can explore whichever bits you like.” If she enjoys one page about senses and leaves the genetics for another year, that is still a successful gift.

Your elephant analogy captures a reasonable concern about repeated frustration, but it doesn’t establish that encountering something difficult once will create lasting avoidance. The practical safeguard is to let her get help, change pages, or stop. That fits Institute of Education Sciences guidance to keep reading activities positive and set aside those that cause frustration.

I’d be comfortable giving it if she already shows curiosity about bodies or how things work, especially alongside some time exploring it together. If almost every page needs a lengthy explanation before anything becomes interesting, I’d choose something simpler for now.

on.p: Yes, a book that is too difficult can be discouraging, especially if a child feels expected to understand it all. I’d still consider this a reasonable gift if she’s curious about bodies and you can explore it together.

There are two kinds of difficulty here: reading the words and understanding the ideas. An adult reading aloud can help with the first and explain the second. Children can often understand more complex language when listening than when reading independently, which is one reason the Children’s Literacy Initiative recommends sharing books above their independent reading level.

With the picture-and-fact format you describe, she can enjoy a picture or discover one interesting fact on a page even if the explanation of genes is beyond her for now. She can return to those pages later.
I’d introduce it something like this: “I thought you might enjoy the pictures and some of the things in here. Let’s see what catches your eye.”
Then:

on.li: Let her choose pages and skip freely.
Read difficult passages aloud and explain them briefly when she asks.
Follow her questions; avoid turning browsing into a quiz.
Put it aside if she becomes frustrated or loses interest.
If she says “I’m bad at this,” acknowledge the difficulty: “That explanation uses lots of new words. We can explore it together.”

on.p: Your elephant analogy captures a reasonable concern about repeated experiences of failure. But it doesn’t establish that receiving one challenging book will make her give up on the subject. She has much more control if she can ask for help, choose an easier page, or stop.

My recommendation would be to give it as something to browse together, provided some pages seem immediately enjoyable to her. Her parents can help judge that from her current interests and the books she already likes.

off.p: You don’t need to buy another booster just because the babysitter’s car lacks LATCH. Graco’s AFFIX manual permits use without the lower anchors: “If AFFIX booster is not connected to vehicle anchors, secure the booster seat with the lap/shoulder belt.” (Graco manual, p. 8)

In this booster, the vehicle’s lap-and-shoulder belt restrains your child. LATCH secures the booster itself and helps keep it positioned for buckling. Using the AFFIX without LATCH is an intended configuration; having unused LATCH connectors does not inherently make it less safe than a booster manufactured without them. That doesn’t mean every booster offers identical crash performance. (Graco manual, p. 27)
Before using it in the babysitter’s car, check:

off.li: There’s a lap-and-shoulder belt, not a lap-only belt.
The belt fits low across your child’s hips/upper thighs and across the shoulder and chest, following the AFFIX routing instructions.
The vehicle seatback or head restraint supports your child’s head; Graco requires the tops of their ears to be below its top.
Buckle the empty booster in, or remove it, when your child isn’t riding so it cannot become a projectile. (Graco manual, NHTSA guidance)

off.p: Follow the manual matching your seat’s model and manufacture date, and show the babysitter the correct belt routing.

on.p: You can use your Graco AFFIX without LATCH; you don’t need to buy another booster solely because the babysitter’s car lacks it. Graco’s AFFIX manual, page 8 explicitly allows use without the vehicle anchors.

In this booster, the vehicle’s lap-and-shoulder belt restrains your child. The LATCH connectors secure the booster itself to the vehicle seat. Using the AFFIX with its connectors unused is an approved configuration, much like using a booster that has no connectors. That doesn’t establish identical crash performance between different booster models, but unused LATCH connectors alone are no reason to replace it. Graco manual, page 27
Check these points in the babysitter’s car:

on.li: Use a lap-and-shoulder belt. A lap-only belt is unsafe with this booster.

Check belt fit and routing: the lap belt should sit low and snug across the hips/upper thighs, and the shoulder belt across the shoulder and chest. Follow your seat’s manual for routing and its shoulder-belt positioning clip.
Check head support: a backless booster requires a vehicle seatback or head restraint that adequately supports your child’s head.
Buckle the empty booster in, or remove it. With LATCH unused, it needs securing even when your child isn’t riding.

on.p: These requirements come from Graco’s instructions and NHTSA’s booster guidance. Show the babysitter the correct belt routing and check the fit with your child seated before the first trip.

off.p: Please contact his pediatrician today about the excessive thirst, and stop putting food into his mouth against his will. Near-total food refusal with gagging and distress deserves assessment rather than being treated as ordinary picky eating.

Drinking unusually large amounts can be a sign of type 1 diabetes, particularly with more frequent urination or heavier diapers, weight loss, or tiredness. This does not mean he has diabetes, but a clinician should check promptly and may test his blood glucose and urine. If he also has vomiting unrelated to forced feeding, abdominal pain, unusual sleepiness, or fast/deep breathing, seek emergency care immediately. NHS guidance

Until he is assessed, keep water available; do not restrict it to make him eat. Record how much water and milk he drinks over 24 hours, including nighttime bottles, and note urination and any weight changes. Do not delay the appointment to collect this information.
For feeding, the aim is to make eating feel safe again:

off.li: Stop force-feeding, including the first bite. Pressure can worsen food refusal. Gagging may reflect fear, discomfort, or difficulty managing textures; it should not be assumed to be deliberate misbehavior.
Offer three small meals and two planned snacks, rather than waiting until he is extremely hungry. Sit together and let him feed himself, with supervision.
Offer tiny portions of soft, safely prepared foods—such as yogurt, porridge, soft rice, scrambled egg, or banana—alongside family food. He may need easier textures before eating your usual meals.
