Let him touch, smell, or taste food without requiring a bite. End calmly when he is done, and offer it again another day. You choose what and when to offer; he chooses whether and how much to eat. AAP feeding advice

off.p: Ask the pediatrician to review his growth and nutrition, possible pain or constipation, and chewing/swallowing skills. A pediatric feeding therapist and dietitian may help with persistent refusal and gagging. NHS feeding guidance

Milk can suppress appetite, and excessive cow’s milk can contribute to iron deficiency. General guidance is about 473–750 mL (16–24 ounces) daily, but because he currently relies on milk, do not abruptly remove his main calorie source or try to “wait him out.” Arrange an individual nutrition plan. AAP milk guidance

To loosen the bedtime attachment, gradually move milk earlier in the routine, practice offering it in an open or straw cup, then brush his teeth and use cuddles, stories, or songs for settling. Avoid leaving a milk bottle in bed. Coordinate reductions with his clinician so his nutrition remains adequate. AAP bottle-weaning guidance

on.p: Please arrange a pediatric assessment today because of the excessive thirst and very limited eating. Unusual thirst can be a sign of diabetes, particularly with frequent urination, very wet diapers, tiredness, or weight loss. A clinician can check his blood glucose and urine. Avoid restricting his water while awaiting assessment. NHS guidance

Seek emergency care now if the thirst is accompanied by repeated vomiting, abdominal pain, fast or deep breathing, or unusual sleepiness. These can signal a serious diabetes complication. NHS guidance

Stop putting food into his mouth by force, including the first bite. Pressure can worsen food refusal, and feeding while he is crying or resisting can be unsafe. Gagging is a distress signal; it does not establish that he is deliberately trying to vomit.

Persistent refusal and gagging deserve a feeding assessment. Ask his pediatrician to review his growth and nutrition and consider referral to a pediatric feeding specialist, such as a speech-language therapist trained in feeding and swallowing. Feeding therapy can help with chewing, texture tolerance, and comfortable eating. ASHA guidance
Meanwhile, try these steps:

on.li: Offer three small meals and two planned snacks at predictable times. Eat together and let him feed himself while seated upright.
Offer tiny portions of soft, safely prepared foods, including something he has previously accepted. Let him touch or taste them at his own pace.
You choose what and when to offer; he chooses whether and how much to eat. End the meal calmly when he becomes distressed.

Measure his milk intake. Large amounts can reduce appetite. General toddler guidance limits milk to about 16–24 ounces (475–710 mL) daily, but because he currently eats so little, agree on a nutrition plan before substantially reducing his main calorie source. American Academy of Pediatrics guidance

on.p: For the bottle attachment, start practicing with a straw or open cup during the day. Gradually move the evening milk earlier, then follow it with toothbrushing, a story, and cuddles. Use that predictable routine to help him settle. Milk bottles during sleep increase tooth-decay risk. Coordinate bottle removal with his clinician so he continues getting adequate nutrition. AAP bottle-transition guidance

Approximately how much milk and water does he drink in 24 hours, how long has this been happening, and is he urinating more or losing weight? These details will help the clinician; please seek assessment while gathering them.

off.p: That sounds tiring, especially when you’re already holding and comforting him. You can work toward a calmer bedtime while continuing to rock or pat him. His crying alone doesn’t tell us whether he’s itchy, overtired, not sleepy yet, or finding the transition difficult.

Start with his physical comfort. Eczema itching can interfere with sleep, so arrange a review with his pediatrician if it is still troublesome despite treatment. Follow his prescribed skin-care plan, include moisturiser in the evening routine, and avoid overheating or irritating clothing. Sleep disruption is a reason to reassess eczema treatment. NHS eczema guidance
Try the following consistently over the next week or two:

off.li: Make the last 30 minutes predictable. Dim the lights, stop active play and screens, then use the same short sequence: skin care, pyjamas, teeth, one book, a song and cuddles. Start winding down about 30 minutes before he *usually falls asleep*, rather than spending a long time trying to make him sleep earlier. Once settling improves, move the routine earlier gradually if needed. NHS bedtime guidance

Offer a cuddle without making him stay still. If “holding firm” means restraining him while he struggles, ease off. Support him securely, but let him change position. If he pushes away, try sitting beside his cot with a gentle hand or quiet voice. Some movement before sleep is okay; he doesn’t have to lie motionless to settle.

Respond to escalating distress with a brief reset. Pick him up if that helps, check for itching or discomfort, and offer a quiet cuddle before trying again. Keep the lights low and avoid restarting play. You can continue rocking him to sleep if that suits you—independent sleep does not have to be the immediate goal.

Check the timing. For several days, note naps, when the routine starts, when he actually falls asleep, and whether he scratches. If he’s already tearful and exhausted before bedtime, try starting 10–15 minutes earlier. If he’s happily active for a long time, bedtime or a late nap may need adjusting. Change one thing at a time.

off.p: Judge progress by whether he seems more relaxed and needs less effort to settle, rather than expecting no tears immediately.

Seek prompt medical advice if his eczema becomes painful, hot, swollen, blistered or oozing, particularly with fever. If bedtime distress persists after his skin is comfortable and the routine is consistent, ask his pediatrician to check for other sources of discomfort. NHS guidance

on.p: That sounds exhausting, especially when you’re happy to comfort him and he still seems distressed. I’d start with his skin comfort, then adjust the bedtime routine and timing. Crying alone cannot tell you whether he’s itchy, uncomfortable, or struggling to settle.

on.li: Have his eczema treatment reviewed. Tell his pediatrician or dermatologist specifically about the nightly crying and sleep difficulty. Eczema itching can delay sleep and cause night waking, and his treatment plan may need adjusting. Follow his prescribed skin care, keep him comfortably cool, and use loose, soft sleepwear. American Academy of Dermatology guidance

Use a short, predictable wind-down. Start about 30 minutes before he usually falls asleep. For example: prescribed skin care, pajamas, brush teeth, one book, then a quiet song and cuddle. Dim the lights and keep active play and screens out of this period. Repeat the same sequence each night so he can learn what comes next. NHS bedtime guidance

Match bedtime to when he can actually fall asleep. For several days, note his naps, when you start settling him, when he falls asleep, and whether he scratches or seems uncomfortable. If he consistently stays awake until a particular time, begin the routine shortly before that time. Once settling becomes easier, gradually move it earlier if needed. Keep morning waking and naps reasonably consistent. NHS guidance

Offer comfort that allows him to move. You can keep rocking or patting if it helps. If “holding firm” means restraining his arms or body while he struggles, stop using that to make him sleep. Try a relaxed cuddle; if he pushes away, let him change position in a safe cot while you stay nearby and speak softly. If distress escalates, pause to check his comfort and soothe him before trying again. Avoid pressing him down or restricting his breathing.

on.p: Aim first for a calmer bedtime. You can work on reducing rocking later, if you want to. Give a consistent routine several nights, while responding to signs of discomfort.
Seek prompt medical care if his eczema becomes painful, hot, swollen, blistered or oozing, particularly with fever or illness. NHS eczema guidance
What time does he wake in the morning, when and how long does he nap, and when do you start bedtime? Those details would help judge whether timing is contributing.

off.p: At 2 years old, it’s normal not to understand “yesterday,” “today,” and “tomorrow” reliably. Understanding time develops gradually; using the words can come before understanding their meaning.
A rough guide is:

off.li: Around 2–3: Children begin using time words and understanding simple sequences—something happened already, or something comes next. “Yesterday” may mean almost any past event, and “tomorrow” may mean any future event.

Around 3–4: Some understand yesterday and tomorrow when connected to their own experiences—for example, yesterday’s visit to Grandma or tomorrow’s outing. A recent study found this understanding in 3-year-olds, although abstract questions were harder. Child Development study

Through the preschool and early school years: Understanding becomes more consistent, including that tomorrow becomes today, and today becomes yesterday. The precise meaning of “exactly one day ago/from now” can take longer to master. These are broad ranges, not deadlines. Research on learning time words

off.p: Recognizing that life moves through routines comes before understanding days as calendar units. Your child may anticipate meals, bedtime, or a familiar outing without yet understanding how many days have passed.
For now, make time concrete:

off.li: “First we eat, then we go outside.”
“Yesterday we went to the park. Today we’re staying home.”
“Tomorrow, after your nighttime sleep, we’ll see Grandma.”

off.p: Use these naturally alongside familiar events, without expecting correct answers or testing them. At this age, mixing up the words is expected.

on.p: At 2 years old, it is normal for a child to have only a partial understanding of “today,” “yesterday,” and “tomorrow.” Understanding develops gradually, and children often start saying these words before they understand their meanings accurately. Developmental research review
A rough guide is:

table: Begins using time words and distinguishing some things that happened from things that will happen. “Yesterday” and “tomorrow” are often used loosely.
Increasingly understands that yesterday is in the past and tomorrow is in the future. Correct use remains inconsistent.
Becomes more precise about which day an event happened and how days relate to each other. Understanding continues to improve through the early school years.

on.p: These are broad ranges. Research finds that performance depends on the language a child speaks and how the question is asked. Understanding that “tomorrow is in the future” develops earlier than consistently understanding “tomorrow is exactly the next day.” Study of children aged 3–7

For “Do they understand that days are passing?”, the understanding emerges in pieces: remembering an event, anticipating another event, and learning how those events fit into successive days. A 2-year-old may remember a visit or anticipate a familiar activity while still being unsure which day it belongs to.
You can help by connecting time words to concrete experiences:

on.li: “Yesterday we went to the park.”
“Today we’re going shopping.”
“Tomorrow, after your sleep tonight, Grandma will visit.”

on.p: For immediate plans, try “After lunch, we’ll go outside.” As your child gets older, a simple picture calendar can make successive days easier to discuss.
Confusing these words at age 2 is expected. Keep using them naturally; accurate understanding develops over the next several years.

off.p: Having your own fears go unnoticed sounds painful. Your experience may help you notice a child’s distress, while leaving room for their experience to differ from yours.
The most helpful thing is repeated, dependable care over time. A child may hear “you’re safe here” long before they can feel it. You can help by:

off.li: Making daily life predictable. Keep routines for meals, school and bedtime. Explain who will care for them, when you’ll return and any changes in plans. Keep small promises.

Allowing feelings without demanding explanations. Try: “It makes sense that you’re worried after having to move before. You haven’t done anything wrong.” Offer conversation, play or quiet company without pressing them to tell their story.

Staying caring during difficult behavior. Fear can appear as clinginess, withdrawal, anger or extreme independence. Set calm limits while keeping connection: “I won’t let you hit. I’m here to help you calm down.” Never threaten to send them away as punishment.
Letting closeness develop at their pace. Offer choices and regular time together; don’t require hugs, affection or calling you “Mom” or “Dad.” If you lose your temper, apologize and reconnect.

off.p: These approaches reflect the American Academy of Pediatrics’ guidance on parenting after trauma.

Be especially careful with promises about permanence. In foster care, promise what you control: “My job is to care for you while you’re here. I’ll tell you what I know about what happens next.” Avoid promising they will never move again when that decision isn’t yours. Work with their caseworker to explain transitions honestly and preserve safe connections with siblings, birth family and previous caregivers. They can care about you and still miss those people.

Before taking a placement, ask the agency about training, caregiver support and access to a therapist experienced in foster care, adoption, grief and trauma. Seek help early if anxiety, sleep problems or distress interfere with everyday life; support can involve both you and the child. The National Center for Adoption Competent Mental Health Services emphasizes this shared, relationship-focused support.

Make room for your own support, too. A child’s withdrawal or an eventual departure may touch your earlier losses. Having an adult space to process those feelings can help you stay available to the child without needing them to reassure you.

on.p: Having your own fears go unnoticed sounds painful. Your experience may help you notice a child’s distress; leave room for their experience to differ from yours.

The most useful foundation is repeated, predictable care, with room for the child’s grief. Trust can grow slowly after several separations, even when a child is safe and loved. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends consistent routines, patient responses, and help tailored to the child’s history. AAP guidance on parenting after trauma
In everyday life:

on.li: Make small promises and keep them. Explain who will collect them from school, what happens at bedtime, and when you’ll return after going out. Give advance notice of changes. Familiar routines provide something dependable.
Let them name what hurts. You might say, “You miss your mum. Would you like to tell me about her?” Let them choose when to talk. Give them permission to love and miss previous caregivers.

Let closeness develop at their pace. Offer time together through play, reading, or an activity they enjoy. Ask before hugs and respect their answer. Keep offering care even when they seem distant. These approaches follow the AAP’s recommendations to offer choices and remain available and responsive. Parenting after trauma

Keep care steady during difficult behavior. Set calm limits: “I won’t let you hit. I’m here to help you calm down.” Never threaten to send them away or withdraw affection as punishment. After you lose your temper, acknowledge it and repair: “I shouted. That was wrong. Next time I’ll pause and lower my voice.” AAP guidance on emotional safety and discipline

Help preserve safe connections. Work with the caseworker to support relationships with birth family and siblings under the child’s care plan. Around visits, explain the plan and provide a familiar welcome afterward. A quiet snack or shared activity can help with the transition. AAP guidance on family visits

on.p: Be especially careful about promises of permanence in foster care. You may have limited control over placement decisions. Offer reassurance you can honor: “My job is to care for you while you’re here. You can ask me questions, and I’ll tell you what I know.” If a move is planned, work with the caseworker to prepare the child and preserve familiar belongings and safe relationships.

Arrange support early. Ask the agency and pediatrician about a therapist experienced in childhood trauma, foster care, and adoption, especially if fear disrupts sleep, school, or daily life. Caregiver involvement can help you learn responses suited to that particular child. AAP guidance for foster and adoptive families

You deserve support, too. Before fostering, consider counseling or an adoptee support group to explore what a child’s rejection, attachment, or departure might bring up for you. Share your story gently when it helps, and let the child tell you what their experience means to them.

off.p: You’re reasonable to want a clear plan for your daughter’s learning. But a Spanish-heavy kindergarten classroom, by itself, is not a reason to assume she’ll fall behind or fail to learn English reading and writing.

Some dual-language programs deliberately start with most instruction in Spanish and increase English instruction over later grades. They aim for literacy in both languages, and some enroll children who start with little Spanish. Your daughter doesn’t necessarily need fluent Spanish to begin; the program needs to be designed to support her current level. California Department of Education

There is reassuring evidence: a lottery-based study in Portland found that students assigned to dual-language programs had stronger English reading results by fifth and eighth grade, without significant disadvantages in math or science. That supports the approach, but it doesn’t guarantee the quality of this particular classroom or tell you what her English reading will look like this year. RAND research brief
The next step is to get specifics from the teacher and the school’s bilingual-program coordinator. “I’ll help her” is reassuring, but you need to know how. Ask:

off.li: What kind of program is this? Is it dual-language immersion intended to develop reading and writing in both languages, or a different bilingual model?
When is English literacy explicitly taught? What English reading and writing skills should she develop in kindergarten, and how does that change in later grades?
How will you support her limited Spanish? Ask about pictures, demonstrations, routines, small groups, and ways to check that she understands.
What do Spanish-only assessments measure? How will they distinguish difficulty understanding Spanish from difficulty understanding a concept? How will they track her progress in both languages?
When will we review her adjustment and progress? Arrange an early check-in and ask what would trigger extra support.

off.p: At home, keep English reading enjoyable: read together, talk about stories, play with rhymes and letter sounds, and encourage drawing and simple writing. Your husband can share Spanish books and conversation. You can support both languages without turning evenings into another school day.

Watch whether she increasingly understands routines, participates, makes friends, and learns—not just whether Spanish initially feels hard. Persistent distress, inability to follow activities despite support, or little progress deserves a prompt meeting rather than indefinite reassurance.

With your husband, you might say: “I want her to be bilingual too. I need us to understand how the school will support her Spanish and teach her to read and write in English.” That gives you a shared question to take to the school.

I wouldn’t request a transfer solely because most instruction is in Spanish. I would base that decision on the school’s literacy plan, the support it actually provides, and how your daughter responds.

on.p: Your concerns are reasonable. You want your daughter to understand her lessons and learn to read and write in both languages. I would ask for a clear plan before deciding whether to change classes.

A Spanish-heavy kindergarten can be part of a well-designed dual-language program. Some programs begin with most instruction in Spanish and gradually increase English instruction in later grades. They include native English speakers, so full Spanish fluency at entry is not necessarily expected. California Department of Education

Your concern about English reading this year deserves a specific answer. Programs differ: some teach literacy in both languages from the beginning; others introduce formal English reading later. For example, Edison Language Academy begins literacy instruction in Spanish and introduces formal English reading in second grade. That illustrates why “two days in English” alone doesn’t tell you what your daughter will learn. Edison’s program description
Ask for a meeting with the teacher and the school’s bilingual-program coordinator. Bring your husband, and ask:

on.li: What kind of program is this? Is it designed for children entering with limited Spanish, and how was her placement determined?
When will she receive explicit English reading and writing instruction? What are the kindergarten goals in each language?
What does “I’ll help her” mean in practice? Ask about pictures, demonstrations, small-group instruction, and help understanding directions.
How will assessments account for her Spanish level? A Spanish-only task may leave you unsure whether she struggled with the concept or the language.
When will we review her progress? Arrange an early check-in and ask what additional support or placement options are available.

on.p: At home, keep reading and talking with her in English. Your husband can share Spanish books, games, and conversation. The American Academy of Pediatrics encourages families to continue using their home languages and reading together. Keep it enjoyable and ask the teacher how home activities can support classroom learning. AAP guidance
With your husband, you might say: “We both want her to know both languages. I want us to understand how this school will support her Spanish and teach her English reading.”

If the school offers a concrete plan and your daughter is participating and progressing, I’d be comfortable giving the program a chance. If she remains distressed, cannot access lessons despite support, or the English-literacy timetable doesn’t meet your family’s goals, revisit the placement promptly. You can value bilingualism and still choose the classroom that best fits her needs.

off.p: It is heartbreaking to hold your baby while she screams and feel unable to help. Crying from colic is not known to shrink a baby’s brain, and her continuing to cry does not mean your comforting has failed. Colic generally resolves without harming a baby’s health or development. Mayo Clinic

Cortisol is a normal stress hormone; a temporary increase is not evidence of brain damage. The research behind frightening claims about stress and brain development concerns prolonged adversity, such as abuse or neglect, without adequate supportive caregiving. Your holding, rocking, and responding are meaningful support—even when they cannot stop the crying. Harvard Center on the Developing Child

You do not need to meet a 10-second deadline. Responding promptly to a newborn is recommended, but that is not a stopwatch rule. You cannot spoil her by comforting her, and no parent can soothe every cry. Briefly watching ordinary squirming is reasonable; newborns still need substantial help settling. American Academy of Pediatrics

Evening crying, difficulty settling, and a red face can all occur with colic, which usually improves by about 3–4 months. However, six hours of inconsolable crying each day deserves another conversation with her paediatrician, especially if they did not know the full duration. They can reassess her feeding, growth, and possible other causes. If she is currently crying continuously for hours and cannot be consoled, seek prompt medical advice rather than assuming every episode is colic. NHS, Seattle Children’s

Seek urgent medical care for a temperature of 38°C/100.4°F or higher in a baby under 3 months, poor feeding, markedly fewer wet nappies, or green vomit. Call emergency services for trouble breathing, blue/grey colour, or unusual floppiness or difficulty waking. AAP, Seattle Children’s, NHS

Keep using gentle comfort and take turns with another caregiver if possible. If you become overwhelmed, put her on her back in an empty, safe cot and take a few minutes to regroup; never shake her. Taking a short break is recommended, responsible care. Your job is to offer care and safety—you do not have to make every cry stop. AAP

on.p: Hearing your newborn scream for hours is heartbreaking, especially when you’re doing everything you can to comfort her. Crying from colic has not been shown to shrink a baby’s brain. NHS guidance describes no known damage from colic crying. Holding and rocking her are appropriate ways to help, even when she keeps crying. NHS colic guidance

Cortisol is part of the body’s normal stress response. A temporary rise does not establish brain injury. Research about harmful “toxic stress” concerns prolonged, excessive stress, particularly when supportive caregiving is absent. Caring, responsive relationships help buffer that stress response. That research does not establish that a baby crying with colic while being comforted suffers brain damage. Harvard Center on the Developing Child

You do not need to meet a 10-second deadline. Paediatric guidance recommends responding promptly to newborns, but sets no such cutoff. Newborns often need help settling, and no parent can stop every episode of crying. Your care still matters when she remains upset. American Academy of Pediatrics

Evening crying, difficulty settling and a red face can fit colic, which usually improves by around three to four months. Because you describe six hours of inconsolable crying every day, contact her paediatrician again, making sure they know its duration. Ask them to review feeding, weight gain and possible causes of discomfort. If she is currently crying continuously and cannot be consoled for over two hours, seek prompt medical advice. NHS, AAP symptom guidance

Get urgent medical assessment for a temperature of 38°C/100.4°F or higher in a baby under three months, poor feeding, markedly fewer wet nappies, or repeated vomiting. Call emergency services for difficulty breathing, blue or grey colour, unusual limpness or difficulty waking her. AAP, NHS

For now, check hunger and her nappy, then try gentle rocking in a quiet, dim room. Arrange someone you trust to take a shift if possible. If you become overwhelmed or too sleepy to hold her safely, place her on her back in an empty cot with a firm, flat mattress and take a short break. Never shake a baby. Taking that break is recommended care for an exhausted parent. AAP guidance

off.p: Eleven is a reasonable age for a first pocketknife, provided it comes with instruction and supervised use. I would base the decision on his behaviour with tools and rules, rather than wait for a particular birthday.

From what you describe, I would consider giving him one this Christmas, initially keeping it with the family camping equipment and letting him use it with you. Ownership can come before permission to carry it independently.
The most useful readiness checks are whether he can:

off.li: Open, use and close it safely, including keeping fingers out of the folding blade’s path.
Stop immediately when asked and put it away when distracted.
Accept restrictions on where he takes it and who may handle it.
Resist showing off when friends encourage him.

off.p: His interest in its status among peers is understandable, but his response to a “no neighbourhood carry or showing off” rule would be especially informative. Being good-natured does not necessarily tell you how he will behave when excited or under peer pressure.

Make the gift include practical lessons: a stable working position, cutting away from himself and others, keeping others beyond reach, closing it before moving, and cleaning and storing it afterwards. Start with simple tasks together. The UK Scouts explicitly teach knife and multitool skills, with appropriate supervision and secure storage, which supports treating this as a teachable outdoor skill. Scouts’ tool-training guidance
The main legal distinctions are:

off.li: Purchase: Most knives cannot be sold to under-18s. GOV.UK describes an exception for non-locking folding pocketknives with a cutting edge no longer than 3 inches (7.62 cm). The sale restriction is not a blanket rule that children cannot own such a pocketknife.

Public carry: That same type of pocketknife ordinarily does not require a “good reason” for carrying it. A locking blade or longer cutting edge falls outside that exception and generally requires a good reason.

Conduct: Even an otherwise lawful pocketknife must not be used threateningly. “Swiss Army Knife” is a brand description, not a legal category: check the actual model’s blade and locking mechanism. Government guidance on buying and carrying knives

off.p: For Sea Cadets, ask his unit’s adult staff what they permit before he brings it. Their activity rules may be stricter than the law. I would also make school, neighbourhood outings and visits to friends off limits under your family rules.

The beginner model does have a purpose: its rounded tip reduces the opportunity for puncture injuries, although the cutting edge still needs careful handling. It also offers useful camping tools, including a saw on the model linked here. A standard model can be reasonable if it fits his hands and he can operate it confidently; extra functions are useful only if he has a use for them. The page for your proposed model was not included, so I cannot assess that particular choice. Victorinox’s beginner model
I would defer if he resists those boundaries. If he accepts them and demonstrates safe handling, another year of age alone is unlikely to add as much as practice with you.

on.p: Eleven can be an appropriate age for a Swiss Army Knife used on supervised camping trips. I would make the gift conditional on learning safe use and accepting clear rules about where it stays and when it comes out.
For your son, the most useful readiness test is whether he can:

on.li: Follow safety instructions consistently, including when friends are watching.
Open, use and close the tools with control.
Keep fingers and other people clear of the blade’s path.
Accept that you store it between approved activities.

on.p: You can assess those things during a supervised practice session before Christmas. UK Scouts teach knife skills to young people and require adult supervision during knife use. Their knife-skills guidance provides a useful starting point.

The peer-status motive deserves a direct conversation. My condition would be: no carrying it around the neighbourhood, taking it to school, lending it to friends or showing it off. You could give him ownership while retaining control of storage and transport. If he resists those conditions, I would defer the gift; another birthday alone would tell you little about his readiness.
There are several legal points to consider:

on.li: Most knives cannot be sold to under-18s. GOV.UK identifies an exception for non-locking folding pocketknives with a cutting edge no longer than 3 inches (7.62 cm).
That same type has an exception to the general requirement for a good reason to carry a knife in public. A locking blade requires a good reason even when it is short.
Any knife can be illegal to carry as a weapon or use threateningly. The pocketknife exception does not protect that behaviour.

on.p: These distinctions appear in GOV.UK’s knife guidance. The under-18 sales restriction is not a general requirement to wait until 18 before giving a child an ordinary pocketknife. Northern Ireland has separate legislation and official guidance, so check the applicable rules if that is where you live.

Ask his Sea Cadet unit about its policy before buying. Its rules may restrict personal knives, specify permitted models or require leaders to hold them. Legal permission to carry a pocketknife does not establish permission to bring it on a cadet expedition.

The first-timer model does have a practical benefit: a rounded blade tip removes the sharp point and reduces the puncture hazard. It still needs careful handling. Victorinox’s My First Victorinox also includes a saw and can opener, so it offers useful camping functions.

I cannot assess the more versatile model because your message contains no product link. Check its cutting-edge length, whether its blade locks, and whether your son can comfortably operate it. A non-locking blade can fold onto fingers under pressure, which should be part of his training.

Given what you describe, I would consider the gift this Christmas, paired with instruction, supervised use and parent-controlled storage. His willingness to keep those rules would be my deciding factor.

off.p: Remind children when a rule is relevant, and adjust the frequency to how reliably they can use it. There isn’t a universal “every X days” schedule.
A practical approach is:

off.li: When introducing a rule: explain it briefly, say why it matters, and demonstrate what to do.
Before the relevant situation: give a short reminder—for example, before entering a busy park or crossing a road.
While they are learning: prompt calmly when needed and acknowledge success: “You checked with me before leaving. Thank you.”
Once it becomes a habit: reduce reminders. Revisit it when circumstances change, they seem uncertain, or they make a mistake.

off.p: For safety rules that rarely come up naturally, add occasional, brief practice. Ask “What would you do if…?” and let the child demonstrate the response. Being able to recite a rule is different from being able to apply it. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children recommends conversations and role-play for this purpose. NCMEC guidance
For your example, I would replace “Don’t talk to strangers” with something more specific:
> “Before going anywhere with anyone, check with me—or the adult looking after you—and get permission, even if you know the person.”

That gives children a clear action and also covers familiar people. A blanket ban on talking to strangers can make it harder for a lost child to ask for help. Teach whom to approach, such as a store employee or a parent with children. NCMEC safety scenarios

You could practice: “Someone says they have a puppy around the corner. What do you do?” Help the child rehearse saying, “I need to ask my parent first,” and returning to you. Keep it calm and predictable rather than staging a frightening surprise test.

Without seeing the video’s methods, I wouldn’t treat it as evidence for how often reminders are needed. And even a child who answers every practice question correctly still needs supervision appropriate to their age; remembering rules cannot carry the whole responsibility for safety.

on.p: Remind children when the rule is about to matter, and repeat it according to how much help they still need. There is no single useful schedule for every age and rule. Toddlers and preschoolers need frequent reminders; the CDC recommends clear rules, consistent responses from caregivers, and specific praise when children follow them. CDC guidance
A practical approach is:

on.li: When introducing a rule: explain it briefly, demonstrate it, and ask your child to show you what to do.
Before the relevant situation: give a short reminder. Before entering a playground, for example: “Check with me before leaving this area.”
When they forget: calmly prompt the action you expect.
When they follow it: acknowledge the behavior: “You checked with me before going over there. Thank you.”
As it becomes familiar: reduce routine prompting, and revisit it when circumstances change.

on.p: For your example, I would change “Do not talk with strangers” to “Get my permission before going anywhere with anyone.” The original rule can discourage a lost child from asking for help, and someone the child knows can also pose a risk. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children recommends permission-based rules and teaching children whom to approach for help, such as a store employee with a nametag. NCMEC guidance

Practise briefly through friendly role-play: “Someone offers to show you a puppy around the corner. What do you do?” Let your child rehearse saying, “I need to ask my parent,” and coming back to you. Repeat occasionally and before relevant outings; increase practice if they seem unsure. NCMEC specifically recommends role-play to practise these skills.

A child’s ability to recite a rule gives you only part of the picture: applying it in an exciting or confusing situation also takes practice. Reminders and rehearsal support safety, but young children still need adult supervision.
The YouTube video alone cannot establish how often reminders are needed. Its methods and editing would matter, and a staged encounter does not provide a reliable reminder schedule.

off.p: That sounds frightening for both of you. Fear of monsters is common at six, but Sammy’s increasing distress and disrupted sleep deserve attention. Arrange an appointment with his pediatrician soon; fears that interfere with sleep or everyday activities may need extra support. American Academy of Pediatrics

His words alone can’t tell us whether he’s describing imagination, a nightmare, or an actual person. When he’s calm, gently ask, “Tell me what happened,” “Who do you mean by ‘he’?” and “What did you see or hear?” Let him explain in his own words without suggesting answers. If he identifies someone who has threatened or hurt him, take that seriously and seek help to keep him safe.
For now:

off.li: Comfort him: “I can see you’re scared. I’m here with you.” Avoid teasing, punishment, or confirming that a monster exists.
Keep bedtime predictable, avoid frightening videos and games, and offer a nightlight or familiar toy. Work toward sleeping in his bed gradually, with your support.
Avoid turning repeated monster searches into a bedtime requirement; focus on helping him feel safe and settle.
Note when episodes happen, whether he’s fully awake, his exact words, and any recent stress or changes. Bring this to the appointment.

off.p: These approaches follow pediatric guidance on reassurance, routines, and gradually managing fears. AAP guidance on childhood fears

If he reports seeing or hearing a pursuer while fully awake, contact his pediatrician promptly. This can have several explanations and does not automatically mean a severe mental illness. Seek urgent medical care if he becomes confused, acutely unwell, or behaves dangerously; call emergency services if there is an immediate threat. American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
Was he fully awake during last week’s episode, and has he described who “he” is?

on.p: Fear of monsters is common at six, and a child’s imagination can make those fears feel very real. Sammy’s worsening distress, disrupted sleep, and episode of running to you screaming deserve an appointment with his pediatrician or GP soon. Persistent fear that affects everyday life is a reason to seek help. NHS guidance

I can understand why that episode frightened you. His words alone can’t tell us whether he was imagining something, reacting to a real person, or experiencing something else. When he’s calm, gently ask, “Tell me what happened,” and “What do you mean by ‘he’?” Let him describe it in his own words; avoid suggesting a person or repeatedly questioning him. If he identifies someone who chased, threatened, or hurt him, take that seriously and keep him away from that person while seeking help.
For now:

on.li: Reassure him calmly: “I can see you’re frightened. I’m here with you.”
Use a predictable bedtime routine, a nightlight, and a comforting toy. Avoid frightening videos or stories.
Keep reassurance brief and gradually reduce repeated monster searches, which can reinforce the fear. Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia
Note when episodes happen, whether he is fully awake, what he says, and any changes at school or home. Bring those notes to his appointment.

on.p: If he says he actually sees or hears someone while fully awake, contact his doctor promptly. Such experiences have several possible causes and need assessment. Seek urgent medical care if he becomes confused, develops fever with unusual behavior, or cannot be kept safe. If an actual person poses an immediate threat, call emergency services. AACAP guidance
Was Sammy fully awake during the episode last week, and does he describe *seeing or hearing* “him,” or feeling afraid that something might be there?

off.p: You can keep supporting the friendship while setting firmer limits on visits. I would pause sleepovers until you’ve spoken with the parents, and invite the friend to your house meanwhile.

With your son, start with curiosity and take his answer seriously. Being frightened by Harry Potter doesn’t prove he was frightened by this movie. He may have experienced it differently with a friend, or he may be reluctant to admit discomfort. You don’t need to settle that to establish your rule.
Choose a relaxed moment and say something like:
> “Thanks for telling us about the movie. You’re not in trouble for telling us. What did you think of it? Was there anything you didn’t understand or wanted to ask about?”

Listen without pressing him to describe disturbing scenes or admit fear. If he says he was fine, accept that and leave the door open: “Okay. If anything bothers you later, you can always tell us.” Frightening content can bother children later or cause nightmares, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Then explain the boundary separately:

> “We don’t allow that kind of movie yet. That rule applies at friends’ houses too. Next time, you can say, ‘My parents don’t let me watch this—let’s do something else.’ You can also call us, and we’ll help.”

Don’t make his willingness to report what happened a reason to punish him. If the rule wasn’t clear before, make it clear now. Give him a practical way to reach you, but remember that supervising adults also need to uphold the boundary; a nine-year-old shouldn’t carry that responsibility alone.
With the parents, be specific and calm. First establish what happened, including whether they knew what the children were watching. Avoid opening with a judgment about their overall parenting.

> “Our son told us the boys watched *Slither*. We don’t allow him to watch R-rated movies or adult horror. We should have discussed movie rules before the sleepover. For future visits, could you check with us before showing anything beyond PG?”

Also address the bike and neighborhood rules directly: he needs his helmet, and you need an agreed area where he can play and a clear understanding of who is supervising. The AAP specifically recommends discussing supervision and media limits before visits in its playdate guidance.

Their response should guide your decision. If they understand and reliably respect your limits, start with shorter daytime visits. If they dismiss the rules or say they can’t enforce them, keep the friendship going at your home or through outings you supervise.
You don’t need them to adopt your parenting approach. You do need confidence that they’ll respect your boundaries while caring for your son.

on.p: You can set a firm boundary about movies and keep supporting the friendship. I would pause sleepovers and visits at their house until you’ve spoken with the parents; invite the friend to yours meanwhile.

With your son, start by accepting his account of how he feels. Being frightened by *Harry Potter* doesn’t establish that this movie frightened him. A calm conversation gives him room to tell you more:
> “Thanks for telling us what you watched. What did you think of it? Was there anything that bothered you or that you didn’t understand?”
Listen, and answer whatever he actually asks. Avoid repeatedly asking whether he was scared or telling him he must have been. Then explain your boundary:
> “We don’t allow that movie at your age. You’re not in trouble for telling us. We’ll talk with your friend’s parents about what you can watch when you visit.”

Give him a practical way to handle another uncomfortable situation: “You can say, ‘My parents don’t let me watch this,’ suggest something else, or call us. We’ll come get you whenever you need us.” Make sure he knows how to reach you, and let the hosting parents know about that arrangement.

Over the next few days, notice how he sleeps and behaves. If he brings up frightening images, acknowledge the feeling, explain that the scene was created with actors and effects, and offer comfort. Frightening media can bother children days afterward, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. If distress persists or interferes with everyday life, contact his pediatrician.
Talk to the parents privately, after you’ve had time to settle your anger. Establish what happened and make your expectations specific:

> “He told us the boys watched *Slither*. We’re concerned because we don’t allow him to watch R-rated movies. We’re glad they’ve become friends, and we’d like to agree on what happens during visits. Please check with us before showing anything beyond [your chosen limit]. Can you make sure that happens?”

Discuss the outdoor rules too: he needs his helmet, agreed boundaries for where he can go, and the supervision you expect. The AAP specifically recommends discussing supervision and media rules before playdates.

Their response should guide your decision. If they take your concerns seriously and can reliably follow those rules, you could try a short daytime visit. If they dismiss the rules or say they cannot enforce them, keep visits at your home. Explain that arrangement to your son calmly, and continue welcoming his friend.

off.p: At two, a calm, immediate limit is more useful than a telling-off. You can teach him that pushing is unacceptable while keeping your time together warm and enjoyable.

Two-year-olds are still learning self-control and often play *alongside* other children rather than with them. This incident doesn’t show that his mother is educating him badly or that missing nursery caused it. The American Academy of Pediatrics explains these age-typical social behaviours.
When he pushes:

off.li: Stop the pushing gently. Move between the children or gently block his hands.
Use one short, firm sentence: “I won’t let you push. Pushing hurts.” Keep your voice calm.
Check on the other child. Your son can watch you model caring: “Are you okay?”
Give him an alternative: “You want some space. Say ‘space, please,’ or come to Daddy.”
If he pushes again, pause the play. Stay with him somewhere quieter: “We’re taking a break so everyone is safe.” Try again when he is calm.

off.p: These steps follow guidance to stop hurtful behaviour, teach an alternative, and supervise closely. He will need many repetitions. ZERO TO THREE’s toddler guidance.

His smile doesn’t establish that he was mocking you or understood what you meant. You can’t reliably infer his feelings from that expression. Don’t increase the shouting to get a frightened reaction; judge success by whether you stopped the pushing and helped him practise something better.

With only two days a month, concentrate on a few consistent rules, plenty of play together, and noticing specific good behaviour: “You touched him gently.” Stay nearby during playdates, and let him watch or play separately without forcing interaction.
You can also repair the shouting simply: “Daddy shouted. I’m sorry. Next time I’ll use a calm voice. I still won’t let you push.” Being affectionate and setting firm limits can go together.

on.p: At two, the useful response is to stop the pushing calmly and show him what to do next. Wanting him to be afraid of you sets the wrong goal: you want him to learn how to treat other people. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends calm limits and teaching, and advises against shouting and shaming. AAP discipline guidance

Two-year-olds are still developing language and impulse control. Pushing can happen when another child gets too close or interrupts their play. His smile alone cannot tell you whether he understood your correction or how he felt about it. You can keep the same calm limit whatever his facial expression. ZERO TO THREE’s guidance on toddler aggression
Next time:

on.li: Stop the push immediately. Move between the children or gently block his hands. Say, in a firm, ordinary voice: “I won’t let you push. Pushing hurts.”
Check on the other child. Briefly comfort them and make sure they are okay.
Give your son an alternative. “If you want space, say ‘space’ or come to Daddy.” Help him move away. He can decline to play; he needs your help to do that safely.
If he pushes again, pause the interaction. Take him a little distance away and stay with him while he settles. Try again when he is ready, with you close enough to intervene.
Notice safe behavior. Be specific: “You waited,” or “You touched him gently.”

on.p: These steps follow the approach of stopping aggression, setting a brief limit, and teaching an alternative. Expect to repeat them many times. ZERO TO THREE’s guidance on self-control

Also, nursery attendance alone does not explain this incident. At two, playing alongside other children and struggling to share are common. Short, supervised opportunities to play near another child are reasonable practice. AAP guidance on social development at two

With only two days together each month, focus on warm, predictable time together and a few consistent limits. You can enjoy him and intervene when someone gets hurt. If you shouted, a simple repair helps: “I shouted earlier. I’m sorry. Next time I’ll use a calm voice. I’ll still stop you from pushing.”

off.p: Your first idea is a good starting point. I’d frame the policy around supervision, safety, and a reasonably quiet office, while accepting that some noise from children is normal.

I’d adjust your second idea: speak privately to the parent, describe the noise without blaming the child, and offer practical choices. Saying the child is “interfering with the surgeons” can sound accusatory.
A consistent approach for staff could be:

off.li: Set expectations before the visit. “If you bring children who need supervision, please bring another adult to care for them while you’re with the clinical team. Our staff cannot supervise children.” Include this in appointment reminders, with an invitation to call if arrangements are difficult.

Offer quiet activities early. Coloring materials, books, or a device with headphones may help. Pediatric dental guidance supports distraction and individualized approaches for anxious children, although that guidance concerns children receiving care. AAPD guidance
Respond to sustained disruption, rather than every squeal or cry. Running near doors, persistent shouting, or noise preventing a clinical conversation warrants intervention.

Speak to the supervising adult kindly and directly. “I know waiting can be hard for children. The sound is carrying into the treatment rooms. Could you help bring the volume down? We have some coloring materials, or you could take a short break outside. We can coordinate with you so you don’t miss being called.”

Escalate unresolved situations to you. If the parent is receiving treatment and there is no other caregiver, staff should involve you and the clinical team to arrange a safe pause or discuss rescheduling. Children shouldn’t be left alone in the lobby.

off.p: I wouldn’t make “Are they hungry or thirsty?” part of the standard script. Let the parent identify what might help; if the child is also a patient, staff should check any fasting instructions before suggesting food or drink. Likewise, an outdoor break should be an option only when the accompanying adult can safely leave.

Build in flexibility for distress, disability, and sensory needs: “Is there anything that would help your child feel more comfortable?” A child receiving care may need clinical support rather than a noise reminder.

For patients who complain, staff can simply say: “I understand the noise is uncomfortable. We’re addressing it, and we can offer a quieter place to wait if one is available.” That acknowledges their concern without criticizing the family.

on.p: Your advance notice is a useful starting point. I’d give staff a consistent process: set expectations, speak privately to the accompanying adult, offer practical help, and involve you if the disruption continues.

on.li: Before the appointment: “If children will accompany you, please bring another adult to supervise them while you’re receiving care. Our staff cannot provide childcare.” Include this in appointment reminders so families can plan.
Set a reasonable threshold: Allow ordinary talking and brief crying. Address sustained shouting, running, or behavior that affects care or safety. Apply the same expectations to all visitors.

Speak calmly to the parent: “The sound is carrying into the treatment rooms. Could you help your child lower their voice? We have some coloring materials available.” Avoid saying the child is “interfering with the surgeons,” which can sound accusatory.

Offer an outside break when feasible: “If a short walk would help, we can coordinate with you about when to return.” Confirm that the supervising adult can leave and that the child stays with them. If the parent is receiving treatment, speak with the accompanying caregiver.

If it continues: Have staff bring the situation to you. Assess whether a quieter waiting space, an adjusted appointment time, or rescheduling a nonurgent visit would help. The clinician should assess urgency before care is postponed.

on.p: I’d leave hunger and thirst to the parent unless they raise it. If the child is the patient, staff should check preoperative instructions before offering food or drink.

For sedation visits, explain supervision and escort arrangements during scheduling. AAOMS guidance requires a responsible adult escort for discharge after surgery and anesthesia; your office should make sure the family’s childcare arrangements also allow that person to fulfill the escort role. AAOMS patient assessment guidance

Give staff room to respond to individual needs, including sensory distress or disability. A quieter space or shorter wait may help. If you’re in the U.S., disability-related policy adjustments may also be required. DOJ guidance on reasonable modifications
The tone to aim for is: “We understand waiting can be difficult for children. Please help us keep the office calm so everyone can receive care.”

off.p: You’re not out of sync, but neither is your son unreasonable for asking. With necessities covered, $12 a week may be adequate; whether it is depends on local prices and what you expect him to buy. His friends’ $20 is useful context, but it doesn’t settle the question.
I’d decide this with him using a small budget:

off.li: Ask what the extra $8 would make possible. Is he missing occasional outings, saving for a game, or mainly wanting the same amount as his friends? Social activities are a legitimate consideration, even though they’re optional.
Compare what each allowance covers. A friend getting $20 might also pay for transport or lunches. Include any spending money you give your son outside his allowance.
Price a realistic month together. Choose a few ordinary activities and a savings goal. An allowance should let him make some choices while still requiring tradeoffs—not buy everything he wants.

Agree on an amount and a review date. You could keep $12, try an intermediate amount, or trial $20 for two months. Review whether it supports the agreed activities and savings, without approving every purchase.

off.p: This approach fits the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s guidance: discuss plans for allowance money, explain differing family priorities, and help teens practise spending, saving, and planning. See its allowance conversation guide and resources for teenagers. Those are more useful here than a universal age-based dollar figure.

Your concern about smoking deserves a direct conversation of its own. Friends’ tobacco use is a recognized risk factor, so your concern has a basis. But that doesn’t establish that your son will smoke—or that keeping his allowance at $12 will prevent it. The CDC identifies peer use, access, and parental involvement among the factors affecting youth tobacco use.

Ask calmly whether he has been offered cigarettes or vapes, what he thinks about them, and how he would handle an offer. State your rule clearly, while making it possible for him to tell you about pressure or experimentation. Avoid treating his request for more money as evidence of misconduct.
You can also distinguish a purchase you consider poor value from something dangerous. Spending his money on a disappointing game can teach him judgment; tobacco needs a firm boundary.
You might say:

> “I’m willing to review your allowance. Let’s look at what you’d like it to cover and what those things cost. Your friends’ allowances are one piece of information. I’m also concerned about smoking, and I want us to talk openly about that.”

My recommendation is to hear his budget before deciding. If $12 allows reasonable recreation and saving, keeping it is defensible. If it routinely excludes him from ordinary activities you support, an increase is worth considering.

on.p: $12 a week can be a reasonable allowance for discretionary spending. Whether it is sufficient depends on local prices, what you pay for separately, and what you want him to learn about managing money. His friends’ $20 is useful context, but you can set your family’s amount on those grounds.
I would handle the allowance request and the smoking concern in separate conversations.
For the allowance, try this:

on.li: Ask what the extra $8 would make possible. Have him price a typical month of activities and anything he wants to save toward. Being unable to join an occasional outing deserves consideration; wanting every purchase his friends make calls for a discussion about priorities.
Compare what the allowances cover. A friend’s $20 might include lunches or transport. Also count any extra spending money you give your son between allowance payments.
Agree on a predictable amount and review date. You could keep $12, agree to an intermediate amount, or try $20 for six weeks. Base the decision on his proposed budget and review how it worked.
Give him room to make ordinary mistakes. If he spends his fun money early, let him wait until the next payment. A purchase you consider poor value can become a useful lesson.

on.p: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a regular allowance, budgeting discussions, and limits on extra money for discretionary purchases. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau similarly emphasizes pairing allowance with guidance about spending and saving. Neither linked resource prescribes a dollar amount for a 14-year-old. AAP guidance, CFPB guidance.

Keeping the allowance at $12 cannot guarantee that he will avoid smoking: he could save money or receive cigarettes from friends. His friends’ smoking also does not establish that he intends to smoke. Ask what he thinks about it, whether anyone has offered him cigarettes, and how he would respond. State your expectations about smoking and vaping clearly. CDC guidance supports clear expectations, knowing his friends and activities, and maintaining a relationship in which he feels comfortable talking to you. CDC guidance for parents.
You might say: “I’m willing to review your allowance. Show me what you’d like it to cover, and we’ll work through the costs together.”
Your current amount is defensible. Giving his request a fair hearing will make the decision easier to explain—and give him practice making a reasoned case.

off.p: A separate room from birth is generally discouraged for infant sleep safety. Calling it “psychological abuse,” however, goes beyond the evidence. Those are two different claims, and parenting debates often mix them together.

Current American Academy of Pediatrics and NIH guidance recommends that babies sleep in the parents’ room, on their own separate sleep surface, for at least the first six months. Room sharing is associated with a lower risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). The baby should sleep on their back, on a firm, flat infant mattress, without pillows, loose bedding, or soft toys. Sharing a room and sharing an adult bed have different safety implications. NIH safe sleep guidance

Psychologically, the important issue is the pattern of care the child receives. Babies need reliable feeding, comfort, affection, and responsive interaction. A separate bedroom tells you very little about whether those needs are being met. Research on the harm of neglect concerns persistent absence of responsive care; it does not establish that a bedroom arrangement, by itself, constitutes neglect. Harvard’s explanation of responsive caregiving

There is also some reassuring evidence about helping older infants learn to sleep. A small randomized trial involving 43 babies aged 6–16 months found that two behavioral sleep interventions improved sleep without detecting differences in attachment or emotional and behavioral problems at follow-up. That is limited evidence, and it does not justify applying the same methods to newborns or ignoring hunger, illness, or distress. The randomized trial

The cultural disagreement partly reflects different ideas about what good parenting should accomplish. In some settings, independent sleeping symbolizes autonomy and a place within the household. In others, sleeping close together symbolizes belonging, protection, and parental availability. Research on Japanese mothers’ sleeping arrangements illustrates how these choices relate to cultural values about interdependence and independence. These are tendencies, with substantial variation within cultures. Study of sleeping arrangements and cultural values

My interpretation is that arguments become especially moralistic when people treat a familiar practice as proof of love: “A loving parent would never let a baby sleep alone,” or “A good parent would teach independence immediately.” Neither slogan adequately distinguishes infant safety, developmental needs, and family preferences.
The other advice you mention also needs unpacking:

off.li: Responding warmly and holding a distressed baby are consistent with responsive care. That does not imply an obligation to provide uninterrupted physical contact.
Avoiding harsh verbal treatment is sound advice. An absolute rule against ever raising your voice is a much broader claim.

“Never discipline” depends on the meaning of discipline. Newborns need care rather than punishment. As children grow, clear limits, redirection, and appropriate consequences are compatible with warmth. The AAP explicitly recommends positive discipline and advises against hitting, threatening, humiliating, and shaming. AAP discipline guidance

off.p: Parental health belongs in this picture too. Caregiver stress can make responsive parenting harder; supporting caregivers helps children. Unlimited sacrifice of sleep and health is therefore a poor general standard for good parenting. Harvard’s guidance on supporting families

For a newborn, the practical recommendation is a separate crib or bassinet in your room. Later sleeping arrangements can be chosen around the child’s needs and the family’s circumstances, without treating the number of bedroom walls as a measure of parental love.

on.p: For a newborn, sharing the parents’ room on a separate infant sleep surface is the recommended arrangement. Calling a separate bedroom “psychological abuse” goes beyond what the evidence establishes. Your question brings together sleep safety, emotional attachment, and cultural expectations about parenting.

The safety issue is fairly clear. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends room sharing for at least the first six months, with the baby in their own crib or bassinet. Room sharing is associated with a lower risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) and makes feeding and comforting easier. Place the baby on their back on a firm, flat surface, with no pillows, loose blankets, or soft toys. Sharing an adult bed carries additional risks. AAP safe-sleep guidance

The psychological question concerns how caregivers respond to the child over time. Warm, dependable, responsive relationships support development. A bedroom arrangement alone tells you little about whether a child receives that care: parents can respond promptly to a baby in another room, and a baby sleeping nearby can still experience neglect. Attachment research supports responsive relationships; it does not establish a requirement for continuous physical contact. Harvard’s explanation of responsive relationships

Age matters here. Newborns need frequent care, and the AAP advises responding promptly to crying during the first few months. Evidence about sleep interventions in older infants cannot simply be applied from birth. For example, a 2016 randomized trial involving 43 babies aged 6–16 months found improved sleep with two behavioral approaches and no significant differences in attachment at follow-up. Its small sample limits certainty, and it did not test newborns sleeping in separate rooms. Gradisar and colleagues

The cultural disagreement partly reflects different ideas about what good parenting should accomplish. Some families see early separate sleeping as a step toward independence and a way to protect parents’ sleep. Others see nighttime closeness as an ordinary expression of care and belonging. Research on Japanese mothers illustrates how sleeping arrangements connect to values about family relationships and mothers’ roles, including disagreement within the same culture. These are tendencies, not rules that describe every family. Study of Japanese mothers’ sleeping arrangements and values

My interpretation is that these customs become morally charged because people treat their familiar arrangement as evidence of love or competence. Someone who associates closeness with safety may interpret separation as abandonment; someone who values early independence may interpret prolonged sharing as a problem. Those interpretations need evidence before becoming claims about harm.
The broader advice you mention also deserves scrutiny:

on.li: Comforting a young baby: supported. Babies need help managing distress.

Never disciplining a child: depends on what “discipline” means. Pediatric guidance recommends calm teaching, consistent limits, and age-appropriate consequences. It discourages hitting, humiliation, and harsh yelling. AAP discipline guidance

Unconditional sacrifice of parents’ health: not a sound general requirement. The AAP explicitly encourages rest, help from others, and a brief break with the baby safely in their crib when a caregiver becomes overwhelmed. AAP guidance on responding to crying

on.p: For a family making this decision, the practical starting point is room sharing with a separate crib for the first six months, responsive care, and shared caregiving that protects parents’ ability to function. Later sleeping arrangements can take account of the child’s needs and the family’s circumstances.

off.p: Explain your concerns, but make it a conversation rather than an ultimatum. Your unease is understandable: eight years can mean a substantial difference in independence and influence when one person is 17.

However, “you can’t have anything in common,” “he must want a family,” and “he’s only after one thing” are assumptions she can dispute. His business success also tells you little about how he treats a partner. Focus on her freedom, his behaviour, and whether the relationship supports her future.
You could say:

> “I’m glad you’ve told me. I’d like to understand what you like about him. I’m concerned because you’re at different stages of life, and I want you to have room for friends, education, travel and your own decisions. How does he feel about your plans? Whatever happens, you can always come to me.”

Then listen. Over a few conversations, explore whether she feels comfortable disagreeing with him, saying no to sex, spending time with friends, and pursuing university or work elsewhere. Ask how they met and how long they’ve known each other, without turning it into an interrogation.

The most useful evidence is how he responds to her independence and boundaries. Pressure for sex or commitment, monitoring her phone, jealousy, isolation, or making her feel indebted because of money or gifts are concerns. Healthy relationships allow both people to make choices freely. NSPCC guidance
Practical steps you can take:

off.li: Invite him to meet you in an ordinary, relaxed setting. Notice whether he respects her opinions and ambitions.
Keep reasonable household arrangements about coming home and communicating, without making every disagreement about him.
Offer help accessing contraception and sexual-health advice privately. NHS contraception services are free and confidential. NHS guidance
Tell her explicitly that you will help if she ever feels uncomfortable or needs collecting, even if she has ignored your advice.

off.p: If you see signs of coercion or exploitation, seek advice from the NSPCC on 0808 800 5000, rather than handling it solely as a family disagreement.

You can be honest that you’re worried without requiring her to defend the relationship whenever she talks to you. Keeping that connection gives you a better chance of helping her assess it—and of hearing about problems early.

on.p: Talk to her about your concerns, and keep yourself someone she can safely confide in. An eight-year gap at 17 deserves careful attention because of the possible difference in independence, experience and influence.

Some of your conclusions go beyond what you know, though. They may have interests in common; being 25 doesn’t establish that he wants marriage or children soon; and his age alone doesn’t establish his motives. Owning a successful business tells you little about how he treats a partner. Focus on what you can learn and observe.
Start with curiosity, privately and when you’re calm: how did they meet, how long have they known each other, what does she enjoy about being with him? Listen before giving your view. You could say:

> “I love you, and I want to understand this relationship. I’m concerned because you’re 17 and he’s further into adult life. Your plans for university, travel and work matter, and I want you to feel free to pursue them. How does he respond when you disagree with him or want time with your friends?”

That last question matters. A healthy relationship includes respect, freedom to make choices and consent given freely. Watch for pressure to have sex, jealousy, monitoring her phone, isolation from friends, or pressure to abandon education or become financially dependent. These behaviours warrant action. NSPCC guidance on healthy relationships
Practical steps you can take:

on.li: Get to know him. Invite him over for an ordinary meal. Observe whether he listens to her, respects her decisions and supports her plans.
Keep boundaries clear and proportionate. Discuss arrangements for going out, getting home and visitors. Avoid threats, humiliation or making her defend him through repeated arguments.
Support her own future. Keep helping with applications, friendships and activities she values. Ask what *she* wants over the next few years.

Make sexual-health support accessible. Have a calm conversation about consent, contraception and condoms. Offer help accessing a clinic if she wants it. NHS sexual-health services are free and confidential, with exceptions for serious safety or welfare concerns. NHS confidentiality guidance

on.p: Tell her explicitly: “You can call me for a lift or tell me something has gone wrong, even if we’ve disagreed about him.”
If you see coercion, fear or exploitation, seek advice promptly from the NSPCC on 0808 800 5000. You can also call to discuss concerns while you’re still unsure. NSPCC advice
You can be honest that the age gap worries you while staying involved and listening. She needs to know both that you take her feelings seriously and that your help remains available.

off.p: You don’t need to track him down simply because a family member is pressuring you. Your son’s questions deserve honest, reassuring answers; they don’t necessarily mean he needs immediate contact with his biological father.

You’re already doing something valuable by welcoming his questions and helping him understand that families look different. You could also give him a more concrete explanation: “You have a biological dad, but he isn’t part of our lives right now. I don’t know why he hasn’t been in touch. It’s nothing you did, and it isn’t your job to change it. You can always ask me about him.” Let his questions guide how much you explain.

I would gently adjust the message about your fiancé. Saying “he can be your dad whenever you say so” may put a big decision on a five-year-old’s shoulders. Instead: “He loves you and wants to help care for you. You don’t have to call him Dad.” Their relationship can develop without your son having to decide anyone’s role.

Years without contact tell you his father hasn’t shown up, although they can’t tell you exactly why or whether that might change. If you ever choose to reach out, make the initial contact privately, without telling your son or promising a meeting. Before involving your son, consider whether his father can offer safe, consistent involvement and respect your son’s pace. If there’s a history of violence, threats, or coercion, that changes the decision substantially.

For now, continuing the conversation with your son is a reasonable choice. You can tell your relative: “I’m taking his questions seriously. I’ll consider contact based on his needs and his father’s ability to be consistently involved. Please stop pushing me, and don’t make promises to him or contact his father on our behalf.” You don’t have to make a permanent decision today.

on.p: Based on what you’ve described, I wouldn’t recommend tracking him down solely because a relative is pressuring you. Your son’s questions deserve attention, and you can give him that attention while deciding separately whether contact would benefit him.

His father’s years of silence tell you he hasn’t participated in parenting. They don’t tell you exactly why, or whether he would be dependable now. I’d base any decision on his ability to offer safe, consistent involvement.

Your explanation about different families gives your son room to ask questions. I’d also make space for his particular feelings: he can love his family and still feel sad or curious about his biological father. You might say:
> “You have a biological dad, but he hasn’t been here as you’ve grown up. I don’t know why he hasn’t stayed in touch. You didn’t cause that. You can always ask me questions or tell me how you feel.”

Keep answers short and follow his questions. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends simple, honest explanations, reassurance that children aren’t responsible for parents’ separation, and patient listening. Its guidance concerns separation and divorce, but those communication principles are useful here too. AAP guidance

I’d gently adjust the message about your fiancé. “He can be your dad when you say so” puts a significant decision on a five-year-old. You could say: “He loves you and wants to help care for you. You can call him what feels comfortable.” Let their relationship develop, with the adults taking responsibility for commitment and care.

If you eventually choose to reach out, make the initial contact privately, before creating expectations for your son. Assess whether his father can sustain contact, then consider a gradual introduction. Any history of abuse or safety concerns would need to shape that decision.

For the relative, a clear boundary is reasonable: “I’m listening to his questions and thinking carefully about what would help him. Please stop pressing me to contact his father, and don’t make promises to him about it.”
You can leave contact alone for now and revisit it as your son’s questions and wishes develop. You don’t have to settle his entire future relationship with his father today.

off.p: Yes—telling his teacher and asking her to get help if she notices symptoms is entirely appropriate. You’re sharing information she needs to care for him at school. The reasonable boundary is asking her to notice and respond during normal supervision; continuous monitoring or medical assessment needs a separate arrangement with the school.
It’s reasonable to:

off.li: Explain that colds can trigger his asthma, even though he usually has no symptoms.
Describe his specific warning signs, especially ones he may not report himself.
Ask her to contact the nurse or designated staff member promptly if he has breathing difficulties, worsening coughing, or seems unusually unwell.
Ask that he be allowed to report symptoms and get help immediately.

off.p: For ongoing care, involve the school nurse—or whoever handles health needs if there isn’t one. Provide a written asthma action plan from his clinician, arrange access to prescribed rescue medication under school procedures, and confirm who responds when the nurse is unavailable. NIH guidance specifically recommends sharing the action plan with school staff. NIH: Asthma in Children
A short email could say:

> Hi [Teacher], > > [Child] has asthma that is usually quiet but can flare up significantly when he has a cold. He has a cold and cough today, although he seemed well enough for school this morning. > > If you notice increased coughing, difficulty breathing, or that he seems unusually tired or unwell—or if he tells you his breathing feels difficult—please contact the nurse/designated staff member promptly. We’re available at [numbers] if he needs to come home. > > I’m also contacting the nurse to confirm his asthma plan and medication arrangements. Please let me know if there’s a school procedure we should follow. Thank you for helping us keep him safe.

For obvious breathing distress, the arrangement should be to bring help to him and keep an adult with him, rather than send him to the office alone. Severe symptoms require the school’s emergency response, without waiting for a parent to arrive. NIH: Managing Asthma—A Guide for Schools

Finally, whether he is well enough to attend is a separate decision from what the teacher can reasonably do. If he needs frequent breathing checks to remain safe, speak with his clinician and the school nurse before relying on classroom supervision.

on.p: Yes—explaining his asthma and asking the teacher to get help if symptoms appear is appropriate. A brief message with specific signs and a clear next step gives her something practical to act on.
You can reasonably ask her to:

on.li: Take his report of breathing trouble seriously and arrange prompt help from the nurse or designated staff member.
