Act if she notices worsening coughing, wheezing, difficulty breathing, or difficulty participating in normal activities.
Have the school contact you if he becomes unwell or needs to come home.

on.p: The boundary is the level of care involved. Constant observation, scheduled breathing assessments, and treatment decisions need an agreed school health plan and appropriately trained staff. Medication administration should follow that plan and school policy.

Because his attacks can become severe, contact the school nurse or office as well as the teacher. Ask who handles asthma symptoms, who covers when the nurse is absent, and what paperwork is needed for his prescribed reliever inhaler and spacer. These are questions the CDC specifically recommends parents ask schools.

Arrange a written asthma action plan with his clinician and give the school a copy. It should specify his warning signs, prescribed treatment, and when to call you or emergency services. NHLBI’s school guidance recommends keeping this plan on file and making sure relevant staff know it.
You could email:

> Hi [Teacher], > > [Name] has asthma that is usually triggered by colds. He has a cough and cold today, and these illnesses can sometimes cause significant breathing problems for him. > > If you notice his cough worsening, wheezing, difficulty breathing, or that he seems increasingly unwell—or if he tells you his breathing feels difficult—please arrange prompt help through the school’s health procedure. Please have the school contact us if he needs assessment or collection; we’re available at [numbers]. > > I’ll also contact the nurse/office to confirm his asthma plan and medication arrangements. Thank you for helping us look after him.
Teach your son to tell an adult immediately when breathing feels difficult. At six, he will still need adults to recognize and respond to symptoms.

One important safety detail: a child struggling to breathe should have an adult stay with him while help is summoned. Severe breathlessness, trouble speaking or walking because of it, or blue/gray lips warrant emergency help immediately; staff should not wait for a parent’s reply. The CDC asthma action plan identifies these as emergency signs.
If he already has breathing difficulty, follow his action plan and seek medical advice promptly. His clinician’s guidance and the school’s illness policy should guide attendance during future colds.

off.p: A trial of 9:30 PM could be reasonable, depending on when she needs to wake up. There’s no single correct bedtime for every 12–13-year-old.
At 12, the recommended sleep range is 9–12 hours; at 13–18, it’s 8–10 hours. Those age cutoffs are guidelines—her sleep needs won’t suddenly drop on her birthday. CDC sleep recommendations
For example, if she wakes at 6:30 AM:

off.li: 9:00 PM allows 9½ hours in bed.
9:30 PM allows 9 hours.
10:00 PM allows 8½ hours.

off.p: Actual sleep will be shorter if she takes time to fall asleep.

I’d agree together to try 9:30 for a week or two, keeping her wake-up time consistent. Check whether she wakes reasonably easily, stays alert at school, and feels rested. If she becomes noticeably tired or struggles more in the mornings, move bedtime earlier again.
It’s also normal for puberty to shift sleepiness later. Keep a quiet wind-down routine and put screens away an hour before bed. American Academy of Pediatrics guidance

Starting high school alone isn’t a reason to move bedtime later—an earlier school start might mean she needs the same bedtime. What time does she get up on school days, and does she actually fall asleep around 9 now?

on.p: A 9:30 bedtime could be a reasonable trial, depending on when she needs to wake up. At age 12, the recommended sleep range is 9–12 hours; at ages 13–17, it’s 8–10 hours. Allow time to fall asleep when working backward from her morning alarm. CDC sleep recommendations
For example, if she wakes at 6:30 AM:

on.li: 9:00 PM gives her 9½ hours in bed.
9:30 PM gives her 9 hours.
10:00 PM gives her 8½ hours.

on.p: Puberty can shift her body clock later, so her request is understandable. Starting high school alone isn’t a reason to move bedtime later; her wake-up time and sleep needs should guide the decision. American Academy of Pediatrics

You could agree together to try 9:30 for two weeks, provided it leaves enough sleep time. Keep the morning alarm consistent and notice whether she wakes reasonably easily and stays alert during the day. If mornings become harder or she’s regularly tired, move bedtime earlier again. That gives her some say and makes the decision something you can assess together.

off.p: You can revise an ill-chosen consequence and still maintain a firm boundary. Consistency matters, but it needn’t mean enforcing every decision you make in frustration. You can teach him both that limits matter and that people take responsibility for mistakes. The American Academy of Pediatrics explicitly recommends cooling down, apologizing, and explaining what you’ll do differently when you make a disciplinary mistake. AAP guidance
When you’re both calm, you could say:

> “You kept watching after I told you to stop, so there will be a consequence. But I made a mistake when I included the iPad you need for school. You’ll have it for schoolwork. Recreational use is off limits until [specific day and time]. I’m responsible for making the consequence reasonable.”

If you also think a week without recreational use is excessive, shorten it openly. You don’t need to pretend that was your original intention. Choose a consequence you consider reasonable and can actually enforce, rather than retaining the week simply to defend your authority.

Separate school access from entertainment access. Use parental controls to restrict recreational apps and websites while leaving school resources available; if the device is school-managed, ask the school what restrictions are possible. At home, keep it with you outside schoolwork periods. Agree on a clear end date so restoring access doesn’t become another negotiation. The AAP recommends clear family media rules supported by parental controls. Family media plan guidance

He may still say his tantrum “worked.” You can calmly repeat your explanation without trying to win that argument. Your subsequent behavior—maintaining the revised boundary—will make the distinction clearer.

Also, his distress needn’t be either entirely sincere or entirely calculated. You can acknowledge it without changing the limit: “I understand you’re worried about school. You’ll have what you need for class. Videos are still unavailable.” Comforting him doesn’t require restoring entertainment privileges.

For next time, decide the stopping rule and a modest consequence beforehand, ideally involving him in planning the transition. A timer, a predictable handover routine, and praise when he stops successfully give him something concrete to practise. Keep disagreements about his mother’s approach between the adults; the boundary in your care can stand on its own.

on.p: You can revise the consequence and still maintain a firm boundary. Your son needs the iPad for school, and acknowledging that you overlooked this is a reasonable correction. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises parents to set reasonable consequences and, when they make a mistake, acknowledge it and explain what will happen next. AAP guidance
When you are both calm, you could say:

> “I’ve thought about what I said. Taking away the iPad completely would interfere with school. That was my mistake, and I’m sorry. You’ll have it for schoolwork. Because you continued watching after I told you to stop, recreational use is suspended until [day and time].”

Choose a duration you consider reasonable now. You can shorten the week if you think it was excessive; you do not have to preserve a poor decision to prove that you follow through. Explain the revised consequence once, then apply it predictably.
Make school access practical:

on.li: Ask the teacher which apps and websites he needs, and whether the school can help restrict recreational access.
Use parental controls to limit entertainment while preserving school tools. Coordinate changes if the device is managed by the school.
At home, keep the iPad with you outside agreed schoolwork periods.

on.p: Parental controls and clear family media rules are also part of the AAP’s media-plan guidance.

If he becomes upset again, you can offer comfort while holding the limit: “I know you’re upset. I’m here to help you calm down. Recreational use resumes on Saturday.” Acknowledging his feelings does not require changing the consequence. His distress may include both frustration and real worry about school; you needn’t settle his motives to enforce the rule.

For future evenings, set the stopping time and consequence beforehand. For example: “Videos finish at seven. If you keep watching, tomorrow’s video time is cancelled.” Then help him practise stopping and acknowledge it when he does. Keep explanations focused on the rules you enforce, and leave judgments about his mother out of the conversation.

off.p: At two, a child can understand “don’t throw” and still lack the self-control to stop when upset. Your empathy and advance warnings are useful; add a predictable, immediate limit on throwing, then teach alternatives when he’s calm. This fits the American Academy of Pediatrics’ guidance on toddler aggression.
Try the same sequence each time:

off.li: Make the situation safe immediately. Move the object out of reach, gently block the throw if possible, or move him away from breakables. For now, put heavy objects, appliances, and fragile items beyond his access—not just the valuable ones. Don’t ignore dangerous throwing.
Use one short sentence: “You’re mad. I won’t let you throw the cup.” Then put the cup away. Avoid explaining, questioning, or negotiating while he’s throwing.

Help him settle while keeping the original limit. Stay nearby in a safe space. Offer a hug if he wants one; don’t insist. Candy stays unavailable, and bedtime still happens. Comfort and a firm boundary can coexist. AAP tantrum guidance and CDC guidance on consequences support intervening in unsafe behavior and avoiding giving in to tantrums.

Practice a replacement when he’s calm. Pick something simple: saying or signing “mad,” asking “help,” or coming to you. Rehearse it in play: “The block fell! I’m mad. Help, please.” During the next frustration, prompt that same response early.

Notice small successes. “You were upset and handed me the cup. That was safe.” Praise attempts, even if he’s still crying. Later, help him repair what he safely can—such as wiping a spill together. Adults handle broken glass.

off.p: Keep your transition warnings, and add small choices within the boundary: “Bedtime now. Walk or be carried?” Both parents should use roughly the same response. Clear rules, redirection, and praise are central to AAP discipline guidance.

Time-out is an option for dangerous behavior, but it doesn’t replace teaching what to do instead. If you use it, keep it brief and predictable; the CDC describes how. You don’t need to keep adding punishments because he remains upset.
Measure progress by safer behavior, not by whether he stops crying. Being disappointed without throwing is a success.

Since this has lasted several weeks and involves potentially dangerous objects, it’s reasonable to discuss it with his pediatrician now—especially if it’s escalating, causing injuries, or you’re struggling to keep everyone safe. The AAP specifically recommends seeking help in those circumstances.

on.p: At two, children still need an adult’s help to stop an angry impulse. Keep the empathy, and pair it with an immediate, consistent safety limit. Your goal is to prevent the throw and gradually teach him what to do when frustrated. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends calm limits, teaching alternatives, and praising gentle behavior. AAP guidance
Try the same sequence each time:

on.li: Make the area safe. Put breakable and heavy objects out of reach, including ordinary cups and the sewing machine. During predictable triggers such as bedtime, stay close enough to intervene. For now, his surroundings need to account for the impulse control he currently has.

Stop the action promptly. Block access to the object or remove it calmly. If necessary, guide him away to a safe area and stay nearby. Use a short statement: “I won’t let you throw the cup. I’m putting it away.” Use only the physical intervention needed for immediate safety; avoid a prolonged struggle.

Name the feeling once, then reduce the talking. “You’re angry because you wanted candy. I’m here.” Offer a cuddle if he wants one; give him some space if touch upsets him more. Toddlers have difficulty taking in new information during a tantrum, so save explanations for after he settles. NHS guidance on emotions
Keep the original limit. Candy stays unavailable; bedtime still happens. Comfort him while maintaining that decision. Giving in to end a tantrum can encourage its repetition. NHS tantrum guidance

Teach and practice when he is calm. Pick one simple alternative: saying “mad” or “help,” or coming to you for comfort. Practice during play, then prompt it at the first signs of frustration. Notice small successes specifically: “You were angry and put the cup down gently.” After a mess, help him do a small, manageable cleanup task. Adults should handle broken glass.

on.p: Your advance warnings and choices are worth continuing: “It’s bedtime. Do you want to walk or be carried?” A successful limit may still involve crying. Look for fewer throwing attempts and more use of the alternative over time.

Because this has continued for several weeks and involves potentially dangerous objects, arrange a conversation with his pediatrician now. Ask for help assessing triggers and developing a consistent behavior plan. Seek help sooner if he injures anyone or you cannot keep everyone safe; these are reasons the AAP recommends consultation. AAP guidance

off.p: You can teach him while using your own right hand. He needs to see how a shape or letter is made; he doesn’t need to copy which hand you use.

At three, keep the emphasis on enjoyable drawing, scribbling, and simple shapes rather than neat handwriting. These activities develop the control he will later use for letters. Play dough, painting, and building with blocks also help develop hand skills. American Academy of Pediatrics guidance
A practical approach is:

off.li: Sit beside him, facing the same direction. Draw a large, simple shape on your own paper, slowly describing the movement: “Start here, go down, then across.” Let him try on his paper with whichever hand he chooses. This gives him the same view of the shape you have.
Start with something he enjoys. Draw roads, circles for wheels, or lines for rain. When he becomes interested in letters, demonstrate one at a time using the same approach.

Keep examples visible. Put the shape or letter above his drawing space or to its right, where his left hand won’t cover it. NHS occupational therapy guidance specifically recommends placing copying examples on the right for left-handed children. Left-handed writing advice

Help him position the paper comfortably. Try placing it slightly to his left and rotating it a little clockwise, with his right hand holding it steady. Adjust it so he can see what he is drawing without twisting his wrist. NHS handwriting guidance

off.p: Let him choose his hand rather than asking him to switch to the right. NHS guidance explicitly advises allowing a child’s left-hand preference. Getting ready to write
Your role is to show the movement, make the activity inviting, and help him get comfortable. You don’t need to become proficient at left-handed writing yourself.

on.p: You can help him by demonstrating the movement and shape, then letting him copy with his preferred hand. At three, start with playful drawing and simple strokes; his pencil grip will develop over time. Let him choose which hand to use, and avoid encouraging him to switch to his right. NHS pre-writing guidance
For teaching together:

on.li: Sit beside him, facing the same direction. Draw a large line slowly and describe the movement: “Start here; go down.” Give him space to try it himself.

Try demonstrating simple strokes with your left hand. A vertical line or circle is enough to begin with. Evelina London’s occupational therapists recommend using the child’s preferred hand when demonstrating alongside them.
Keep the example visible. Put your drawing above his working area so his left hand does not cover it.
When he becomes interested in letters, show the starting point and stroke direction. For English, continue teaching writing from left to right.

on.p: These demonstration techniques follow Evelina London’s handwriting guidance, pages 15–16.

Help with the physical setup too. Position the paper slightly to his left and turn it clockwise until its left edge roughly follows his forearm. As his grip develops, holding the pencil a little farther from the tip can help him see his marks. Encourage his right hand to steady the paper. Evelina London’s left-handed writing advice

For now, a useful activity is drawing together: you make a line for rain or a circle for a face, and he adds his own. Short crayons, chalk and finger painting all offer ways to practise controlling movements. Follow his interest and stop when he loses enthusiasm. NHS guidance on getting ready to write

off.p: The evidence does not support the blanket claim that daycare makes children antisocial or emotionally unstable. There are studies finding small behavioral differences, but the results are mixed, and care quality matters.

“Antisocial” also needs clarification: researchers usually measure externalizing behaviors, such as aggression, disobedience, and impulsivity. These are different from being shy, preferring solitude, or having an emotional disorder.
Three useful findings:

off.li: Some older research found small associations with behavior problems. The US NICHD study followed children from infancy into adolescence. More hours in nonparental care were associated with slightly greater impulsivity and risk taking at age 15; higher-quality care was associated with fewer acting-out behaviors and better academic outcomes. This was observational research, so it cannot establish that daycare caused the differences. Vandell and colleagues, 2010

A larger, newer analysis found no association between daycare hours and behavior problems. It combined seven studies involving 10,105 toddlers and preschoolers across five countries. By examining whether changes in each child’s daycare hours accompanied changes in behavior, it reduced some of the problems with comparing different families. The average association was essentially zero. However, this does not settle every question about starting care in infancy or particular care settings. Rey-Guerra and colleagues, 2023

Daycare does not automatically undermine attachment. A study of 1,153 infants found no overall effect of childcare amount, type, quality, or starting age on attachment security at 15 months. Some combinations of less responsive parenting and adverse childcare conditions were associated with less secure attachment, which makes the findings more nuanced than “daycare damages the parent–child bond.” NICHD, 1997

off.p: For your decision, I would give more weight to the actual care your son receives than to the daycare label. Look for warm, responsive caregivers, enough staff to give babies individual attention, consistent caregivers, and clear communication about feeding, sleep, and distress. ChildCare.gov’s selection guide

A “meh” first week tells you little about long-term development. At 8 months, separation anxiety can make starting care difficult. Familiarization visits and a brief, predictable goodbye can help. Ask caregivers whether he settles after you leave, accepts comfort, and has comfortable periods of feeding, sleeping, and exploring. Persistent distress throughout the day deserves a conversation with the caregivers and, if needed, his pediatrician. American Academy of Pediatrics guidance

These studies do not provide a basis for saying your wife needs to leave her job to prevent antisocial behavior. Your family’s preferences, finances, and the quality of the available care are better grounds for that choice.

on.p: The evidence does not support the broad claim that daycare children are “often antisocial and emotionally unstable.” Some studies have found small increases in particular behavior problems; findings vary with the study, care setting, and outcome measured.

“Antisocial” also needs unpacking. Researchers usually measure *externalizing behaviors*, such as aggression, disobedience, or impulsivity. Those findings do not establish that children become withdrawn or unable to form relationships.
Three studies help explain the picture:

on.li: The US NICHD study followed children from infancy. Its 2010 follow-up found that more hours of nonparental care were associated with slightly greater impulsivity and risk-taking at age 15. Higher-quality care was associated with fewer acting-out problems. The differences were small, and this observational study could not establish that childcare caused them. Vandell and colleagues, 2010

A newer analysis combined seven studies involving 10,105 toddlers and preschoolers across five countries. It examined whether changes in a child’s daycare hours predicted changes in that same child’s behavior. It found no association between hours and externalizing problems. This strengthens the evidence against a simple “more daycare causes more aggression” claim, although it does not directly settle the question of starting daycare at eight months. Rey-Guerra and colleagues, 2023

Research specifically on infants examined attachment at 15 months. The NICHD researchers found no overall effect of childcare attendance on attachment security. They did find increased insecurity in combinations involving less responsive parenting and poorer-quality care, more hours, or multiple care arrangements. That points to the importance of the child’s overall caregiving environment. NICHD Early Child Care Research Network, 1997

on.p: For your decision, the quality of the actual care available deserves close attention. Look for warm, responsive caregivers who comfort your son, small groups, and stable staff. The American Academy of Pediatrics identifies these as key indicators of quality. Your family’s finances and both parents’ preferences also belong in the decision. AAP guidance

As for the “meh” first week: separation anxiety commonly develops around this age. One week gives you limited information about how he will settle. Ask staff how he behaves after drop-off, whether they can comfort him, and how he feeds, sleeps, and engages during the day. A predictable goodbye routine can help. AAP separation guidance
These studies do not establish that your wife needs to leave her job to protect your son’s emotional development. They support evaluating the care he receives and how he responds over time.

off.p: Make the gift about something he gets to do and own, rather than whether it’s new. A Technic set he has seen on a shelf can feel quite different when it becomes his to build, change, and play with.
You can still give him the pleasure of unwrapping and discovering it:

off.li: If he enjoys building, dismantle the set, check that the pieces are there, and put them in bags in a wrapped box with the instructions.
If he prefers playing with finished models, give it assembled. You could include a little challenge: “Can you make this lift a load?” or “Let’s build an obstacle course for it.”
Add a short personal note: “I really enjoyed building this, and I thought you’d enjoy the gears and moving parts. Now it’s yours.”

off.p: Present it confidently, without apologizing that it’s second-hand or explaining that you don’t want to buy more Lego. “I wanted you to have this” is a good message. Offering to build together can make the gift special, provided he’s also free to explore it on his own.

The important part is that it really becomes his—including permission to take it apart, combine it with other Lego, and make something you never intended. Your history with it adds meaning, but shouldn’t create an obligation to preserve it or love it as much as you did.
You can create an inviting experience; you can’t guarantee appreciation. If his reaction is quieter than you hoped, give him time rather than trying to persuade him that he ought to be excited.

on.p: Make the gift about becoming his to build and use. He has seen your models on display; taking ownership and discovering how they work can still be a new experience.
For the Lego, I’d suggest:

on.li: Choose one set that fits his interests and ability. Giving him your whole collection at once could make it harder for any one set to feel special.

Prepare it for a fresh build. Check the pieces, clean them if needed, and dismantle the model into bags. Include the instructions and put everything in a box you can wrap. Opening a present can still be fun when its contents are second-hand.
Tell him briefly why you chose it for him. For example: “I enjoyed building this, and I thought you’d like the working gears. It’s yours now.”
Offer time together. “Would you like us to start building it this afternoon?” That gives the present an experience to look forward to.
Let him decide what happens to it. Rebuilding, modifying, and combining it with his other Lego are ways of enjoying the gift.

on.p: If he particularly enjoys taking things apart, you could give it assembled, with the instructions wrapped alongside it.
Be honest about its history, and keep the story light. “This was mine, and now I want you to have it” is enough; a speech about its sentimental value can make it feel like something he must preserve.
You can make the handover thoughtful, but you can’t guarantee appreciation. Give him room to discover what he likes about it, even if his first reaction is quieter than you hoped.
